My favourite thing in the museum is the mail van. It is marvellous inside — little wooden shelves on every wall, each one labelled, and a rail down the middle for the sacks.
The guide was unusually generous with her time. She let us ask questions until the bell went, and she answered the silly ones as seriously as the good ones.
We are going back in October with the year below. It is the one school trip that nobody in our class has ever complained about.
qs: How much of the museum do most school trips manage?
About half.
What is inside the mail van?
Little labelled wooden shelves on every wall and a rail down the middle for the sacks.
What did the guide do with the silly questions?
She answered them as seriously as the good ones.

write.task: Are museums worth visiting? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Transport Museum
paras: The transport museum is enormous, and nobody warns you about this in advance. It takes a full day to walk round it properly, at a reasonable pace, without stopping for lunch, and most school trips in practice manage somewhere around half of it before the coach has to leave.

There is a tram from 1902 that visitors are allowed to climb into and sit in. The seats are wooden, upright, and extremely hard, and it is genuinely remarkable to stand in it and consider that people once rode right across a city on those seats twice a day without apparently thinking anything of it.

The single best thing in that building is the mail van. It is marvellous inside: small wooden shelves running the length of every wall, each one labelled in faded ink, and a brass rail down the centre of the floor that the sacks were slung from while the train was moving.

Our guide was unusually generous with her time. She let us ask questions right up until the bell went for the next group, and — this is the part I remember — she answered the silly ones exactly as seriously as she answered the good ones.
We are going back in October with the year below us. It is, as far as anybody can establish, the only school trip in the history of our class that not one person has ever complained about.
qs: Why do school trips only see half the museum?
The coach has to leave before they can finish.
What is remarkable about the tram seats?
People rode right across a city on them twice a day without thinking anything of it.
What does the narrator particularly remember about the guide?
She answered the silly questions as seriously as the good ones.

write.task: Write a report on how people travelled a hundred years ago. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Quiet Poet
paras: There is a poet who lives in the house at the end of our road.
She is very quiet. She does not create a fuss about anything.
Once a year she reads her poems in the hall by the science block.
The room is always full. People come from three villages to sit on hard chairs.
She never explains a poem. She says the poem has already done that.
qs: Who lives at the end of the road?
A poet lives there.
Where does she read her poems?
In the hall by the science block, once a year.
Why does she not explain her poems?
She says the poem has already done that.

write.task: Should a poet explain her poems? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Quiet Poet
paras: There is a poet living in the end house on our road. She has been there longer than anybody else on the street and she creates no fuss whatsoever about any of it.
She is extremely quiet. You can pass her in the lane and she will nod and say nothing, and it does not feel rude.
Once a year, in November, she reads her poems in the hall beside the science block. The event is not advertised anywhere except on one piece of paper in the post office window.
The room is always completely full. People come in from three villages and sit on hard plastic chairs for an hour and a half without complaining.
She has never once explained a poem afterwards. If somebody asks what one means she says, quite kindly, that the poem has already answered that.
qs: How is the reading advertised?
On one piece of paper in the post office window.
How long do people sit on the hard chairs?
An hour and a half.
What does she say if asked what a poem means?
That the poem has already answered that.

write.task: Write about going to the reading. Use time-order words and describe what the room was like.

g4.title: The Quiet Poet
paras: There is a poet living in the end house on our road. She has been there longer than anybody else on the street, she grows a great many beans, and she creates absolutely no fuss about any part of her life, including the part that other people find interesting.

She is extremely quiet. You can pass her in the lane and she will nod and say nothing at all, and somehow it does not read as rudeness. It reads as a person who has decided that not everything requires a sentence.

Once a year, in the second week of November, she reads her poems in the hall beside the science block. The event is advertised nowhere except on a single sheet of paper taped inside the post office window, and it has never needed any more than that.

The room is always completely full. People come in from three villages and sit on hard plastic chairs for an hour and a half, and in all the years we have been going I have never once seen anybody leave early or look at a watch.

She has never explained a poem. If somebody asks her afterwards what a particular one was about, she says — quite kindly, and without any suggestion that it was a stupid question — that the poem has already answered that as well as she can.
qs: What does the author say her silence reads as?
A person who has decided that not everything requires a sentence.
What has the narrator never seen at a reading?
Anybody leave early or look at a watch.
How does she decline to explain a poem?
Kindly, without suggesting the question was stupid.

write.task: Should art be explained? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: Eight Days of Rain
paras: It rained for eight days without stopping. The weight of the water bent the fence.
Our neighbour built a small wall of sandbags across the end of the drive.
On the eighth night the river came up and stopped two feet from the door.
In the morning the sky was blue, as though nothing had happened.
We spent a week clearing the field. The fruit trees had survived, which was the main thing.
qs: How long did it rain?
Eight days without stopping.
What did the neighbour build?
A small wall of sandbags across the end of the drive.
What survived the flood?
The fruit trees survived.

write.task: Tell what happened over the eight days, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Eight Days of Rain
paras: It rained for eight days without a break. By the fourth the weight of water in the ground had bent two whole sections of the back fence over at an angle.
Our neighbour, who has lived here longest and has seen it before, built a wall of sandbags across the end of the drive on the sixth day and told us to move everything upstairs.
On the eighth night the river came up over the bank and stopped about two feet from the back door. Nobody in the house slept.
In the morning the sky was a clear blue and the water had dropped eight inches, as though the entire week had been somebody else's idea.
We spent the following week clearing the field. The fruit trees had survived, roots and all, which was the thing everybody had been most worried about.
qs: What had bent by the fourth day?
Two whole sections of the back fence.
Why did the neighbour know what to do?
He has lived there longest and has seen it before.
What had everybody been most worried about?
Whether the fruit trees would survive.

write.task: Explain what people should do when a flood is coming. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Eight Days of Rain
paras: It rained for eight days without a genuine break. By the fourth day the sheer weight of water in the ground had pushed two entire sections of the back fence over at an angle, and nobody suggested going out to fix them.

Our neighbour has lived on this road for fifty-one years and has seen the river come up three times. On the sixth day he built a wall of sandbags across the end of the drive without being asked, and then came and knocked and told us, in about nine words, to move everything we cared about upstairs.

On the eighth night the river came over the bank. It crossed the field, crossed the lane, and stopped about two feet from the back door, and there it sat for six hours. Nobody in the house slept, and nobody suggested that anybody should try.

In the morning the sky was a flat clear blue, the water had dropped eight inches overnight, and the whole thing had the air of something that had been somebody else's idea entirely and was now being denied.

We spent the following week clearing the field of everything the river had carried in. The fruit trees had survived, roots and all, which was what everybody had privately been most worried about and nobody had said out loud.
qs: How long has the neighbour lived there and how often has he seen this?
Fifty-one years, and he has seen the river come up three times.
How long did the water sit two feet from the door?
Six hours.
What had nobody said out loud?
That they were worried about the fruit trees.

write.task: Write the eighth night from inside the house. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Impossible Shelf
paras: Dad said the shelf would be impossible to put up without help. He was incorrect.
I measured the wall twice and marked it in pencil. It was not complicated.
The first hole was imperfect. I filled it and moved along two inches.
The second one was fine. The shelf went up and it is completely level.
Dad has not commented on it. He has put three books on it, which is a kind of comment.
qs: What did Dad say about the shelf?
That it would be impossible to put up without help.
What went wrong with the first hole?
It was imperfect, so it was filled and moved two inches.
How do you know Dad approves?
He has put three books on the shelf.

write.task: Was Dad wrong to say it was impossible? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Impossible Shelf
paras: Dad announced that the shelf in the back room would be impossible to put up without a second pair of hands. He was, as it turned out, incorrect about that.
I measured the wall twice, marked both ends in pencil, and checked the marks against each other. None of it was complicated. It was simply slow.
The first hole came out imperfect — slightly off the line and a shade too wide — so I filled it, let it set, and moved along two inches.
The second was fine. The brackets went on, the shelf went up, and when I put the spirit level across it the bubble sat exactly in the middle.
Dad has not commented on the shelf at any point. He has, however, put three books on it, which in this house counts as a review.
qs: What did Dad say was needed?
A second pair of hands.
What was wrong with the first hole?
It was slightly off the line and a shade too wide.
How did the narrator check it was level?
With a spirit level — the bubble sat exactly in the middle.

write.task: Explain how to put up a shelf. Group your steps in order and use topic words like measure, level and bracket.

g4.title: The Impossible Shelf
paras: Dad announced over breakfast that the shelf in the back room would be impossible to put up without a second pair of hands, and that we would therefore wait until his brother was down in June. He was incorrect about this, as I established that afternoon.

I measured the wall twice, marked both ends in pencil, and then checked the two marks against each other with a length of string, because measuring twice is only useful if you compare the answers. None of this was complicated. It was simply slow, and slow is not the same thing as impossible.

The first hole came out imperfect. It was a few millimetres off the line and a shade too wide for the plug, which I could see immediately and which there was no point arguing with. I filled it, left it to set for an hour, and started again two inches along.

The second was clean. The brackets went on square, the shelf went up on top of them, and when I laid the spirit level across the front edge the bubble came to rest dead in the centre and stayed there.
Dad has not commented on the shelf at any point in the eleven days since. He has, however, put three books on it, and in this house that is a review.
qs: Why did Dad want to wait until June?
So his brother could help.
Why did the narrator use a length of string?
Measuring twice is only useful if you compare the answers.
What does the author mean by 'slow is not the same thing as impossible'?
The job was difficult and time-consuming but could be done alone.

write.task: Should you try something difficult alone first? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Musician Next Door
paras: A musician moved in next door in the spring. She practises every day at six.
At first we were suspicious. Nobody wants an hour of scales from the next room.
But she is an exceptional player, and the sound is delicious rather than annoying.
My mother, who is cautious about everybody, now leaves her windows open on purpose.
It is official. We are the only street in town with free music every evening.
qs: When does the musician practise?
Every day at six.
Why were they suspicious at first?
Nobody wants an hour of scales from the next room.
What does the mother do now?
She leaves her windows open on purpose.

write.task: Is it good to have a musician next door? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Musician Next Door
paras: A musician moved into the house next door in the spring, and within a week we had worked out that she practises every single day at six in the evening.
At first the whole street was suspicious about it. Nobody actively wants an hour of scales coming through a party wall, however much they like music in theory.
She turned out to be an exceptional player. What comes through the wall is not scales and it is not practice noise. It is delicious, and I have not found anybody on this road who disagrees.
My mother is cautious about everybody and everything on principle. She now opens the kitchen window at ten to six, deliberately, and then pretends she opened it for the air.
It is more or less official at this point. We are the only street in this town with a free concert every evening, and nobody wants her to move.
qs: How soon did they learn her routine?
Within a week.
Why was the street suspicious?
Nobody wants an hour of scales through a party wall.
What does the mother pretend?
That she opened the window for the air.

write.task: Explain how to be a good neighbour. Group your points and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Musician Next Door
paras: A musician moved into the house next door at the end of March, and within about a week the entire street had independently worked out that she practises every single day, without exception, at six o'clock in the evening.

The initial reaction was suspicion, and it was not unreasonable. Nobody actively wants an hour of scales coming through a party wall every evening of their life, however warmly they may feel about music as a general proposition.

She turned out to be an exceptional player. What comes through that wall is not scales and it is not the sound of somebody practising. It is delicious, in the most precise sense of that word, and in four months I have not met one person on this road who takes a different view.

My mother is cautious about every new thing on principle and has been for as long as I have known her. She now opens the kitchen window at ten minutes to six, quite deliberately, and then informs anybody present that she has opened it for the air.

It is more or less official at this point. We are the only street in this town with a free concert every evening of the week, and the one thing everybody here agrees on is that nobody wants her to move.
qs: How did the street learn her routine?
Independently, within about a week.
Why does the author call the suspicion 'not unreasonable'?
Nobody wants an hour of scales through a party wall every evening.
What is the one thing everybody agrees on?
That nobody wants her to move.

write.task: Should there be rules about noise in a neighbourhood? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: Admitted and Forgotten
paras: I had been forgetting things all term. I admitted it to my teacher in November.
She was not upset. She said the beginning of a fix is noticing.
We set up a system. Everything I was committing to went straight in one notebook.
By the end of term I had not forgotten a single thing. I was quite surprised.
She said the notebook was not magic. She said I had simply stopped relying on luck.
qs: What had the narrator been doing all term?
Forgetting things.
What did the teacher say the beginning of a fix is?
Noticing.
What went into the notebook?
Everything the narrator was committing to.

write.task: Write three facts about the notebook system. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: Admitted and Forgotten
paras: I had been forgetting things all term. Homework, kit, a library book that was eventually found behind a radiator. I admitted all of it to my teacher in the second week of November.
She was not upset in the slightest, which I had not expected. She said that the beginning of any fix is noticing, and that most people never get that far.

Then we set up a system, which took about ten minutes. Everything I was committing to — every deadline, every item, every promise — went straight into one notebook, immediately, before I did anything else.
By the end of that term I had not forgotten one single thing. I was more surprised about this than anybody else was.
She said afterwards that the notebook was not magic and never had been. She said I had simply stopped relying on luck, and that luck had never been very good at the job anyway.
qs: Where was the library book found?
Behind a radiator.
What does the teacher say most people never do?
Get as far as noticing the problem.
What did the teacher say the real change was?
That the narrator stopped relying on luck.

write.task: Write about a habit you changed. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: Admitted and Forgotten
paras: I had been forgetting things all term and it had been getting steadily worse. Homework, kit, a permission slip, a library book that was eventually recovered from behind a radiator in a state the librarian described as unfortunate. In the second week of November I admitted the whole of it to my teacher.

She was not upset in the slightest, which was not what I had braced for. She said that the beginning of any fix at all is noticing that something needs fixing, and that a great many people go their entire lives without getting that far.

Then we set up a system, and the whole thing took about ten minutes. Everything I was committing to — every deadline, every item, every promise made in a corridor — went into one notebook, immediately, before I did anything else at all. Not later. Immediately.

By the end of that term I had not forgotten one single thing. I was considerably more surprised by this than she appeared to be, and I remember checking the notebook twice in the last week convinced that something must have slipped.

She told me afterwards that the notebook was not magic and had never been magic. She said I had simply stopped relying on luck to hold my commitments for me, and that luck had never been especially good at that particular job.
qs: How did the librarian describe the book's state?
Unfortunate.
What is the one rule of the system?
Write it down immediately, before doing anything else.
What did the narrator do in the last week of term?
Checked the notebook twice, convinced something must have slipped.

write.task: Is writing things down better than remembering them? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Elephant Photograph
paras: There is a photograph of an elephant on the wall of our school hall.
My grandfather took it. He was a photographer for a newspaper for thirty years.
The elephant is standing in a river with its trunk up, and the light is orange.
People stop in front of it every day. Nobody ever walks straight past.
I like that a photograph taken before I was born can still stop a person in a corridor.
qs: Who took the photograph?
The narrator's grandfather took it.
What is the elephant doing?
Standing in a river with its trunk up.
What do people do in front of it?
They stop. Nobody walks straight past.

write.task: Should schools put photographs on the walls? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Elephant Photograph
paras: There is a large photograph of an elephant on the wall of our school hall, in a plain black frame, with no label beside it at all.
My grandfather took it. He was a photographer for a newspaper for thirty-one years and this was, by his own account, the only picture he ever took that he was satisfied with.
The elephant is standing chest-deep in a river with its trunk raised, and the light coming across the water is a deep orange that nobody has ever been able to reproduce in a print.
People stop in front of it every single day. I have watched this happen for four years. Nobody walks straight past it, not even the people who have seen it a thousand times.
I like that a photograph taken twenty years before I was born can still stop a person halfway down a corridor.
qs: What is missing from the frame?
There is no label beside it at all.
What did the grandfather say about this picture?
It was the only one he ever took that he was satisfied with.
What has the narrator watched for four years?
People stopping in front of the photograph every day.

write.task: Write a report on photography. Group related information into sections and use topic vocabulary.

g4.title: The Elephant Photograph
paras: There is a large photograph of an elephant on the wall of our school hall. Plain black frame, no label, no explanation, no name anywhere on or near it. It has hung there since before any pupil currently in the building arrived.

My grandfather took it. He worked as a photographer for a newspaper for thirty-one years and, by his own account, which he gave rarely and without much elaboration, it was the only picture he ever made that he was genuinely satisfied with.

The elephant is standing chest-deep in a river with its trunk raised, and the light coming low across the water behind it is a particular deep orange that he said no print he ever ordered managed to reproduce properly. He had six made. He kept the closest one and gave the rest away.

People stop in front of it every single day. I have watched this happen for four years now, from the bench by the door, and I have never once seen somebody walk straight past — not visitors, and not the people who have passed it a thousand times.
What I like about it is this: a photograph taken twenty years before I was born, by a man who is no longer here, can still stop a stranger halfway down a corridor on a Tuesday morning.
qs: How many prints were made, and what happened to them?
Six — he kept the closest one and gave the rest away.
Where does the narrator watch from?
The bench by the door.
What does the narrator find remarkable about the photograph?
That it can still stop a stranger, years after it was taken and after the photographer has died.

write.task: Write about an object that means something to your family. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Myth in the Gym
paras: There is a myth in our school that the gym was built on top of an old well.
Every pupil hears it in the first week. Nobody has ever checked it.
Last year a system of cracks appeared across one corner of the floor.
The caretaker lifted a board. There was no well. There was a very old pipe.
The myth has not changed at all. People still tell it, and they tell it better now.
qs: What is the myth?
That the gym was built on top of an old well.
What did the caretaker find?
No well — a very old pipe.
What happened to the myth after that?
It has not changed. People still tell it, and tell it better.

write.task: Should people keep telling a story that is not true? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Myth in the Gym
paras: There is a myth in our school that the gym was built directly on top of an old well, and that on quiet afternoons you can hear water underneath the floor.
Every new pupil hears this within about a week of arriving. In the whole history of the school, as far as anybody can establish, nobody has ever checked it.
Last year a system of fine cracks appeared across one corner of the floor and the caretaker was sent in with a crowbar to find out why.
He lifted three boards. There was no well. There was a very old iron pipe with a slow leak in it, which had been quietly soaking the joists for years.
The myth has not altered in the slightest. People still tell it, and since the pipe they tell it rather better.
qs: What is supposed to be heard on quiet afternoons?
Water underneath the floor.
Why was the caretaker sent in?
A system of fine cracks had appeared in the floor.
What was actually under the boards?
A very old iron pipe with a slow leak.

write.task: Write the moment the boards came up. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Myth in the Gym
paras: There is a myth in our school, and it is a good one, that the gym was built directly over the top of an old well, and that on very quiet afternoons in winter you can stand in the centre circle and hear water moving underneath the floor.

Every new pupil is told this within about a week of arriving, usually by somebody only a year older who heard it the same way. In the entire history of the building, as far as anybody has been able to establish, not one person has ever gone and checked.

Last year a system of fine cracks spread out across one corner of the floor, in a pattern the head described as concerning, and the caretaker was sent in with a crowbar and told to find out what was underneath.

He lifted three boards. There was no well, and there never had been. There was a very old iron pipe with a slow leak in it, which had been quietly soaking the joists for a number of years that nobody wanted to estimate out loud.

The myth has not altered in the slightest. People still tell it to new pupils in the first week, and since the business with the pipe they tell it considerably better, because now there is a part where men come with crowbars.
qs: Who usually passes the myth on?
Somebody only a year older who heard it the same way.
How did the head describe the cracks?
Concerning.
Why is the myth told better now?
Because now there is a part where men come with crowbars.

write.task: Do stories matter even when they are not true? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Rhino in Autumn
paras: The rhino at the wildlife park has a name but nobody uses it.
In autumn she stands by the fence for hours and watches the leaves come down.
The keeper says it is not a mystery. She likes movement, and leaves move.
There is a rhythm to it. A leaf falls, she turns her head, she waits for the next one.
I could watch her do that all day. I am told that I have.
qs: What does the rhino do in autumn?
She stands by the fence and watches the leaves come down.
What does the keeper say?
That it is not a mystery — she likes movement, and leaves move.
What is the rhythm?
A leaf falls, she turns her head, she waits for the next one.

write.task: Write three facts about the rhino. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Rhino in Autumn
paras: The rhino at the wildlife park has an official name on the sign by her enclosure, and nobody who works there has used it in years. She is simply the rhino.
In autumn she comes and stands against the fence on the north side for hours at a time, facing the beech trees, watching the leaves come down.
The keeper says there is no mystery in it at all. Rhinos have poor eyesight and are drawn to movement, and in October everything in that corner of the park is moving.
There is a rhythm to the way she does it. A leaf comes loose, she turns her head and follows it all the way to the ground, and then she waits, perfectly still, for the next one.
I could watch her do that all afternoon. My sister tells me that on one occasion I did.
qs: Why does nobody use her name?
She is simply the rhino to everyone who works there.
What does the keeper give as the reason?
Rhinos have poor eyesight and are drawn to movement.
What does she do between leaves?
She waits, perfectly still, for the next one.

write.task: Write an afternoon at the wildlife park. Use time-order words and describe what you could see and hear.

g4.title: The Rhino in Autumn
paras: The rhino at the wildlife park has an official name, printed on the sign beside her enclosure, and nobody who actually works there has used it within living memory. To the keepers, to the regulars, and eventually to everybody, she is simply the rhino.

Every autumn she comes and stands against the fence on the north side of her paddock for hours at a stretch, facing the line of beech trees beyond it, watching the leaves come down. She does this in no other season.

The keeper says there is no mystery in it whatsoever, and he says this slightly impatiently, as though people ask him too often. Rhinos see poorly and are strongly drawn to movement, and in October every single thing in that corner of the park is moving.

There is a rhythm to the way she does it that is difficult to look away from. A leaf comes loose somewhere up in the beeches, she turns her enormous head and follows it the whole way down to the grass, and then she stops and waits, entirely still, for the next one.
I could watch her do that for an entire afternoon. My sister informs me that on at least one occasion I did exactly that, and that she asked three times to go and look at the otters.
qs: How does the keeper answer the question?
Slightly impatiently, as though people ask too often.
In what season does she do this?
Autumn, and no other season.
What does the sister's detail reveal?
That the narrator really did watch for a whole afternoon and ignored her.

write.task: Write a report on an animal's behaviour. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Telescope on the Roof
paras: My aunt is a biologist, but her real passion is the telescope on her roof.
She built the platform herself and photographs the sky from it on clear nights.
She has a catalogue of every photograph, organised by date and by what is in it.
She let me look through it once at Saturn. I did not say anything for a while.
She said that was the correct response and made me a cup of tea.
qs: What is the aunt's job?
She is a biologist.
What did she build herself?
The platform for the telescope on her roof.
What did the narrator see?
Saturn.

write.task: Tell what happened on the roof, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Telescope on the Roof
paras: My aunt is a biologist by profession, and that is what she will tell you if you ask. Her real passion is the telescope bolted to a platform on her roof.
She built the platform herself over two summers, and she photographs the sky from it on every clear night she can manage, which in this country is not many.
She keeps a catalogue of every photograph she has ever taken, organised by date, by what is in the frame, and by how satisfied she was with it, which is the column she consults most.
She let me look through the telescope once, at Saturn, when I was nine. I remember not saying anything at all for quite a long time.
She said afterwards that this was the only correct response to a first view of Saturn, and then she went downstairs and made us both a cup of tea.
qs: How long did the platform take to build?
Two summers.
Which column does she consult most?
How satisfied she was with the photograph.
What did she say about the narrator's silence?
That it was the only correct response to a first view of Saturn.

write.task: Write a report on how telescopes work. Group related information into sections and use topic vocabulary.

g4.title: The Telescope on the Roof
paras: My aunt is a biologist by profession and will tell you so within a minute of meeting you, usually before her name. Her actual passion, as anybody who has spent an evening at her house knows, is the telescope bolted to a timber platform on her roof.

She built the platform herself across two summers, working alone, and she now photographs the sky from it on every clear night she can get, which in this part of the country amounts to considerably fewer nights a year than she would like.

She keeps a catalogue of every photograph she has ever taken up there. It is organised by date, by what is in the frame, and — the column she consults far more than either of the others — by how satisfied she was with the result at the time.

She let me look through the telescope once, at Saturn, the autumn I turned nine. What I remember is not the planet. What I remember is not saying anything whatsoever for what must have been well over a minute, which is a long time at that age.

She said afterwards that silence was the only correct response to a first view of Saturn, and that anybody who starts talking straight away has not really looked. Then she went downstairs and made us both a cup of tea and did not mention it again.
qs: What does she tell people before her name?
That she is a biologist.
Which column does she consult far more than the others?
How satisfied she was with the result at the time.
What does she say about people who talk straight away?
That they have not really looked.

write.task: Should everybody get the chance to look through a telescope? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Antique Machine
paras: There is an antique machine in the window of the shop on the corner.
It is unique. The man in the shop says there is no other one like it in the country.
It has a brass plaque on the side with a date and a name in French.
Nobody knows what it was for. The chef next door thinks it made chocolate.
I hope nobody ever finds out. It is better as a question.
qs: Where is the machine?
In the window of the shop on the corner.
What is on the brass plaque?
A date and a name in French.
What does the chef think?
That it made chocolate.

write.task: Is it better to know or not to know what the machine did? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Antique Machine
paras: There is an antique machine in the window of the shop on the corner, and it has been there since long before we moved to this town.
It is unique. The man who owns the shop says, and he says it often, that there is not another one like it anywhere in the country.
It has a brass plaque screwed to one side with a date, 1883, and a name in French that nobody local has ever managed to pronounce the same way twice.
Nobody knows what it was for. The chef at the restaurant next door is certain it made chocolate. The man in the shop thinks it pressed flowers.
I hope that nobody ever establishes the answer. It is a far better object as a question than it would be as a fact.
qs: What date is on the plaque?
What are the two theories?
The chef says chocolate, the shop owner says it pressed flowers.
Why does the narrator hope nobody finds out?
It is a better object as a question than as a fact.

write.task: Write a story about what the machine was really for. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Antique Machine
paras: There is an antique machine standing in the window of the shop on the corner, brass and iron and about the size of a sewing machine, and it has been in that window since considerably before we moved to this town.

It is unique. The man who owns the shop says so, and he says so frequently and at length to anybody who slows down outside, and as far as anybody has been able to check he is entirely right: there is not another one like it recorded anywhere in the country.

There is a brass plaque screwed to one side of it carrying a date, 1883, and a name in French which nobody local has ever managed to pronounce the same way twice, including the French teacher at our school, who has tried.

Nobody knows what the thing was for. The chef at the restaurant next door is absolutely certain it was built to make chocolate and will explain the mechanism to you unprompted. The man in the shop maintains it pressed flowers. A woman from the museum came and looked at it for an hour and left without saying anything at all.
I hope sincerely that nobody ever establishes the answer. It is a far better object as a question than it could ever be as a fact, and I think the man in the shop quietly agrees with me.
qs: How big is the machine?
About the size of a sewing machine.
What did the woman from the museum do?
Looked at it for an hour and left without saying anything.
Why does the narrator think the shop owner agrees?
Because the mystery is what brings people to the window.

write.task: Should every mystery be solved? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: A Month of Mondays
paras: One month last winter, something went wrong with every single Monday.
The oven broke. The front door stuck. My brother lost a glove, twice.
My mother started to wonder whether we should simply skip Mondays altogether.
Then one Monday nothing happened at all. We came home and sat down and nothing broke.
We talked about that quiet Monday for weeks. It was the best one we had.
qs: What went wrong that month?
The oven broke, the front door stuck, and a glove was lost twice.
What did the mother wonder?
Whether they should skip Mondays altogether.
Why was the quiet Monday the best one?
Because nothing went wrong at all.

write.task: Tell what happened over the month, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: A Month of Mondays
paras: For one month last winter, something went wrong with every single Monday, without exception, and we started keeping a list.
The oven broke on the first one. The front door stuck shut on the second, with all of us inside. On the third my brother lost a glove, found it, and lost it again before tea.
By the fourth Monday my mother had begun to wonder aloud whether the sensible thing would simply be to skip Mondays altogether and go straight from Sunday to Tuesday.
Then came a Monday when absolutely nothing happened. We came home, we sat down, nothing broke, nothing stuck, nobody lost anything.
We talked about that one quiet Monday for weeks afterwards. It remains, by some distance, the best Monday any of us can remember.
qs: What did the family start keeping?
A list.
What happened on the second Monday?
The front door stuck shut with all of them inside.
Why is a Monday where nothing happened memorable?
Because every other Monday that month had gone wrong.

write.task: Are quiet days better than exciting ones? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: A Month of Mondays
paras: For one month last winter, something went wrong on every single Monday without a single exception, and after the second one we started keeping a list on the back of a calendar.

The oven broke on the first. The front door stuck shut on the second, with all four of us inside the house and my father pulling at it for twenty minutes before anybody thought of the back door. On the third my brother lost a glove, found it again under the stairs, and lost the same glove a second time before tea.

By the fourth Monday my mother had begun to wonder aloud, in a tone that was only partly joking, whether the sensible course of action would be to skip Mondays altogether and move straight from Sunday to Tuesday.
Then came a Monday on which absolutely nothing happened. We came home. We sat down. Nothing broke, nothing stuck, nobody lost anything, and at no point did anybody have to go and find a tool.

We talked about that one quiet Monday for weeks afterwards, and we still bring it up. It remains, by a considerable distance, the best Monday that anybody in this family can remember, and nothing whatsoever occurred on it.
qs: Where was the list kept?
On the back of a calendar.
What did nobody think of for twenty minutes?
The back door.
What is the irony of the best Monday?
Nothing whatsoever happened on it.

write.task: Write about an ordinary day you remember. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: Worth the Work
paras: My grandmother worked the same patch of ground for forty years.
She says the first word of gardening is patience and the second is work.
Nothing in that garden arrived quickly. The apple tree took nine years to fruit.
She never once said it was not worth it. Not in all the time I knew her.
The tree is still there. Every autumn the whole world seems to come and pick from it.
qs: How long did she work the ground?
Forty years.
How long did the apple tree take to fruit?
Nine years.
What did she never say?
That it was not worth it.

write.task: Write three facts about the garden. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: Worth the Work
paras: My grandmother worked the same patch of ground behind her house for forty years, and by the end of it she knew every corner of that garden the way you know a room in the dark.
She used to say that the first word of gardening is patience and the second word is work, and that most people manage one of the two.
Nothing in that garden ever arrived quickly. The apple tree she planted the year my father was born took nine years to produce a single apple worth eating.
She never once said that it had not been worth it. Not in all the years I knew her, and not even in the last ones, when she could only get out there with help.
The tree is still standing. Every autumn half the world seems to turn up with a basket, and nobody is ever turned away.
qs: How well did she know the garden?
The way you know a room in the dark.
What does she say most people manage?
One of the two — patience or work.
What happens every autumn now?
Half the world turns up with a basket and nobody is turned away.

write.task: Is slow work worth doing? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: Worth the Work
paras: My grandmother worked the same patch of ground behind her house for forty years, and by the end of that time she knew every corner of it the way a person knows a familiar room in the dark — where the step is, where the ground turns heavy, which bed holds the water after rain.
She used to say that the first word of gardening is patience and the second word is work, and that most people manage one of the two and then wonder why the thing has not happened.

Nothing in that garden ever arrived quickly, and she did not expect it to. The apple tree she planted in the year my father was born took nine full years before it produced a single apple that was worth the trouble of picking.

She never once said that it had not been worth it. Not in all the years I knew her, and not in the last two either, when she could only get out there with somebody holding her arm and could do very little once she arrived.
The tree is still standing and still cropping. Every autumn what feels like half the world turns up at that gate with a basket, and in forty years nobody has ever been turned away from it.
qs: Name two things she knew about the ground.
Where the step is and which bed holds water after rain.
What do most people do, according to her?
Manage one of patience or work, then wonder why nothing happened.
What does the last line show about her?
That she was generous with what her long work produced.

write.task: Is patience the most important quality? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Performance
paras: Our class gave a performance in the village hall at the end of the year.
There was a long silence before it started. The audience was patient.
My part was small, but the difference between knowing it and not knowing it was everything.
The applause at the end went on for ages. My father stood up, which was embarrassing.
On the way home nobody mentioned the mistakes. There had been several.
qs: Where was the performance?
In the village hall at the end of the year.
What happened at the end?
The applause went on for ages and the father stood up.
What did nobody mention on the way home?
The mistakes, of which there had been several.

write.task: Tell what happened at the performance, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Performance
paras: Our class gave a performance in the village hall at the end of the summer term, in front of an audience made up almost entirely of relatives.
There was a long silence before it began, the kind where somebody clears a throat and everybody else decides not to. The audience was extremely patient about it.
My own part was small — four lines and a bit of carrying things on — but the difference between knowing those four lines and not knowing them turned out to be the entire evening.
The applause at the end went on for an embarrassing length of time. My father stood up, alone, in the second row, which I have not fully recovered from.
On the way home nobody mentioned the mistakes. There had been a considerable number of them, and we all knew it, and not one person said a word.
qs: Who made up the audience?
Almost entirely relatives.
What was the narrator's part?
Four lines and carrying things on.
What did everybody avoid saying on the way home?
Anything about the mistakes.

write.task: Should people point out mistakes afterwards? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Performance
paras: Our class gave a performance in the village hall at the end of the summer term, in front of an audience composed almost entirely of relatives, several of whom had driven a considerable distance to be disappointed.

There was a long silence before it began — the particular kind of silence in which one person clears a throat and every other person in the room immediately decides not to. The audience was extraordinarily patient all the way through it, which in hindsight was the first act of generosity of the evening.

My own part was small. Four lines, and some carrying of furniture on and off between scenes. But the difference between knowing those four lines and not knowing them turned out, for me, to be the difference between the whole evening working and not.

The applause at the end continued for an embarrassing length of time. My father stood up, alone, in the second row, and remained standing, and I have not entirely recovered from it and do not expect to.

On the walk home not one person mentioned the mistakes. There had been a considerable number of them, some of them substantial, and every single one of us knew exactly what they had been, and nobody said a word about any of it.
qs: What does the author say about the relatives who drove far?
That they had come a considerable distance to be disappointed.
What was the first act of generosity?
The audience's patience during the long silence.
What does the final paragraph show about the families?
That they chose kindness over honesty about the mistakes.

write.task: Write the performance from a parent's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue and sensory details.

g2.title: The Thing I Was Taught
paras: My uncle taught me to fish when I was eight. It was the only thing he ever taught me.
We caught nothing at all for three whole days. I thought about giving up.
He said he had brought me here to learn to wait, not to learn to catch.
On the fourth day I caught one. It was small and I put it back.
I have thought about what he said far more often than I have fished.
qs: Who taught the narrator to fish?
The narrator's uncle.
How long did they catch nothing?
Three whole days.
What did the uncle say he had brought the narrator there to learn?
To wait, not to catch.

write.task: Write three facts about what the uncle taught. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Thing I Was Taught
paras: My uncle taught me to fish the summer I was eight. It is the only thing he ever taught me directly, and he never offered to teach me anything else.
We caught nothing for three entire days. Not a bite, not a nibble, nothing. By the second afternoon I had thought seriously about asking to go home.
On the evening of the third day he said, without any particular emphasis, that he had not brought me out there to learn to catch fish. He had brought me out to learn to wait.
On the fourth morning I caught one. It was about the length of my hand, and after we had both looked at it properly I put it back in the river.
I have thought about what he said that evening a great deal more often than I have been fishing, and I am nearly certain that was the point.
qs: How old was the narrator?
Eight.
What did the uncle say on the third evening?
That he had brought the narrator out to learn to wait, not to catch.
What happened to the fish?
They looked at it and put it back in the river.

write.task: Is waiting a skill worth learning? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Thing I Was Taught
paras: My uncle taught me to fish the summer I turned eight. It is the only thing he ever taught me directly, and in the twenty years since he has never once offered to teach me anything else, which I have come to think was deliberate.

We caught nothing for three entire days. Not a fish, not a bite, not so much as a serious nibble. By the second afternoon I had thought hard about asking to be taken home, and had got as far as working out how to phrase it.

On the evening of the third day, with the light going and neither of us having said anything for about an hour, he remarked — without any particular emphasis, as though it had just occurred to him — that he had not brought me out there to learn to catch fish. He had brought me out there to learn how to wait.

On the fourth morning I caught one. It was about the length of my hand and nothing whatsoever to be proud of, and after the two of us had looked at it properly for a while I leaned over the side and put it back into the river.

I have thought about what he said that evening considerably more often than I have actually been fishing, which cannot be an accident. He was not a man who said a great deal, and he appears to have chosen that sentence carefully and then waited three days to use it.
qs: Why does the narrator think the uncle taught nothing else?
They have come to think it was deliberate.
How had the second afternoon nearly ended?
The narrator had worked out how to ask to be taken home.
What does the last line suggest about the uncle?
That he planned the sentence and waited three days for the right moment.

write.task: Write about something somebody taught you. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue and sensory details.

g2.title: The Fish in the Dish
paras: Josh has a shop. In the shop he has fish in a dish.
A man came in and said he had a wish. He had a wish for a big fish.
Josh got him the big fish. It did not fit in the dish.
So Josh got a sack. He did a dash to the back of the shop and got the sack on it.
The man got his fish. Josh had to wash the dish. The shop was a shambles, but the man was not sad.
qs: What does Josh have in his shop?
He has fish in a dish.
What was the man's wish?
He had a wish for a big fish.
Why did the fish not go in the dish?
It did not fit.

write.task: Tell what happened in the shop, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Fish in the Dish
paras: Josh runs the fish shop on the corner, and everything in it is laid out in shallow white dishes on crushed ice.
A man came in one morning and said he had one wish: the biggest fish in the shop, for his mother's birthday.
Josh fetched it. It was so long that it would not fit in any dish he had, and the tail hung over the end of the counter.
He dashed out to the back, came back with a sack, and got the whole thing wrapped before it slid off onto the floor.
The man left delighted. Josh spent the rest of the morning washing dishes and mopping up melted ice, and he says it was worth it.
qs: How is the fish displayed?
In shallow white dishes on crushed ice.
Who was the big fish for?
The man's mother, for her birthday.
What did Josh do for the rest of the morning?
Washed dishes and mopped up melted ice.

write.task: Was the big fish worth the trouble? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Fish in the Dish
paras: Josh runs the fish shop on the corner of Mill Street, and everything in that shop is laid out in shallow white dishes on crushed ice, rearranged twice a day so the display never looks picked over.
A man came in on Tuesday morning and said he had exactly one wish, which was the biggest fish in the shop, and that it was for his mother, and that it was her eightieth birthday on Thursday.

Josh went and fetched it from the back. It was so long that it would not sit in any dish he owned. The tail hung off the end of the counter and the head pushed up against the till, and both of them stood there looking at it for a moment.
He dashed out the back for a sack, came back at speed, and got the whole thing wrapped and parcelled about four seconds before it would have slid off the counter and onto the floor.

The man left delighted, carrying it in both arms. Josh spent the remainder of that morning washing out dishes and mopping melted ice off the tiles, and he says, without any hesitation, that it was entirely worth it.
qs: How often is the display rearranged, and why?
Twice a day, so it never looks picked over.
What two details show how long the fish was?
The tail hung off the counter and the head pushed against the till.
How close did the fish come to falling?
About four seconds.

write.task: Write the morning from the man's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: Much for Lunch
paras: Chad had a chat with his chum at lunch.
Chad had a chop. His chum had a chip and a bit of rich ham.
“That is not much,” said Chad. “Have an inch of my chop.”
His chum did. Then he had much of it, and then he had a lot of it.
Chad had the chip. It was not much of a lunch, but it was a chat.
qs: Who did Chad have lunch with?
His chum.
What did Chad have for lunch?
Chad had a chop.
What did Chad end up eating?
Chad had the chip.

write.task: Was Chad right to share his lunch? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: Much for Lunch
paras: Chad had a chat with his chum over lunch on the bench outside the chip shop.
Chad had a chop wrapped in paper. His chum had one chip and a chunk of rich ham, which was not much of a lunch by anybody's measure.
“That is not much,” Chad said, and pushed the paper across. “Have an inch of this.”
His chum took an inch. Then he took a chunk. By the time the chat had got going properly he had worked his way through most of it.
Chad ate the chip. It was not much of a lunch, but he says the chat was the point and the lunch was not.
qs: Where were they sitting?
On the bench outside the chip shop.
What did the chum bring?
One chip and a chunk of rich ham.
What does Chad say was the point?
The chat was the point and the lunch was not.

write.task: Explain how to be a good friend at lunchtime. Group your points and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Much for Lunch
paras: Chad had a chat with his chum over lunch on the bench outside the chip shop, which is where the two of them have eaten on a Thursday for most of a year.

Chad had a chop wrapped in paper from home. His chum had one chip and a chunk of rich ham, which was not much of a lunch by any reasonable measure, and which he was making a considerable show of enjoying.
“That is not much,” Chad said, and pushed the paper across the bench without making anything of it. “Have an inch of this.”

His chum took an inch. Then, a little later, he took a chunk. By the time the chat had got properly going he had worked his way through the better part of the whole chop, and neither of them had remarked on it once.

Chad ate the chip. It was not much of a lunch and he was hungry by three. He says the chat was the point and the lunch was not, and that if you have to choose between them it is not a difficult choice.
qs: How long have they eaten there on Thursdays?
Most of a year.
What was the chum doing about his small lunch?
Making a considerable show of enjoying it.
Why did Chad push the paper across 'without making anything of it'?
So his chum would not feel awkward about accepting.

write.task: Is it better to share or to keep what is yours? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Moth on the Path
paras: Beth and I went on a thin path in the sun.
A moth sat on the path. It was thin and it did not run off.
“Do not tap that moth,” said Beth. “That moth is not in our path. We are in its path.”
So we went round it. Then we had a bath to get the mud off.
The moth was on the path when we got back. Beth said that moth was then a pal.
qs: What was on the path?
A moth was on the path.
What did Beth say?
Not to tap the moth, because it was not in their path.
Was the moth still there later?
Yes, it was on the path when they got back.

write.task: Tell what happened on the path, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Moth on the Path
paras: Beth and I walked the thin path along the north side of the hill on Thursday, the one that runs between the gorse.
About halfway along there was a moth sitting in the middle of the path with its wings flat. It did not move for us at all.
“Do not step on that,” Beth said, in a tone that did not leave anything to discuss. “It is not in the way. We are.”
So we went round it, one at a time, and carried on, and came back the same way three hours later after a bath in the stream at the bottom.
The moth was still there, in exactly the same spot, wings flat. Beth said that by then it counted as somebody we were on good terms with.
qs: Where does the thin path run?
Along the north side of the hill, between the gorse.
What did Beth say about who was in the way?
That the moth was not in the way — they were.
How long were they gone?
Three hours.

write.task: Should people move out of the way for small animals? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Moth on the Path
paras: Beth and I walked the thin path along the north side of the hill on Thursday afternoon, the one that runs between the gorse and is barely wide enough for one person to pass another.

About halfway along, in the exact middle of the path, there was a moth sitting with its wings flat out against the ground. It was pale and quite large and it did not move for either of us, or for the dog, or for anything else.
“Do not step on that,” Beth said, in the particular tone that does not leave anything open for discussion. “It is not in the way. We are in the way.”

So we went round it, one at a time, with some difficulty, and carried on to the top. We came back down the same path about three hours later, after a bath in the stream at the bottom of the far side that neither of us had planned on.

The moth was still there. Same spot, same wings, no sign whatsoever of having moved an inch in either direction. Beth said that by that stage it counted as somebody we knew, and we went round it again without a word.
qs: How wide is the path?
Barely wide enough for one person to pass another.
What exactly did Beth say about who was in the way?
That the moth was not in the way — they were.
Why did they go round it a second time without a word?
They had already agreed the moth had the right to be there.

write.task: Write the walk from the moth's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: Which One, Whiz?
paras: My pup is Whiz. When we get to the shop, Whiz has to pick.
“Which one?” I ask him. “Which one do you want?”
Whiz sits. He will not pick. He does not get why I ask.
When I pick for him, he whips his back legs about. Then he is not sad.
So now I do not ask which one. I just pick. Whiz is a pup, not a man.
qs: What is the pup called?
The pup is called Whiz.
What does the narrator ask him?
Which one do you want?
Why does the narrator stop asking?
Because Whiz is a pup and will not pick.

write.task: Should pets get to choose things? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: Which One, Whiz?
paras: My dog is called Whiz, which was a hopeful name given to an animal that has never once hurried anywhere.
When we get to the pet shop I hold up two things and ask him which one he wants. I have been doing this for two years.
Whiz sits down. He will not pick, and he gives every impression of not understanding why anybody would ask him to.
When I give up and pick for him, he whips his tail about and is perfectly delighted, whichever one I chose.
So I have stopped asking which. I just pick. Whiz is a dog, and the asking was never for his benefit anyway.
qs: Why is the name hopeful?
He has never once hurried anywhere.
How long has the narrator been asking?
Two years.
Who was the asking really for?
The narrator, not the dog.

write.task: Explain how to choose a toy for a pet. Group your points and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Which One, Whiz?
paras: My dog is called Whiz, which was an optimistic name to give an animal that has not, in six years, hurried anywhere for any reason whatsoever.

When we get to the pet shop I crouch down and hold up two things, one in each hand, and ask him which one he would like. I have been doing this since he was a puppy, which is to say for about two years longer than there has been any evidence it works.
Whiz sits down. He will not pick. He looks at me with an expression of mild, patient confusion, as though I have asked him something in a language he is aware exists but has never studied.

When I eventually give up and choose for him, he whips his tail about and is entirely delighted, and he is exactly as delighted whichever of the two I happened to be holding, which rather settles the question.
So I have stopped asking which. I crouch down, I pick, and we go home. Whiz is a dog, and when I am honest about it the asking was never for his benefit in the first place.
qs: How long has Whiz failed to hurry?
Six years.
What expression does Whiz give?
Mild, patient confusion, as though asked in a language he never studied.
What 'rather settles the question'?
He is equally delighted whichever one is chosen.

write.task: Do animals understand more than we think? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: Tim and the Big Pig
paras: Tim has a pig. The pig is big. It will not fit in the bin.
Tim did dig a pit for it. He hid the lid of the bin in the pit.
The pig did sit in the pit. It did not want to get up.
Tim got a fig. He did hold it up. The pig got up and did run to him.
Now the pig will sit with Tim. Tim will not dig a pit for it.
qs: Who has a pig?
Tim has a pig.
What did Tim dig?
He did dig a pit for the pig.
What got the pig up?
A fig that Tim held up.

write.task: Tell what Tim did, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Tim and the Big Pig
paras: Tim keeps a pig in the bit of field behind his house, and it is a very big pig indeed.
In spring he dug a shallow pit for it to wallow in, which took him most of a Sunday with a spade.
The pig sat down in the pit the minute it was finished and did not get up again for six hours.
Tim tried calling. He tried whistling. In the end he held up a fig, and the pig was out of the pit and across the field in seconds.
The pig now follows him everywhere. Tim has not dug anything since, and he says he does not intend to.
qs: Where does Tim keep the pig?
In the bit of field behind his house.
How long did digging the pit take?
Most of a Sunday.
What finally worked?
Holding up a fig.

write.task: Was the pit a good idea? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: Tim and the Big Pig
paras: Tim keeps a pig in the strip of field behind his house. It is a very big pig, bigger than it has any business being, and it has opinions about where it sits.

In the spring he dug it a shallow pit to wallow in. This took him the better part of a Sunday with a spade and a wheelbarrow, and he finished it in the middle of the afternoon feeling rather pleased with himself.
The pig sat down in the pit within a minute of its completion and did not get up again for six solid hours, which Tim had not anticipated and had no plan for.

He tried calling it. He tried whistling, which has never worked on this pig and did not begin working then. In the end he went and got a fig from the kitchen and held it up, and the pig was out of the pit and halfway across the field before he had finished lifting his arm.
The pig follows him everywhere now, at a distance of about three feet. Tim has not dug anything since that Sunday, and he says, with some feeling, that he has no intention of ever digging again.
qs: How did Tim feel when he finished the pit?
Rather pleased with himself.
What had Tim not anticipated?
That the pig would sit in it for six hours and not get up.
How far behind does the pig follow?
About three feet.

write.task: Write a report on keeping a pig. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Pot on the Cot
paras: Mom got a pot. The pot is hot. She put it on a cot by the tub.
The dog got on the cot. He did not go to the pot.
“Off, dog,” said Mom. “The pot is hot. Do not go on the cot.”
The dog got off. He sat on the rug and did not nod off.
Mom got the pot. The dog got the cot. Not a bad job for a dog.
qs: Where did Mom put the hot pot?
On a cot by the tub.
What did the dog do?
He got on the cot.
What did the dog get at the end?
The dog got the cot.

write.task: Should the dog be on the cot? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Pot on the Cot
paras: Mom took the pot off the stove on Monday and set it down on the folding cot by the back door, which is not where a hot pot goes.
The dog was on that cot within about four seconds. He has never been on it before in his life and he chose that moment.
“Off,” said Mom, in the voice that does not get argued with. “That pot is hot. Get off the cot.”
He got off. He sat down on the rug a foot away and watched the pot with great attention for the next twenty minutes, not nodding off once.
Mom got the pot back to the stove. The dog got the cot, and he has slept on it every night since.
qs: Where did Mom set the hot pot?
On the folding cot by the back door.
How quickly was the dog on the cot?
Within about four seconds.
What happened to the cot afterwards?
The dog got it and has slept on it every night since.

write.task: Write this from the dog's point of view. Use time-order words and include something somebody says.

g4.title: The Pot on the Cot
paras: Mom took the pot off the stove on Monday evening and set it down, without really thinking about it, on the folding cot by the back door. A hot pot does not go on a folding cot. Everybody in the house knows this, including, as it turns out, Mom.

The dog was on that cot within about four seconds. He has never been on the cot before in his entire life. It has stood there for three years and he has walked past it perhaps two thousand times without once showing any interest, and he chose that precise moment to get on it.
“Off,” Mom said, in the particular voice that does not get argued with by anybody, dog or otherwise. “That pot is hot. Get off the cot.”

He got off at once. Then he sat down on the rug about a foot away from the cot and watched that pot with enormous attention for the next twenty minutes, not nodding off even slightly, as though he had been given a job.
Mom got the pot back to the stove where it belonged. The dog got the cot. He has slept on it every single night since, and nobody has suggested otherwise.
qs: How long has the cot been there?
Three years.
Why is the dog's timing remarkable?
He had ignored the cot about two thousand times before.
What does the dog seem to think he has been given?
A job — watching the pot.

write.task: Should pets be allowed on the furniture? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Bug in the Mug
paras: Gus has a mug. The mug is on a rug by the tub.
A bug got in the mug. It did run up and it did run down.
Gus did not want to cut up the bug. He got a bun and put it on the rug.
The bug did run up out of the mug. It did go to the bun.
Gus got his mug. The bug got a bun. Gus is not a bad lad.
qs: Where is the mug?
On a rug by the tub.
What got in the mug?
A bug got in the mug.
How did Gus get the bug out?
He put a bun on the rug and the bug went to it.

write.task: Tell what Gus did, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Bug in the Mug
paras: Gus left his mug on the rug by the tub on Sunday morning, which is how most of the trouble in his life begins.
By the time he came back there was a bug in it, running up the inside and sliding back down again, over and over, getting nowhere.
He did not want to tip it out and he did not want to squash it. So he tore up a bit of a bun and put the crumbs on the rug next to the mug.
The bug stopped running, worked its way up the side one more time, got over the lip, and went straight to the crumbs.
Gus got his mug back and washed it twice. The bug got the bun. Gus says that is about as fair as mornings usually get.
qs: Where did Gus leave his mug?
On the rug by the tub.
What was the bug doing?
Running up the inside and sliding back down, getting nowhere.
What did Gus use instead of tipping it out?
Crumbs from a bun put on the rug.

write.task: Was Gus right to rescue the bug? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Bug in the Mug
paras: Gus left his mug on the rug by the tub on Sunday morning. Leaving things in places they do not belong is how most of the trouble in Gus's life begins, and he is aware of this, and it has never once stopped him.

By the time he came back for it there was a bug in the bottom, running up the smooth inside of the mug and sliding straight back down again, over and over, with enormous effort and absolutely no progress whatsoever.

He did not want to tip it out onto the rug, and he was not going to squash it. So he tore up a bit of a bun that was sitting on the counter and put the crumbs down on the rug about an inch from the mug, and then sat back on his heels and waited.
The bug stopped running. It gathered itself, worked its way up the side one more time, got a grip on the lip, hauled itself over, and went directly to the crumbs without pausing.
Gus got his mug back and washed it twice, with care, before using it again. The bug got the bun. Gus says that is about as fair as a Sunday morning generally manages to be.
qs: What does Gus know about himself?
That leaving things where they do not belong causes his trouble, and it never stops him.
How is the bug's effort described?
Enormous effort and absolutely no progress whatsoever.
What did Gus do after waiting?
Nothing — he let the bug climb out on its own.

write.task: Explain how to get an insect out of a house without hurting it. Organise it into steps and connect your ideas.

g2.title: Ten Red Hens
paras: Jed has ten red hens. The hens are in a pen by the hut.
Jed fed the hens. He set the pet bed in the pen.
Ten hens, one bed. Not all the hens got in the bed. One hen did not.
It sat on the pen leg. Jed let it sit. Then it got in the bed as well.
Ten hens, one bed. Jed is a man who can get a job done.
qs: How many hens does Jed have?
Jed has ten red hens.
Where did Jed set the bed?
He set the pet bed in the pen.
Which hen did not get in the bed at first?
One hen sat on the pen leg.

write.task: Write three facts about Jed's hens. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: Ten Red Hens
paras: Jed keeps ten red hens in a pen beside the shed, and he has kept the same ten since the end of September.
He fed them at seven every evening, and in October he set an old pet bed down in the corner of the pen to see what would happen.
Nine of them were in it that same night, pressed together in a heap. The tenth stayed out and sat on the fence rail instead, on her own.
Jed let her be. He has learned not to interfere with hens. She watched the rest of them from the rail for eleven nights.
On the twelfth she got into the bed with the others, and that was the end of it. Ten hens, one bed, nothing said.
qs: How long has Jed kept these ten?
Since the end of September.
Where did the tenth hen sleep at first?
On the fence rail, on her own.
How many nights did she stay out?
Eleven nights.

write.task: Write the eleven nights from the tenth hen's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what she could see.

g4.title: Ten Red Hens
paras: Jed keeps ten red hens in a pen beside the shed. They are the same ten he has had since the end of September, and he can tell them apart, which he says is not a special skill and simply takes paying attention.

He feeds them at seven every evening without fail. In the middle of October he put an old pet bed down in the corner of the pen, not for any particular reason, mainly to see what they would do about it.
Nine of them were in it that same night, pressed into a single heap with no gaps anywhere. The tenth did not go near it. She went up onto the fence rail instead and sat there on her own in the cold.

Jed let her be. He has kept hens for eleven years and the main thing he has learned is not to interfere with them. She watched the other nine from that rail every night for eleven nights, and he did not move her once.
On the twelfth night she got down and got into the bed with the rest of them, and that was the end of the matter. Ten hens, one bed, and nobody had said a word about it to anybody.
qs: What does Jed say about telling the hens apart?
That it is not a special skill and simply takes paying attention.
Why did he put the bed in?
For no particular reason, mainly to see what they would do.
What is the main thing eleven years has taught him?
Not to interfere with hens.

write.task: Is it better to leave something alone or to step in? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Cake on the Lake
paras: Jane made a cake. She made it late, and she made it for the race by the lake.
She gave the cake a name. The name was Mud Cake, as it was the same shade as mud.
Dave came and had a taste. He made a face. Then he had a lot more.
At the gate by the lake, the kids ate the cake in a wave.
Jane made the same cake the next time. That time she made two.
qs: Who made the cake?
Jane made the cake.
What name did she give it?
She gave it the name Mud Cake.
What did Jane do the next time?
She made the same cake, but she made two.

write.task: Tell what happened to the cake, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Cake on the Lake
paras: Jane made the cake late on the Friday, for the race at the lake the following morning, and she was still icing it at eleven.
She gave it a name, because she names everything. It was called Mud Cake, on the grounds that it was exactly the same shade as the path down to the water.
Dave came over and took a taste before anybody else was awake. He made a face that was not encouraging, and then he had a second slice, and then a third.
At the gate by the lake the whole cake went in about four minutes, in a wave of children who had not been told it was coming.
Jane made the same cake again the next weekend. That time she made two, and the second one lasted nearly ten minutes.
qs: When did Jane finish the cake?
She was still icing it at eleven on the Friday night.
Why was it called Mud Cake?
It was the same shade as the path down to the water.
How long did the whole cake last?
About four minutes.

write.task: Was Dave's reaction fair? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Cake on the Lake
paras: Jane made the cake late on the Friday, for the race at the lake the next morning, and she was still icing it at eleven at night with the radio on and everybody else in the house asleep.

She gave it a name, because she names everything she makes and always has. It was called Mud Cake, on the entirely reasonable grounds that it was precisely the same shade as the path that runs down to the water.

Dave came over early and took a taste before anybody else in the house was awake. He made a face that could not fairly be described as encouraging. He then had a second slice, and shortly afterwards a third, and did not revise the face or offer any explanation for either.
At the gate by the lake the entire cake went in about four minutes, in a wave of children who had not been told it was coming and who arrived from three directions at once.
Jane made the same cake again the following weekend. That time she made two of them, and the second one lasted nearly ten minutes, which she considers a substantial improvement.
qs: What was Jane doing at eleven at night?
Still icing the cake with the radio on.
What is odd about Dave's behaviour?
He made an unencouraging face and then ate three slices without explaining.
Why does Jane consider ten minutes an improvement?
The first cake had lasted only four.

write.task: Write a report on planning food for an event. Organise it into sections, develop each with examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Kite and the Pine
paras: Mike has a kite. It is white with a line of red on the side.
He likes to fly it, but it got in a pine at the side of the lane.
Mike did not like that. The kite was up in the pine and he is not tall.
Dad came with a pole. It did take a while, but the kite came down fine.
Mike will fly the kite a mile from that pine the next time.
qs: What does Mike's kite look like?
It is white with a line of red on the side.
Where did the kite get stuck?
In a pine at the side of the lane.
How did it come down?
Dad came with a pole.

write.task: Tell how the kite came down, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Kite and the Pine
paras: Mike's kite is white with a line of red down one side, and he has flown it nearly every week since his birthday.
On Saturday the wind swung round while he was not looking and put it straight into the big pine at the side of the lane.
It was high up. Mike is not tall and the lowest branch is well above his head, and he spent some time pretending he had a plan.
