Dad came out with the window pole, which is nine feet long and not meant for this. It took a while and a good deal of advice from both of them, but the kite came down undamaged.
Mike flies it a good mile from that pine now. He says the wind is better down there, which is not the reason.
qs: How often has Mike flown the kite?
Nearly every week since his birthday.
Why could Mike not reach it?
He is not tall and the lowest branch is above his head.
What is not the real reason he moved?
That the wind is better further away.

write.task: Should Mike fly the kite somewhere else? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Kite and the Pine
paras: Mike's kite is white with a single line of red running down one side, and he has flown it nearly every week since his birthday in April, in conditions ranging from ideal to extremely unwise.

On Saturday afternoon the wind swung right round while he was looking the other way and put the kite straight into the big pine at the side of the lane, about twenty feet up, where it lodged and stayed.

It was well out of reach. Mike is not tall, the lowest branch on that pine is a good way above his head, and he spent several minutes walking round the base of the tree giving a convincing impression of somebody who had a plan.

Dad came out eventually with the window pole, which is nine feet long and was not designed for retrieving anything from a tree. It took a quarter of an hour and a considerable volume of advice from both parties, but the kite came down undamaged and with the line still attached.
Mike flies it a good mile from that pine now, down by the river. He says the wind is better down there. The wind is not better down there, and everybody involved is aware of it.
qs: How high did the kite lodge?
About twenty feet up.
What was Mike really doing while walking round the tree?
Giving a convincing impression of somebody who had a plan.
What does the last line tell you?
Everybody knows the real reason is the tree, not the wind.

write.task: Write the rescue from Dad's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Mole by the Rose
paras: A mole made a hole by the rose. Mom got the hose to fill it up.
“Do not do that,” I said. “That hole is its home.”
Mom did not use the hose. She put a cone on the hole so that no one would fall in it.
The mole did not use that hole. It made a hole by the pole.
Now we have a cone, a pole, a rose, and a mole with a home.
qs: What made a hole by the rose?
A mole made the hole.
What did Mom put on the hole?
She put a cone on it.
Where did the mole make its next hole?
By the pole.

write.task: Write three facts about the mole. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Rope and the Stone
paras: Rose had a rope and one very large stone, and a plan that did not survive contact with the rope or the stone.
She tied the rope to the stone and then tied the other end to the gate pole, on the theory that she could lever it. The stone did not move an inch.
She did not mope about it. She went inside, got a note pad, and sat down at the table to think, which is more than most people do.
What she wrote was this: hose the mud off it first, then roll it rather than drag it. Mud is what is holding it down.
She did exactly that. The stone rolled, and then rode home on a pole and the rope, and it is in her garden now.
qs: What was Rose's first theory?
That she could lever the stone using the gate pole.
What did she do instead of moping?
She got a note pad and sat down to think.
What was holding the stone down?
Mud.

write.task: Is stopping to think better than trying harder? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Rope and the Stone
paras: Rose had a rope, one extremely large stone, and a plan, and the plan did not survive its first contact with either of the other two.

She tied the rope around the stone and then tied the other end to the gate pole, on the theory that she could use the pole as a lever and walk the stone out of the ground. The stone did not move. It did not even acknowledge the attempt.

She did not mope about it, which is the part I find remarkable. She went indoors, got a note pad off the shelf, sat down at the kitchen table and thought about it properly for twenty minutes, which is more than most people manage in a week.
What she wrote down was this: hose the mud off it first, then roll it rather than drag it, because it is the mud holding it and not the weight. Both of those turned out to be correct.

She did exactly that, in that order. The stone rolled over twice, came free, and then rode home on the pole and the rope with two of us steadying it. It sits in her garden now, and she has never once mentioned the lever.
qs: What was wrong with the lever plan?
The stone did not move or even acknowledge the attempt.
What does the narrator find remarkable?
That Rose did not mope about it.
What two things did she write down?
Hose the mud off first, and roll it rather than drag it.

write.task: Explain how to move something heavy safely. Organise it into steps, develop each with examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Cute Mule
paras: June has a mule. The mule is cute. It is not rude, but it is not tame.
June got a tube of mule mash. The mule did not use it.
“Do not be rude,” said June. “I got this for you.”
The mule came up. It did use the tube. Then it sat on June's shoe.
June did not fuss. A cute mule can sit on a shoe if it likes.
qs: What does June have?
June has a cute mule.
What did June get for it?
A tube of mule mash.
What did the mule sit on?
It sat on June's shoe.

write.task: Is the mule rude? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Cute Mule
paras: June keeps a mule in the field behind the house. It is cute in the way that difficult animals often are, and it is not remotely tame.
She bought a tube of the expensive feed in June, which the man in the shop had assured her no animal could refuse. The mule refused it for nine days.
“Do not be rude,” June told it, every morning, holding the tube out at arm's length. “I bought this for you.”
On the tenth morning it came over, used the whole tube in about a minute, and then stood on June's shoe and would not get off.
June did not mind. She says a mule that has decided to stand on your shoe has decided a great deal more than that.
qs: How long did the mule refuse the feed?
Nine days.
What had the man in the shop said?
That no animal could refuse it.
What does June think standing on her shoe means?
That the mule has decided a great deal more than that.

write.task: Write the ten days from the mule's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what it could smell.

g4.title: The Cute Mule
paras: June keeps a mule in the field behind her house. It is cute in the particular way that difficult animals often are, which is to say that it is cute until you want it to do something, and it is not remotely tame and has never pretended to be.

She bought a tube of the expensive feed back in June, on the recommendation of the man in the shop, who assured her at some length that no animal alive could refuse it. The mule refused it, without any apparent effort, for nine consecutive days.

“Do not be rude,” June told it every single morning, standing at the gate with the tube held out at arm's length. “I bought this for you.” The mule would look at the tube, and then at her, and then walk away.

On the tenth morning it came straight over, used the entire tube in something under a minute, and then put one front hoof down on June's shoe and stood there, with its whole weight on it, and would not move.
June did not mind, and still does not. She says that a mule which has decided to stand on your shoe has quietly decided a great deal more than that, and that it is worth waiting nine days for.
qs: In what way is the mule cute?
Cute until you want it to do something.
What did the mule do each morning?
Look at the tube, then at June, then walk away.
What does June think the shoe means?
That the mule has accepted her, and it was worth the nine days.

write.task: Is patience the best way to win an animal over? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Snail on the Rail
paras: There is a snail on the rail at the end of our lane.
It has been there since the rain. It did not fail to stay put.
I gave it a name. The name is Maid, as she sits so plain and still.
Dad said a snail will wait for rain and then it will trail off.
It did rain. Maid left a trail on the rail and went. I did not mind.
qs: Where is the snail?
On the rail at the end of our lane.
What name did the narrator give it?
The name is Maid.
What did the snail do when it rained?
It left a trail on the rail and went.

write.task: Tell what the snail did, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Snail on the Rail
paras: There has been a snail on the rail at the end of our lane since the rain nine days ago, in exactly the same spot.
I gave it a name, which Dad says is a mistake with snails. The name is Maid, because she sits so plain and still.
He explained that a snail will wait out dry weather without moving at all, and then trail off the moment the air gets damp again.
It rained on Friday night. On Saturday morning there was a faint silver trail along the rail and no snail at the end of it.
I do not mind. She waited nine days for that rain and she had earned the right to go.
qs: How long had the snail been there?
Nine days, since the rain.
What does Dad say a snail does in dry weather?
Waits without moving at all.
What was left on the rail?
A faint silver trail.

write.task: Explain how snails survive dry weather. Group your points and use topic vocabulary.

g4.title: The Snail on the Rail
paras: There has been a snail on the rail at the end of our lane since the rain on Tuesday, in precisely the same spot, at precisely the same angle, for nine days without a visible change of any kind.

I gave it a name, which Dad maintains is a mistake to make with snails. The name is Maid, chosen because she sits so plain and still that you could walk past her a hundred times without registering that she is an animal at all.

He explained the reason, which I had not known. A snail will wait out dry weather entirely, sealed against the surface it has chosen, losing nothing, gaining nothing, and will trail off the moment the air turns damp enough to be worth the effort.
It rained hard on Friday night. On Saturday morning there was a faint silver trail running along the rail for about a foot, and at the end of it there was no snail.
I do not mind, and I was not expecting to feel that way. She had waited nine days for that rain. Nothing that waits nine days for anything should have to explain itself when it finally goes.
qs: What makes the snail easy to walk past?
She sits so plain and still she does not register as an animal.
What does a snail do while sealed against a surface?
It loses nothing and gains nothing.
Why does the narrator not mind?
The snail had waited nine days and had earned the right to go.

write.task: Is it worth waiting a long time for something? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: A Day in the Hay
paras: We stay at my gran's in May. There is hay in the big bay of the barn.
We play in the hay all day. Gran will not say no.
One day a gray cat came to play. It did not stay.
It ran away when my brother did a big jump in the hay.
The next day it came back. It may stay if we play in a quiet way.
qs: When do they stay at Gran's?
In May.
Where is the hay?
In the big bay of the barn.
Why did the gray cat run away?
Because the brother did a big jump in the hay.

write.task: Should they play quietly for the cat? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: A Day in the Hay
paras: We stay at my gran's every May, and the best thing about it is the hay stacked up in the big bay at the end of the barn.
We play in it all day and Gran has never once said no, which I think is the whole reason we keep going back.
One afternoon a gray cat came in and sat on a bale to watch us, and it stayed for nearly an hour without moving.
Then my brother took a run and jumped into the stack from the ladder, and the cat was out of the door before he landed.
It came back the next day. It will stay as long as we play in a quiet way, and we have learned to.
qs: What is stacked in the bay of the barn?
Hay.
How long did the cat stay?
Nearly an hour.
What have they learned?
To play in a quiet way so the cat will stay.

write.task: Write the afternoon from the cat's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what it could hear.

g4.title: A Day in the Hay
paras: We stay at my gran's every May for a fortnight, and the best thing about the whole arrangement is the hay stacked right up to the roof in the big bay at the far end of the barn.
We play in it all day, every day, and Gran has never once said no to any of it. I am fairly certain that is the entire reason we keep going back, and I am fairly certain she knows that too.
One afternoon a gray cat came in through the side door, picked a bale near the front, and sat on it to watch us. It stayed for the better part of an hour without moving anything except its eyes.

Then my brother climbed the ladder, took a run at the edge, and jumped into the stack from a height that Gran would not have approved of, and the cat was through the door and gone before he had finished landing.
It came back the following day and sat on the same bale. It will stay for as long as we play in a quiet way, which is a thing we have had to learn, and which has turned out to be worth learning.
qs: How long do they stay in May?
A fortnight.
What did the cat move while watching?
Nothing except its eyes.
What has turned out to be worth learning?
How to play in a quiet way.

write.task: Write a report on how to behave around a nervous animal. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: Three Green Trees
paras: There are three green trees at the end of the street.
A bee went to the trees. We did see it from the steps.
We need to keep the trees. Dad said he will feed them in the week.
Deep in the green there is a nest. We can see the feet of a bird in it.
Three trees, one bee, one nest. That street is the best street.
qs: How many trees are there?
There are three green trees.
What went to the trees?
A bee went to the trees.
What is deep in the green?
A nest, with the feet of a bird in it.

write.task: Write three facts about the trees. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: Three Green Trees
paras: There are three green trees at the end of our street, planted close together, and they have been there longer than any of the houses.
A bee went into them one morning and we watched it from the front steps for a good while before it came out again.
Dad says we need to keep those trees in better condition than we have been, and that he will feed them properly this week.
Deep inside the middle one there is a nest. If you stand underneath and look straight up you can see two feet over the edge of it, and nothing else.
Three trees, one bee, one nest. We keep telling people it is the best street in the town, and we keep being right.
qs: How long have the trees been there?
Longer than any of the houses.
What can you see if you look straight up?
Two feet over the edge of the nest.
What does Dad plan to do this week?
Feed the trees properly.

write.task: Should every street have trees? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: Three Green Trees
paras: There are three green trees at the end of our street. They stand close together, almost touching at the top, and they have been there a great deal longer than any of the houses that now surround them.

A bee went into them on Tuesday afternoon and we sat on the front steps and watched for it to come out, which took a surprisingly long time and which neither of us admitted to enjoying as much as we did.
Dad says we need to keep those trees in rather better condition than we have been keeping them, and that he intends to feed them properly this week, which he has said in previous weeks.

Deep inside the middle one, well above head height, there is a nest. If you stand directly underneath and look straight up you can see two small feet hooked over the edge of it and absolutely nothing else of the bird at all.
Three trees, one bee, one nest. We have told a great many people that this is the best street in the town, and so far nobody has been able to supply a convincing argument against it.
qs: How do the trees stand?
Close together, almost touching at the top.
What did neither of them admit?
How much they enjoyed watching for the bee.
What is implied about Dad's plan?
He has promised to feed them in previous weeks and not done it.

write.task: Write about a tree you know well. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: Tea by the Sea
paras: We eat by the sea each year. Gran makes tea and we each get a peach.
The sand is clean and the sea is near. You can hear it from the seat.
A seal came up. It did not speak, but it did eat a bit of my meal.
“That seal is not weak,” said Gran. “It has a real plan.”
Each year we go back. Each year the seal gets a meal.
qs: What does Gran make?
Gran makes tea.
What came up while they were eating?
A seal came up.
What did Gran say about the seal?
That it is not weak and has a real plan.

write.task: Tell what happened by the sea, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Tea by the Sea
paras: We eat by the sea at least once each year, and Gran brings tea in a flask and a peach for everybody, which she has done since before I can remember.
The sand at that beach is clean and the sea comes in close, so you can hear it clearly from the seat on the wall where we always sit.
A seal came up out of the water last year while we were eating. It did not make a sound. It worked its way up the sand and took a good piece of my meal.
“That seal is not weak,” Gran said, without getting up. “That seal has a real plan and it has used it before.”
We go back each year to the same stretch of beach. Each year the seal gets a meal, and each year Gran brings an extra peach.
qs: What does Gran bring?
Tea in a flask and a peach for everybody.
What did the seal do?
It came up the sand without a sound and took a piece of the meal.
What has changed since?
Gran brings an extra peach each year.

write.task: Should people feed wild animals? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: Tea by the Sea
paras: We eat by the sea at least once each year, and Gran brings tea in a flask and a peach for every single person, which she has done for as long as anybody in this family can actually remember.
The sand on that beach is clean and the sea comes in close at high tide, so that from the seat on the wall where we always sit you can hear it clearly without having to stop talking to do so.

A seal came up out of the water last year while we were in the middle of eating. It made no sound whatsoever. It worked its way up the wet sand in a series of short efforts, arrived at the edge of the blanket, and took a substantial piece of my meal without any sense of hurry.
“That seal is not weak,” Gran said, not getting up, not even putting down her tea. “That seal has a real plan, and from the look of it that seal has used this plan a number of times before.”

We go back every year to the same stretch of beach and the same seat on the same wall. Each year the seal gets a meal. Each year, since then, Gran has carried one extra peach, and nobody has ever discussed why.
qs: What can you do from the seat on the wall?
Hear the sea without stopping talking.
How did the seal move up the sand?
In a series of short efforts, without any hurry.
What has nobody ever discussed?
Why Gran brings one extra peach.

write.task: Write a report on seals. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Goat on the Road
paras: A goat got out and went up the road. It had a coat of thick white hair.
Joan got her coat and went to get it. The goat did not want to go home.
It did eat the oats from her hand. Then it did eat the soap from the load.
“Not the soap,” said Joan. “You can not eat soap.”
The goat went home on the road with Joan. It did moan the whole way.
qs: What was on the road?
A goat was on the road.
What did the goat eat?
It ate the oats from Joan's hand, then the soap.
How did the goat go home?
On the road with Joan, moaning the whole way.

write.task: Tell what the goat did, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Goat on the Road
paras: A goat got out of the top field on Sunday and went straight up the road, which is the one direction nobody wanted it to take.
Joan got her coat and went after it. The goat had no intention of going home and made that perfectly clear by walking faster every time she got close.
In the end she stopped chasing and held out a handful of oats. The goat ate the oats. Then, before she could stop it, it ate a bar of soap off the load in the back of the cart.
“Not the soap,” Joan said. “Nothing eats soap. You cannot eat soap.”
It walked home on the road beside her without any further argument, and it moaned, steadily and without pause, the entire way.
qs: Which way did the goat go?
Straight up the road, the one direction nobody wanted.
How did the goat react when Joan got close?
It walked faster.
What did it do all the way home?
It moaned steadily without pause.

write.task: Was Joan right to stop chasing? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Goat on the Road
paras: A goat got out of the top field on Sunday morning and went straight up the road, which is the one direction out of four that nobody in the house wanted it to take, and which it appeared to have selected deliberately.

Joan got her coat and went after it. The goat had no intention whatsoever of coming home, and it made this clear in the way goats do, which is by walking slightly faster every single time she got within reach of it and then stopping again as soon as she gave up.

In the end she stopped chasing altogether, sat down on the bank, and held out a handful of oats. The goat came over and ate the oats. Then, before she could do anything about it, it ate a bar of soap straight off the load in the back of the cart.
“Not the soap,” Joan said. “Nothing eats soap. There is no animal on this earth that eats soap.” The goat looked back at her with complete composure and finished it.
It walked home along the road beside her afterwards without any further argument at all, and it moaned steadily, without pausing once for breath, for the entire length of the journey.
qs: How did the goat choose its direction?
It appeared to have selected it deliberately, the one nobody wanted.
What is the goat's method of avoiding capture?
Walking faster when approached, then stopping when she gives up.
How did the goat react to being told off?
With complete composure, and it finished the soap.

write.task: Write the morning from the goat's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Crow on the Window
paras: A crow sits on the window sill when the snow falls.
It will not go. It will not show any fear of us at all.
We throw it bits from the yellow bowl. It takes them slow.
Below the window there is a row of its tracks in the snow.
Now we know the crow. It is our crow, and the crow lets us know it.
qs: When does the crow sit on the sill?
When the snow falls.
What do they throw it?
Bits from the yellow bowl.
What is below the window?
A row of its tracks in the snow.

write.task: Tell what the crow does, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Crow on the Window
paras: A crow sits on our window sill whenever snow falls, and it has done so every winter for three years now.
It will not go when we open the window, and it shows no fear of any of us, which is not normal for a crow.
We throw it bits from the yellow bowl on the sill. It takes them slow, one at a time, and never takes more than four.
Below the window there is always a row of its tracks going off across the snow in the same direction, towards the low wall.
Now we know the crow and it knows us. My mother says we should not have named it. We named it anyway.
qs: How long has the crow been coming?
Every winter for three years.
How many bits does it take?
Never more than four.
Where do its tracks go?
Across the snow towards the low wall.

write.task: Should wild birds be fed in winter? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Crow on the Window
paras: A crow sits on our kitchen window sill whenever snow falls. It has done this every winter for three years, and it arrives within about an hour of the first flakes, which nobody has ever been able to explain.
It does not go when we open the window. It shows no fear of any of us whatsoever, which is not normal behaviour for a crow, and which took some getting used to in the first winter.

We throw it bits from the yellow bowl we now keep on the sill for that purpose. It takes them slow, one at a time, turning each one over before swallowing it, and it has never once taken more than four.
Below the window there is always a row of tracks going off across the snow in the same direction, towards the low wall at the end of the garden, and never in any other direction.

Now we know the crow and the crow knows us. My mother says we should never have given it a name, because naming a wild thing is how you end up responsible for it. We gave it a name anyway, four days in.
qs: How soon does the crow arrive?
Within about an hour of the first flakes.
What does it do before swallowing?
It turns each piece over.
What is the mother's argument against naming it?
Naming a wild thing is how you end up responsible for it.

write.task: Write a report on crows. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Jar in the Barn
paras: In the dark of the barn there is a jar on a shelf.
The jar is full of hard bits of glass. Some are sharp.
Gran said her dad put them in the jar. He got them in the yard.
“Do not start on that jar,” she said. “It is far too sharp for hands.”
So the jar sits in the dark. It is a part of the barn now.
qs: Where is the jar?
On a shelf in the dark of the barn.
What is in the jar?
Hard bits of glass, some of them sharp.
What does Gran say?
Not to start on the jar, because it is far too sharp for hands.

write.task: Should the jar be thrown away? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Jar in the Barn
paras: In the dark at the far end of the barn there is a glass jar on a shelf, and it has sat there since long before I was born.
It is full of hard bits of coloured glass, worn smooth at the edges by years in the ground, though some of them are still sharp.
Gran says her father filled it. He turned the pieces up in the yard whenever he dug, and he kept every single one of them.
“Do not start on that jar,” she tells us, every summer. “Parts of it are far too sharp for hands.”
So the jar stays where it is, in the dark, on the same shelf. It is a part of the barn now, as much as the beams are.
qs: How did Gran's father collect the glass?
He turned the pieces up in the yard whenever he dug.
Why are most pieces smooth?
They were worn smooth by years in the ground.
What does the narrator compare the jar to?
The beams of the barn.

write.task: Write about the man who filled the jar. Use time-order words and include something he might say.

g4.title: The Jar in the Barn
paras: In the dark at the far end of the barn, on the third shelf up, there is a large glass jar, and it has stood in that exact spot since a long time before I was born.
It is full of hard bits of coloured glass — green, brown, and a very few blue — most of them worn smooth at the edges by years in the ground, though a small number of them are still perfectly sharp.

Gran says her father filled it over about forty years. He turned pieces up in the yard every time he dug for anything, and rather than throwing them out he carried them in and dropped them into the jar, and he did this until he could not dig any more.
“Do not start on that jar,” she tells us, every summer, in the same words. “Parts of it are far too sharp for hands.” None of us ever has.
So it stays where it is, in the dark, on its shelf. Nobody has emptied it and nobody has suggested emptying it. It is as much a part of that barn now as the beams are.
qs: What three colours are in the jar?
Green, brown and a very few blue.
Over how long did her father fill it?
About forty years, until he could not dig any more.
What has nobody ever suggested?
Emptying the jar.

write.task: Should families keep things that have no use? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Horn by the Barn
paras: There is an old horn on a shelf by the north wall of the barn.
Dad got it at the fort. It is torn at one end.
He will not sort it out. He said it is worth more than it is.
In the morning my brother got the horn. It was not a short note. It went on and on.
Mom came out. “Not before my corn,” she said.
qs: Where is the horn?
On a shelf by the north wall of the barn.
What is wrong with it?
It is torn at one end.
What did Mom say?
Not before her corn.

write.task: Tell what happened in the barn, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Horn on the Porch
paras: There is an old brass horn on the porch by the north door, hanging from a nail that was put there for something else.
Dad bought it years ago from a shop near the fort, for a sum he has never been willing to tell anybody. It is torn at one end and it is not worth much.
He will not throw it out and he will not hear any argument about it. He says it is worth more than it looks, and that this is right about most things on that porch.
On Sunday morning my brother took it down and sounded it, with no warning to anybody. It was not a short sound. It went on for a remarkable length of time.
Mom came out onto the porch in her dressing gown. “Not,” she said, “before I have had my corn.” That is the whole rule now.
qs: Where did Dad buy the horn?
From a shop near the fort.
What has he never been willing to say?
How much he paid for it.
What is the rule now?
No horn before Mom has had her corn.

write.task: Should the horn be allowed on Sunday mornings? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Horn on the Porch
paras: There is an old brass horn hanging on the porch by the north door, from a nail that was driven in for something else entirely and has held the horn for eleven years without complaint.

Dad bought it from a shop near the fort a long time ago, for a sum of money that he has consistently and cheerfully refused to disclose to anybody, including, I believe, Mom. It is torn at one end, the lacquer has gone, and it is worth very little.

He will not throw it out and he will not entertain any argument on the subject. He says it is worth a good deal more than it looks, and that the same is true of almost everything else on that porch, which is a point he is not wrong about.

On Sunday morning my brother took it down off its nail and blew it, without warning anybody in the house of his intentions. It was not a short sound. It went on for a genuinely remarkable length of time and could be heard, we later established, from the end of the road.

Mom came out onto the porch in her dressing gown and stood there for a moment. “Not,” she said, “before I have had my corn.” That has been the whole of the rule ever since, and it has not needed adding to.
qs: How long has the nail held the horn?
Eleven years.
Who does Dad apparently not tell the price?
Anybody, including Mom.
How far could the horn be heard?
From the end of the road.

write.task: Write the Sunday morning from Mom's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Song in the Spring
paras: In the spring a bird sings on the long branch by the swing.
It sings the same song for a long time. It will not stop.
I bring a bit of string and hang it on the branch for the nest.
The bird takes the string. Then it sings the long song again.
That song is the best thing about spring on our bit of land.
qs: Where does the bird sing?
On the long branch by the swing.
What did the narrator bring?
A bit of string for the nest.
What did the bird do with the string?
It took the string.

write.task: Write three facts about the bird. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Song in the Spring
paras: Every spring a bird sings from the long branch above the swing, starting before six and keeping going for most of the morning.
It is the same song every time, repeated without variation, and after the first week you stop hearing it as a sound and start hearing it as the time of year.
In April I took out a length of string, cut it into short bits, and hung them along the branch where the bird could reach them.
It took every one of them over the following three days and then went back to singing the same long song from the same spot.
The nest is above the swing now. That song is the best thing about spring on our bit of ground, and it costs nothing.
qs: When does the bird start singing?
Before six in the morning.
What happens after the first week?
You stop hearing it as a sound and hear it as the time of year.
How long did it take the string?
Over the following three days.

write.task: Write the spring from the bird's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what it could see.

g4.title: The Song in the Spring
paras: Every spring a bird sings from the long branch directly above the swing. It starts before six in the morning and it keeps going, with very few breaks, until something like eleven.

It is the same song each time, repeated without any variation at all, and after about a week of it you stop hearing it as a sound in the garden and begin hearing it as the time of year itself, which is a strange thing to be able to say about a noise.
In the middle of April I took out a length of string, cut it into short pieces of about four inches, and hung them along the branch at intervals where the bird could easily get at them.

It took every single piece over the following three days, one at a time, working from the end nearest the trunk, and then it went back to singing the same long song from precisely the same spot it had used before.

The nest is directly above the swing now, which means nobody can use the swing until July. That song is still the best thing about spring on this bit of ground, and it has never cost us anything but a swing.
qs: How long does the bird sing each day?
From before six until about eleven.
In what order did it take the string?
One at a time, working from the end nearest the trunk.
What does the nest cost the family?
The use of the swing until July.

write.task: Is it worth giving up something for wildlife? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Pink Tank
paras: Hank has a fish tank. The tank has a pink light on the back.
He thinks the fish like it. I think they do not blink at it at all.
A bit of junk sank to the bottom of the tank. Hank got it out.
Then he gave the fish a drink of clean water. He did not thank me for the help.
The pink light is still on. The fish still do not blink.
qs: What does Hank have?
Hank has a fish tank.
What is on the back of the tank?
A pink light.
What sank to the bottom?
A bit of junk.

write.task: Should the tank have a pink light? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Pink Tank
paras: Hank has kept a fish tank on the bank of shelves by his window since the summer, and in September he put a pink light on the back of it.
He thinks the fish like it. I think the fish have not blinked at it once, and I have told him so more than once.
On Sunday a bit of junk sank to the bottom, off the shelf above, and the whole tank went cloudy within the hour.
Hank got it out with a net on a stick, changed half the water, and gave them a clean drink without any help from anybody.
The pink light is still on. The fish still do not blink at it. Hank has not thanked me for my opinion.
qs: When did Hank add the light?
In September.
What happened when the junk sank?
The whole tank went cloudy within the hour.
How did Hank fix it?
With a net on a stick, and by changing half the water.

write.task: Explain how to look after a fish tank. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Pink Tank
paras: Hank has kept a fish tank on the bank of shelves by his bedroom window since the summer before last, and in September he fitted a pink light to the back panel of it, on the grounds that it would be good for them.

He thinks the fish like it. I think the fish have not blinked at that light once in the entire time it has been there, and I have said so to him on at least four separate occasions without any noticeable effect.
On Sunday a bit of junk sank to the bottom of the tank, having fallen off the shelf directly above it, and the water went cloudy within the hour and stayed that way for most of the afternoon.
Hank got the junk out with a net taped to a stick, changed rather more than half the water, and gave the whole tank a proper clean without asking for or receiving any help from anybody in the house.
The pink light is still on. The fish still do not blink at it. Hank has yet to thank me for my opinion on the matter and I have stopped expecting him to.
qs: Why did Hank fit the light?
On the grounds that it would be good for the fish.
How many times has the narrator said so?
At least four separate occasions.
What has the narrator stopped expecting?
To be thanked for the opinion.

write.task: Should you keep giving advice nobody takes? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Duck and the Truck
paras: A duck sat in the back of a truck by the dock.
The truck had a sack of rock in it. The duck sat on the sack.
Jack came to check the truck. He got a shock.
“Off the sack,” said Jack. The duck did not pick itself up.
So Jack sat on the rock and had a snack. The duck kept the sack.
qs: Where did the duck sit?
In the back of a truck by the dock.
What was in the truck?
A sack of rock.
What did Jack do in the end?
He sat on the rock and had a snack.

write.task: Tell what happened by the dock, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Duck and the Truck
paras: There was a duck sitting in the back of a truck down by the dock on Thursday, and it had clearly been there some time.
The truck had a sack of broken rock in it, waiting to go up to the yard, and the duck had made itself comfortable right on top of the sack.
Jack came down to check the truck before taking it up and got a considerable shock when the duck looked back at him.
“Off the sack,” said Jack, with no particular authority. The duck did not pick up one foot.
So Jack sat down on a rock on the dock and had his snack instead, and the duck kept the sack for another forty minutes.
qs: What was in the sack?
Broken rock.
Why did Jack get a shock?
The duck looked back at him from the truck.
Who won?
The duck — it kept the sack for another forty minutes.

write.task: Should Jack have moved the duck? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Duck and the Truck
paras: There was a duck sitting in the back of the truck down by the dock on Thursday morning, and from the state of the truck bed it had clearly been there for a considerable length of time before anybody noticed.

The truck had a sack of broken rock in it, loaded the previous evening and waiting to go up to the yard, and the duck had arranged itself directly on top of the sack with every appearance of ownership.

Jack came down to check the truck before driving it up and got a genuine shock, because he was looking at the tyres and the duck was looking at him, and he did not notice this until he straightened up.
“Off the sack,” Jack said, with no particular authority in his voice and, by his own later account, no real expectation of being obeyed. The duck did not pick up either foot.

So Jack sat down on a rock at the edge of the dock and had his snack instead, which he had been going to eat later anyway. The duck kept the sack for another forty minutes and then left of its own accord.
qs: How could they tell the duck had been there a while?
From the state of the truck bed.
Why did the shock happen?
Jack was looking at the tyres and did not see the duck until he straightened up.
How did the situation end?
The duck left of its own accord after forty minutes.

write.task: Write the morning from the duck's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Patch on the Pitch
paras: There is a bad patch on the pitch by the ditch.
When it is wet you can not catch on that patch. The ball will not come up.
Mitch had a plan. He got sand from the ditch and put it on the patch.
Then we had a match. No one did a bad catch on that patch at all.
Mitch did not brag. He just sat on the bench and had his lunch.
qs: Where is the bad patch?
On the pitch by the ditch.
What was Mitch's plan?
To get sand from the ditch and put it on the patch.
What did Mitch do after the match?
He sat on the bench and had his lunch.

write.task: Was Mitch's plan a good one? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Patch on the Pitch
paras: There is a bad patch on the pitch down by the ditch, and it has been getting worse every winter for about three years.
When it rains you cannot catch anything on that patch. The ball hits it and stops dead instead of coming up, and everybody has learned to avoid it.
Mitch had a plan that nobody expected to work. He fetched sand up from the ditch in a bucket, load after load, and worked it into the patch over two afternoons.
Then we had a match on it. Nobody dropped a single catch on that patch, and two people did not even notice it was there.
Mitch did not brag about any of it. He sat on the bench afterwards and ate his lunch and let other people work it out.
qs: How long has the patch been getting worse?
About three years.
What does the ball do on the patch?
It hits it and stops dead instead of coming up.
How did Mitch behave afterwards?
He did not brag — he sat on the bench and ate his lunch.

write.task: Write the two afternoons Mitch spent fixing it. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Patch on the Pitch
paras: There is a bad patch on the pitch down by the ditch, about eight feet across, and it has been getting steadily worse every winter for something like three years without anybody doing anything about it.

When it rains you cannot catch anything on that patch at all. The ball comes down, hits it, and stops dead rather than coming up, and over three seasons everybody who plays there has quietly learned to avoid standing on it.

Mitch had a plan, and nobody who heard it expected it to work. He fetched sand up from the bottom of the ditch in a bucket, load after load after load, and worked it down into the patch with a rake across two long afternoons.

Then we had a match on it that Saturday. Nobody dropped a single catch on that patch. Two people played the entire match without noticing that it had ever been there at all, which Mitch considered the best possible result.
He did not brag about it, then or since. He sat on the bench afterwards and ate his lunch and let the rest of us work out for ourselves what had changed, which took us most of the afternoon.
qs: How big is the patch?
About eight feet across.
What did Mitch consider the best result?
That two people never noticed the patch had been there.
How long did it take the others to work out what changed?
Most of the afternoon.

write.task: Is it better to fix a problem quietly or to be seen doing it? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Cab and the Cup
paras: Cam got in a cab. He had a cup and a cap.
The cab hit a bad bit of mud. The cup did not hold.
Cam got a wet cap and a wet lap. The cab man did not cut the run.
Cam got out. He had to pat the cab man on the back.
Cam got a cod for his pot. The cup is in the bin.
qs: What did Cam have with him?
A cup and a cap.
What made the cup spill?
The cab hit a bad bit of mud.
What did Cam get for his pot?
A cod.

write.task: Tell what happened in the cab, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Cab and the Cup
paras: Cam got into the cab at the corner with a cup in one hand and a cap pulled down over his hair.
The cab hit a bad patch of road about a mile in, and the cup did not hold anything like as well as he had hoped.
He arrived with a wet cap, a wet lap, and no coffee at all. The driver, to his credit, said nothing whatsoever about it.
Cam did not cut the fare or make any sort of fuss. He paid what was on the meter and thanked the man properly.
Then he went and bought himself a cod and a cob for tea instead. The cup went in the bin on the corner.
qs: How far in was the bad patch of road?
About a mile.
What did the driver do?
He said nothing whatsoever about it.
What did Cam buy instead?
A cod and a cob for tea.

write.task: Should Cam have paid the full fare? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Cab and the Cup
paras: Cam got into the cab at the corner carrying a cup in one hand and wearing a cap pulled down low over his hair, which is how he travels and has always travelled.

The cab hit a bad patch of road about a mile in — a stretch that everybody who drives it knows about and nobody has ever fixed — and the cup did not hold anything like as well as he had been quietly assuming it would.

He arrived at the other end with a wet cap, a comprehensively wet lap, and no coffee whatsoever. The driver, entirely to his credit, said not one word about any of it, either at the time or on arrival.
Cam did not attempt to cut the fare and he did not make any kind of fuss. He paid exactly what was on the meter, added something on top of it, and thanked the man properly before getting out.
Then he walked round the corner and bought himself a cod and a cob for his tea instead, which he says was the better outcome anyway. The cup went in the bin by the lights.
qs: What does everybody who drives that road know?
About the bad patch that nobody has ever fixed.
When did the driver mention it?
Not at any point — not at the time and not on arrival.
What did Cam do beyond paying the meter?
He added something on top and thanked the man properly.

write.task: Write a report on how people should behave in shared transport. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: Ken and the Kid
paras: Ken has a pet kid. The kid is not big.
The kid got in the keg bin and did not get out.
Ken had a kit bag. He got the kit out and put the kid in the bag.
Then the kid got out of the bag as well. It is a kid that can not sit.
Ken is not mad at it. He just got a lid for the keg bin.
qs: What does Ken have?
Ken has a pet kid.
Where did the kid get stuck?
In the keg bin.
What did Ken do at the end?
He got a lid for the keg bin.

write.task: Is a kid a good pet? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: Ken and the Kid
paras: Ken keeps a kid in the yard behind the house. A kid is a baby goat, and this one is about four months old.
In October it got into the keg bin head first and could not get itself back out again, which took Ken twenty minutes to sort out.
He had a kit bag in the shed. He tipped the kit out onto the bench and carried the kid back across the yard in the bag.
The kid was out of the bag before he had put it down. It is not an animal that can sit still for any length of time.
Ken is not angry about any of it. He simply bought a lid for the keg bin, which he says he should have done in the first place.
qs: How old is the kid?
About four months old.
How long did it take Ken to free it?
Twenty minutes.
What did Ken buy afterwards?
A lid for the keg bin.

write.task: Explain how to keep a young animal safe. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Ken and the Kid
paras: Ken keeps a kid in the yard behind his house. A kid is a baby goat, in case that is not obvious, and this particular one is about four months old and has no sense whatsoever.

In the middle of October it got into the keg bin head first, could not reverse out, and stood there with its back legs on the cobbles making a noise that pulled three neighbours to their gates. It took Ken the better part of twenty minutes to work it free.
He had an old kit bag hanging in the shed. He tipped the kit out of it onto the bench, carried the bag across, and got the kid into it to bring it back across the yard without it running off again.
The kid was out of the bag before Ken had finished putting it down on the ground. It is not an animal capable of sitting still for any measurable length of time, and Ken has given up expecting it to.
He is not angry about any of this. He went into town the following morning and bought a lid for the keg bin, which, as he says himself without any prompting, he should have done in the first place.
qs: What brought three neighbours to their gates?
The noise the kid made while stuck.
Why did Ken use the bag?
So the kid would not run off again on the way across.
What does Ken admit without prompting?
That he should have bought the lid in the first place.

write.task: Write the rescue from the kid's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Rock in the Sock
paras: Nick put a rock in a sock.
The sock got in the back of the deck bin. It did not come up.
Nick had to pick at it. He got it up, bit by bit.
The sock did come up. The rock did not. It is in the bin yet.
Nick had to kick the lid. Now the bin has a rock in it.
qs: What did Nick put in the sock?
He put a rock in it.
Where did the sock get caught?
In the back of the deck bin.
What is still in the bin?
The rock is still in the bin.

write.task: Tell what Nick did, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Rock in the Sock
paras: Nick put a rock in a sock in July, for a reason that made sense to him at the time and that he has since declined to explain.
The sock, with the rock still in it, got stuck right down the back of the deck box, wedged behind the hinge where nobody could reach.
He had to pick at it for most of an afternoon with a tack hammer and a length of wire, lying on his front on the decking.
The sock came out in the end. The rock did not. It is still down there behind the hinge, and it is going to stay there.
Nick has to kick the lid to get it shut now. He says the box works fine. The box does not work fine.
qs: When did Nick put the rock in the sock?
In July.
Where exactly did it get stuck?
Behind the hinge at the back of the deck box.
What does the narrator think of Nick's claim?
That the box does not work fine.

write.task: Should Nick fix the box properly? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Rock in the Sock
paras: Nick put a rock in a sock in July. There was a reason for this at the time, and it made complete sense to him, and he has since declined on four separate occasions to explain what it was.
The sock, with the rock still inside it, went down the back of the deck box and wedged itself behind the hinge, in the one position from which nothing can be retrieved by hand from any direction.
He had to pick at it for the better part of an afternoon, lying flat on his front on the decking with a tack hammer in one hand and a bent length of wire in the other, getting slowly more annoyed.
The sock came out at about five o'clock. The rock did not come out at all. It is still down there behind the hinge, and from the look of things it is going to remain there for the life of the box.

Nick has to kick the lid now to get it to shut properly. He maintains, every time anybody mentions it, that the box works perfectly well. The box does not work perfectly well, and everybody who has ever tried to close it knows that.
qs: How many times has Nick declined to explain?
Four separate occasions.
What two tools did he use?
A tack hammer and a bent length of wire.
How does the author contradict Nick?
By saying everybody who has tried to close it knows it does not work.

write.task: Is it better to fix something properly or work around it? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: Puff and the Cuff
paras: Puff is my pup. Puff is off the mat a lot.
Puff will huff and puff at the cat. The cat sits on the sill and will not get off.
Dad had a cuff of mud on his sock. Puff did it.
I had to buff the mud off the cuff. It was a lot of mud.
Puff did not huff at me. Puff had a nap on the bed.
qs: Who is Puff?
Puff is my pup.
What did Puff do to Dad's sock?
Puff got a cuff of mud on it.
Who had to buff the mud off?
I had to buff it off.

write.task: Tell what Puff did, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Puff and the Cuff
paras: Puff is my pup, and Puff is off the mat more often than on it, which is the whole problem in one sentence.
She will huff and puff at the cat for twenty minutes at a stretch. The cat sits on the window sill and does not get off, and has never once got off.
On Sunday Dad came in with a cuff of wet mud on his sock, and there was no real mystery about how it got there.
I had to buff that mud off the cuff with a stiff brush and a bit of soap, and it took most of the stuff in the cupboard.
Puff did not huff at me while I did it. She had a nap on my bed instead, which I think was her way of saying sorry.
qs: How long will Puff huff at the cat?
Twenty minutes at a stretch.
How many times has the cat got off the sill?
Never once.
What did the narrator use to buff the cuff?
A stiff brush and a bit of soap.

write.task: Should Puff be kept off the sill? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: Puff and the Cuff
paras: Puff is my pup, and she is off her mat a great deal more often than she is on it, which is really the whole difficulty stated in a single line.

She will huff and puff at the cat for twenty minutes at a stretch without any sign of getting tired of it. The cat sits on the window sill the whole time and does not get off, and in two years has never once got off.
On Sunday Dad came in from the garden with a cuff of wet mud all the way round one sock, and there was no real mystery about how it had got there, nor any serious effort to pretend otherwise.
I had to buff that mud off the cuff with a stiff brush and a bit of soap, and it used up most of the stuff in the cupboard under the sink before it finally came off clean.
Puff did not huff at me once while I was doing it. She had a long nap on my bed instead, which I have decided to take as her way of offering an apology.
qs: How long has the cat never got off the sill?
In two years.
What was not seriously attempted?
Pretending Puff had not caused the mud.
How does the narrator read the nap?
As Puff's way of offering an apology.

write.task: Write a report on looking after a young dog. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: Nell, Bill and the Well
paras: A big bell sits up on the hill.
Bill can hit the bell. Bill is ten and he is tall.
If Bill hits the bell, it will tell us all to come in.
Nell fell in the mud by the well. Nell did yell a lot.
Bill hit the bell. Nell got up. We all had a hot dish.
qs: Where does the bell sit?
Up on the hill.
What does the bell tell us?
It will tell us all to come in.
Who fell in the mud?
Nell fell in the mud by the well.

write.task: Is the bell a good way to call us in? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: Nell, Bill and the Well
paras: A big iron bell sits at the top of the hill, on a post that was sunk there long before any of us were born.
Bill is the one who rings it, because Bill is ten and tall enough to reach the rope without standing on anything.
When the bell goes, it tells all of us to come in, and we have about four minutes from the first ring to the table.
On Monday Nell fell in the mud by the well just as it rang, and the yell she let out carried further than the bell did.
Bill rang it again anyway. Nell got up, came in filthy, and still sat down to a hot dish with the rest of us.
qs: Why is Bill the one who rings it?
He is tall enough to reach the rope without standing on anything.
How long do they have from the first ring?
About four minutes.
What carried further than the bell?
The yell Nell let out.

write.task: Write the Tuesday from Nell's point of view. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: Nell, Bill and the Well
paras: A heavy iron bell sits at the very top of the hill, hung from a post that was sunk into the ground a long time before any of us were born and that nobody has ever had cause to replace.
Bill is the one who rings it, and has been for a year, because Bill is ten and is tall enough to reach the rope without standing on the bucket that everybody else still needs.
When that bell goes, it tells all of us to come in, and we have worked out that there are about four minutes between the first ring and the moment the food is actually on the table.

On Tuesday Nell fell full length in the mud by the well at the exact moment it started ringing, and the yell she let out from down there carried a good deal further across the fields than the bell itself did.

Bill rang it a second time regardless, which Nell has not forgiven. She got up, came in filthy from the elbows down, and still sat and ate a hot dish with the rest of us without saying a word about any of it.
qs: Why has nobody replaced the post?
Nobody has ever had cause to.
What does everybody else still need?
The bucket, to reach the rope.
What has Nell not forgiven?
That Bill rang the bell a second time.

write.task: Should Bill have rung it again? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: Tess and the Moss
paras: Tess has moss. The moss sits in a tin pot on a shelf.
A cat got in the pot. Now the moss is a mess.
Tess did not fuss at the cat. She did toss it off the shelf.
Tess put the moss back in the pot. She did not miss a bit of it.
The boss of the moss is Tess. The cat is not the boss.
qs: What does Tess have in the tin pot?
Tess has moss in it.
Who made the mess?
A cat got in the pot.
Who is the boss of the moss?
Tess is the boss of the moss.

write.task: Write three facts about the moss. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: Tess and the Moss
paras: Tess grows moss in a tin pot on the shelf by the back door, and she has kept that same pot going since March.
On Thursday the cat got into it with both front feet, and what had been a neat green cushion became a mess in about four seconds.
Tess did not fuss at the cat, which surprised me. She lifted it off the shelf, set it on the floor, and said nothing at all.
Then she pressed the moss back into the pot, piece by piece, and did not miss a single bit of it, and it took her the best part of an hour.
The boss of the moss, as Tess puts it, is Tess. The cat has been informed of this and has not accepted it.
qs: How long has Tess kept the pot going?
Since March.
How quickly did the moss become a mess?
In about four seconds.
How long did it take to press it back in?
The best part of an hour.

write.task: Was Tess right not to fuss at the cat? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: Tess and the Moss
paras: Tess grows moss in a tin pot on the shelf beside the back door, and she has kept that one pot alive and green since March, which is longer than most people manage with anything.
On Thursday the cat got into it with both front feet and then turned round in it, and what had been a neat green cushion became a comprehensive mess in something under four seconds.
Tess did not fuss at the cat, which genuinely surprised me and still does. She lifted it off the shelf without hurrying, set it down on the floor, and said absolutely nothing to it at all.

Then she pressed the moss back into the pot, piece by piece, working from the rim inwards, and she did not miss a single bit of it. The whole business took her the best part of an hour and she never once looked annoyed.
The boss of the moss, as Tess puts it herself, is Tess and not the cat. The cat has been informed of this arrangement on several occasions and has at no point accepted it.
qs: What is longer than most people manage?
Keeping the pot alive and green since March.
How did Tess work when pressing it back?
Piece by piece, from the rim inwards.
How has the cat responded to the arrangement?
It has at no point accepted it.

write.task: Write the Thursday from the cat's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: Buzz and Jazz
paras: A bug can buzz. The buzz of a bug is not a hum.
Dad has jazz on. The jazz has a buzz in it as well.
I had a fizz in a cup. The fizz did buzz on my lip.
The fuzz on the bug is red. The fuzz on my cap is not red.
Dad put the jazz up. All I can get is buzz, buzz, buzz.
qs: What can a bug do?
A bug can buzz.
What did the fizz do on my lip?
The fizz did buzz on my lip.
What colour is the fuzz on the bug?
The fuzz on the bug is red.

write.task: Tell what you can hear in this story, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Buzz and Jazz
paras: A bug can buzz, and the buzz a bug makes is not a hum, whatever my brother says about it.
Dad had jazz on all Saturday, and there is a buzz in the jazz as well, down in the bass where the speaker cone has gone.
I had a glass of fizz at lunch, and the fizz buzzed against my lip in a way I liked more than I expected to.
The fuzz on the bug by the window is a dark red. The fuzz on my winter cap is grey, and the bug is winning.
Dad turned the jazz up after that. For the rest of the afternoon the only thing in that house was buzz, buzz and more buzz.
qs: What does the narrator's brother think?
That a bug's buzz is a hum.
Where is the buzz in the jazz?
Down in the bass, where the speaker cone has gone.
What colour is the fuzz on the cap?
Grey.

write.task: Explain what makes a buzzing sound. Group your ideas and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Buzz and Jazz
paras: A bug can buzz, and the buzz that a bug actually makes is not a hum, whatever my brother may say about it and however confidently he says it.

Dad had jazz on for the whole of Saturday, and there is a buzz in that jazz as well, down in the bass register, where the cone in the left speaker has gone and nobody has done anything about it for three years.

I had a tall glass of fizz at lunch and the fizz buzzed against my lip in a way that I liked considerably more than I had expected to, and I sat there for some time not drinking it in order to keep that going.
The fuzz on the bug by the window is a dark red that is almost brown in the right light. The fuzz on my winter cap is a flat grey, and on any fair comparison the bug is winning by a distance.
Dad turned the jazz up after lunch and left it there. For the entire rest of the afternoon the only thing available in that house, in any room of it, was buzz and buzz and more buzz.
qs: How long has the speaker cone been left?
Three years.
Why did the narrator stop drinking?
To keep the fizz buzzing against the lip.
How does the bug compare with the cap?
The bug is winning by a distance.

write.task: Is loud music at home fair on everybody else? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: Clem and the Clam Club
paras: Clem has a club. The club is just for kids on his block.
At the club we clap when a kid wins a game.
Clem has a clock on a clip by the back step. The clock has a crack in it.
The club met at six. Clem did clip a note on the box by the gate.
Then we had a clam dish. Clem did not clap for that.
qs: Who is the club for?
The club is just for kids on his block.
What is wrong with the clock?
The clock has a crack in it.
What did Clem not clap for?
Clem did not clap for the clam dish.

write.task: Tell what happened at the club, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Clem and the Clam Club
paras: Clem runs a club for the kids on his block, and it has met on the same step every week since the clocks changed.
We clap at the club whenever anybody wins a game, which Clem insists on, and which took the rest of us a while to get used to.
There is a clock on a clip by the back step with a crack right across the glass. It still keeps time. Clem will not replace it.
The club met at six on Friday. Clem had clipped a note to the box by the gate telling everybody so, in handwriting nobody can read.
Then we had clam chowder, which Clem had made himself. Nobody clapped. Clem did not clap for it, and he had made it.
qs: How long has the club met on the same step?
Since the clocks changed.
Why will Clem not replace the clock?
It still keeps time even with the crack.
Who clapped for the clam chowder?
Nobody, not even Clem, who made it.

write.task: Should everybody clap when somebody wins? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: Clem and the Clam Club
paras: Clem runs a club for the children on his block, and it has met on the same back step every single week since the clocks changed, in all weathers and with no exceptions that anybody can remember.
We clap at that club whenever anybody wins a game of anything, which is a rule Clem insists on absolutely, and which took the rest of us the better part of a month to stop finding strange.

There is a clock on a clip by the back step with a crack running right across the glass from one corner to the other. It still keeps perfect time, and for that reason Clem will not hear any suggestion of replacing it.
The club met at six on Friday. Clem had clipped a note to the box by the gate to tell everybody, written in handwriting that nobody present has ever been able to read without help from Clem himself.

Afterwards we had clam chowder, which Clem had made from scratch that afternoon. Nobody clapped for it. Clem did not clap for it either, and Clem had made it, which tells you most of what you need to know.
qs: How long did the clapping rule take to feel normal?
The better part of a month.
Why does the cracked clock stay?
Because it still keeps perfect time.
What does Clem not clapping tell you?
That even the cook knew the chowder was poor.

write.task: Write a report on how to run a club for children. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Flag on the Flat Rock
paras: Flip has a flag. The flag is red with a flat black line on it.
Flip put the flag up on a flat rock by the shed.
A gust of wind did flip the flag flat. It fell off the rock.
A flock of ducks sat on it. The flag got wet and did flop in the mud.
Flip did not flop. He got the flag up and set a stone on it. The flag has not fled yet.
qs: What does the flag look like?
It is red with a flat black line on it.
What did the wind do?
It did flip the flag flat off the rock.
What sat on the flag?
A flock of ducks sat on it.

write.task: Was the flat rock a good spot for the flag? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Flag on the Flat Rock
paras: Flip's flag is red with a flat black line across it, and she made it herself out of an old sheet in about two hours.
She put the flag up on the flat rock by the shed, which is the highest thing in the garden and the obvious place for it.
On Sunday a gust of wind flipped the flag flat and took the whole thing off the rock and into the grass.
A flock of ducks came over from the pond and sat on it, and by the time we got there the flag was wet and flopping in the mud.
Flip did not flop. She washed it, dried it, put it back up, and set a stone on the corner. The flag has not fled since.
qs: What did Flip make the flag from?
An old sheet, in about two hours.
Why is the flat rock the obvious place?
It is the highest thing in the garden.
What stopped the flag blowing off again?
A stone set on the corner.

write.task: Write the Sunday from the ducks' point of view. Use time-order words and describe what they could see.

g4.title: The Flag on the Flat Rock
paras: Flip's flag is red with a flat black line running across the middle of it, and she made the whole thing herself out of an old bed sheet in a little under two hours one wet afternoon.
She put the flag up on the flat rock by the shed, which is the highest point in the garden by a clear margin and therefore the only place anybody seriously considered putting it.
On Sunday morning a single gust of wind flipped the flag flat against the rock and then took the entire thing, pole and all, off the top and down into the long grass at the back.

A flock of ducks came over from the pond within the hour and sat on it, and by the time any of us got out there the flag was soaked and flopping about in the mud with a duck still standing on one corner.
Flip did not flop. She washed it, dried it on the line, put it back up on the rock the same evening and set a heavy stone on the lower corner to hold it. The flag has not fled from that rock since.
qs: How long did the flag take to make?
A little under two hours.
What did the gust take off the rock?
The entire flag, pole and all.
What was still happening when they arrived?
A duck was standing on one corner of the flag.

write.task: Explain how to put up something outdoors so it stays. Organise it into steps and connect your ideas.

g2.title: Stan and the Stump
paras: Stan has a stump out the back. It is all that is left of an elm.
He must get it out. He did his best with a stick, but the stick just broke.
Then Stan got a stone and a post. He did stand on the post and shove.
The stump did not stop him. It came up fast and Stan sat down in the mud.
Stan is a mess of dust and mud. The stump is in the bin at last.
qs: What is the stump left from?
It is all that is left of an elm.
What did Stan try first?
He did his best with a stick, but it broke.
Where is the stump at the end?
The stump is in the bin at last.

write.task: Tell how Stan got the stump out, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Stan and the Stump
paras: Stan has a stump at the back of his garden, which is all that is left of an elm that came down in a storm before he moved in.
He had made up his mind to get it out. He started with a stick, did his best with it for most of an hour, and the stick broke in two.
Then he fetched a stone and a fence post, stood the post against the stump, rested it on the stone, and leaned on the far end as hard as he could.
The stump did not stop him for long. It came up far faster than he expected and Stan sat straight down in the mud behind it.
He stood up a mess of dust and wet soil, with the stump beside him. It went in the bin that afternoon, and the hole is still there.
qs: What happened to the elm?
It came down in a storm before Stan moved in.
How did Stan use the stone?
He rested the fence post on it and leaned on the far end.
What is still there?
The hole where the stump was.

write.task: Explain how a lever works. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Stan and the Stump
paras: Stan has a stump at the far end of his back garden, and it is all that is left of a large elm that came down in a storm a good while before he moved into the house.

He had made up his mind to get the stump out of the ground himself. He started with a stick, did his best with it for the better part of an hour, achieved nothing whatsoever, and the stick eventually broke cleanly in two.

Then he went and fetched a stone and an old fence post. He stood the post against the stump, rested the post across the stone to make a lever of it, and leaned the whole of his weight steadily on the far end.
The stump did not stop him for long after that. It came up a great deal faster than he had allowed for, the post went with it, and Stan sat straight down in the wet mud behind the hole it left.

He stood up a mess of dust and soil from the waist down, with the stump lying beside him and the post still under it. The stump went in the bin that same afternoon. The hole is still there and shows no sign of being filled.
qs: How long did the stick last?
The better part of an hour, before breaking cleanly in two.
What turned the post into a lever?
Resting it across the stone.
What does the hole show no sign of?
Being filled.

write.task: Should Stan have hired somebody instead? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: Max, the Fox and the Box
paras: Max has a big box. The box sat by the shed.
A fox got in the box. The fox did not get up.
Max did fix the box. He cut a gap in the top.
The fox did run! Max had six bits of mud on his hat.
Max did wax the box. The fox can not get in. The fox sits by the box.
qs: What got in the box?
A fox got in the box.
What did Max cut in the top?
He cut a gap in the top.
Where does the fox sit at the end?
The fox sits by the box.

write.task: Tell what the fox did, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Max, the Fox and the Box
paras: Max keeps a big wooden box by the shed, and he has kept it there since the spring without ever quite saying what it is for.
In October a fox got into it overnight and then could not get back out, and it was still in there at six in the morning.
Max fixed the box the same day. He cut a gap in the top, wide enough for a fox and too narrow for the lid to sag.
The fox went out through the gap at once. Max came back in with six separate patches of mud on his hat and did not explain any of them.
He waxed the box afterwards so the rain runs off it. The fox cannot get in any more and sits beside it most evenings instead.
qs: How long has the box been by the shed?
Since the spring.
Why was the gap not cut wider?
So the lid would not sag.
What does the fox do now?
It sits beside the box most evenings.

write.task: Explain how to help an animal that is stuck. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Max, the Fox and the Box
paras: Max keeps a large wooden box by the shed at the bottom of his garden, and it has stood in that exact spot since the spring without him ever quite explaining to anybody what he keeps in it.

In the middle of October a fox got into the box overnight, somehow, and then found that it could not get back out again, and it was still sitting in there at six o'clock the following morning when Max went down.

Max fixed the box the same afternoon. He cut a gap in the top, measured so that it was wide enough for a fox to pass through comfortably and still too narrow for the lid to sag in the middle under its own weight.

The fox went out through the gap more or less at once and did not look back. Max came back into the house with six separate patches of mud on his hat and offered no explanation whatsoever for any of them.

He waxed the whole box afterwards so that the rain runs off the top instead of sitting on it. The fox cannot get in any more, and now sits beside the box most evenings as if it still considers the matter open.
qs: What has Max never explained?
What he keeps in the box.
How was the gap measured?
Wide enough for a fox, narrow enough that the lid would not sag.
What does the fox's behaviour suggest?
That it still considers the matter open.

write.task: Should wild animals be helped out of trouble? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: Quin and the Quick Quack
paras: Quin has a duck. The duck can quack.
The quack is quick and it is big. Quack! Quack! Quack!
Mom had a quiz on the bus at ten. She did not quit it.
The duck did quack at the quiz. Mom did quit it.
Quin had to put the duck in a pen. The duck is quick, but the pen is big.
qs: What can the duck do?
The duck can quack.
What did Mom have at ten?
Mom had a quiz on the bus.
Why did Mom quit the quiz?
The duck did quack at it.

write.task: Should the duck go in a pen? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: Quin and the Quick Quack
paras: Quin has a duck, and the duck can quack in a way that carries across three gardens without any effort at all.
The quack is quick as well as loud. It comes in bursts of three, always three, and it starts at about half past five.
Mom was doing a radio quiz on the bus at ten on Saturday, and she had got seven questions right and had no plan to quit.
The duck quacked for most of the next question, which was the only one she did not hear properly. Mom quit the quiz and has not entered another one since.
Quin has had to put the duck in a pen at the bottom of the garden. The duck is quick, but the pen is big, and the two of them have reached an understanding.
qs: How far does the quack carry?
Across three gardens.
How many quacks come in a burst?
Always three.
How many questions had Mom got right?
Seven.

write.task: Write the Saturday morning from Mom's point of view. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: Quin and the Quick Quack
paras: Quin has a duck, and that duck can quack in a way that carries clean across three gardens and a road without any apparent effort on its part whatsoever.

The quack is quick as well as loud, which is the part people underestimate. It comes in bursts of three, always exactly three, and the first burst arrives at about half past five in the morning regardless of the season.

Mom was doing a radio quiz on the bus at ten o'clock on Saturday, with the window open because the morning was warm. She had answered seven questions correctly in a row and had no intention of quitting at any point.

The duck quacked steadily through most of the eighth question, which was the only one she did not hear properly. Mom quit the quiz there and then and has not entered another one of any kind since that morning.

Quin has since had to put the duck in a pen at the bottom of the garden. The duck is quick and the pen is large, and after some early disagreement the two of them appear to have reached a workable understanding.
qs: What do people underestimate about the quack?
That it is quick as well as loud.
Why was the window open?
Because the morning was warm.
What happened after the early disagreement?
The duck and the pen reached a workable understanding.

write.task: Write a report on keeping ducks near neighbours. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Rabbit in the Basket
paras: Pat has a rabbit. The rabbit naps in a basket on the mat.
A magnet fell in the basket. The rabbit did not like it one bit.
Pat had a napkin in her hand. She put the napkin on top of the magnet.
The rabbit sat up fast. It can not stand a napkin.
Pat had to admit it. The rabbit is the boss of that basket.
qs: Where does the rabbit nap?
In a basket on the mat.
What fell in the basket?
A magnet fell in the basket.
Who is the boss of the basket?
The rabbit is the boss of the basket.

write.task: Tell what happened in the basket, in order. Use first, next, and last.
