g3.title: The Rabbit in the Basket
paras: Pat has a rabbit, and the rabbit naps in a flat basket on the mat by the back door for most of the afternoon.
On Sunday a magnet fell off the fridge and landed in the basket, and the rabbit did not like it one bit.
Pat happened to have a napkin in her hand, so she dropped the napkin over the magnet to hide it.
The rabbit sat up faster than she has ever seen it move. It cannot stand a napkin and never has been able to.
Pat has had to admit it. She is not the one who decides what happens in that basket, and she has stopped pretending otherwise.
qs: How long does the rabbit nap?
For most of the afternoon.
Why did Pat use the napkin?
To hide the magnet in the basket.
What has Pat stopped pretending?
That she decides what happens in the basket.

write.task: Should pets be allowed to decide things? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Rabbit in the Basket
paras: Pat has a rabbit, and that rabbit naps in a flat basket on the mat by the back door for the better part of every afternoon, in a spot it chose itself and has never been persuaded to leave.
On Sunday a magnet fell off the front of the fridge and landed in the basket beside the rabbit, and the rabbit did not like it one bit and made that perfectly plain within about a second.
Pat happened to be holding a napkin at the time, so she dropped the napkin over the magnet to hide it, which struck her as a sensible and rather clever thing to do in the moment.

The rabbit sat bolt upright faster than Pat has ever seen it move in three years. It cannot stand a napkin, has never been able to stand a napkin, and the magnet had in fact stopped being the problem.
Pat has had to admit the whole thing. She is not the one who decides what happens inside that basket, she has not been for some time, and she has finally stopped pretending to visitors that she is.
qs: How did the rabbit choose its spot?
It chose the basket itself and has never left.
Why did the napkin make things worse?
The rabbit cannot stand a napkin, so the magnet stopped being the problem.
What has Pat stopped telling visitors?
That she decides what happens in the basket.

write.task: Write a report on how to keep a rabbit comfortable. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Velvet Helmet
paras: Ben has a helmet. The helmet has velvet on the inside.
Ben has it on when he gets on his bike. He will not let it off at all.
An insect got in the helmet. Ben did not expect that.
The insect sat on the velvet. Ben did not get upset.
He let the insect exit. Then the helmet went back on.
qs: What is inside the helmet?
The helmet has velvet on the inside.
What got in the helmet?
An insect got in the helmet.
What did Ben let the insect do?
He let the insect exit.

write.task: Write three facts about the helmet. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Velvet Helmet
paras: Ben has a helmet with velvet lining the inside of it, which he says is the best part and which nobody else can see.
He puts it on whenever he gets on his bike, and he will not let it off his head between the gate and the end of the lane.
On Wednesday an insect got into the helmet while it hung on the handlebar, and Ben did not expect to find it there.
The insect was sitting on the velvet when he lifted it. Ben did not get upset, and he did not shake the helmet to dislodge it.
He carried it to the hedge and let the insect exit in its own time. Then he put the helmet back on and rode off.
qs: Why can nobody see the best part?
The velvet is on the inside.
How did the insect get in?
The helmet hung on the handlebar and the insect got into it.
Where did Ben let the insect out?
At the hedge, in its own time.

write.task: Write the Wednesday from the insect's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what it could feel.

g4.title: The Velvet Helmet
paras: Ben has a helmet with velvet lining the whole of the inside of it, which he will tell anybody is the best part of the helmet, and which not one person other than Ben has ever actually seen.
He puts it on every time he gets on his bike without being reminded, and he will not let it off his head at any point between the gate and the far end of the lane, whatever the weather is doing.
On Wednesday an insect got into the helmet while it was hanging by its strap from the handlebar outside the shop, and Ben did not expect to find anything in there at all when he picked it up.

The insect was sitting on the velvet when he lifted the helmet to his head and stopped. Ben did not get upset about it, and, which is the part I respect, he did not shake the helmet to get the insect out.
He carried the whole helmet across to the hedge, held it still, and let the insect exit in its own time, which took rather longer than he had to spare. Then he put the helmet on and rode off.
qs: How many people have seen the velvet?
Only Ben.
Where was the helmet hanging?
By its strap from the handlebar outside the shop.
What does the narrator respect?
That Ben did not shake the helmet to get the insect out.

write.task: Is it worth being late to avoid harming an insect? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Picnic and the Kitten
paras: We had a picnic on the grass by the pigpen.
A kitten sat on the rug with us. The kitten did not sit still.
It did insist on the ham. We did not let it in the tin.
In the end the kitten got a bit of ham. We did admit it did win.
Then it went in the pigpen. That is a kitten that will not quit.
qs: Where did they have the picnic?
On the grass by the pigpen.
What did the kitten insist on?
The kitten did insist on the ham.
Where did the kitten go at the end?
It went in the pigpen.

write.task: Should the kitten have got the ham? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Picnic and the Kitten
paras: We had the picnic on the grass by the pigpen, which is not where anybody would choose, but it is the only flat bit.
A kitten came over from the next farm and sat on the rug with us, and it did not sit still for one minute of the afternoon.
It insisted on the ham. We did not let it near the tin, and it tried six different routes to get there.
In the end the kitten got a bit of ham, because my sister gave it one, and we all had to admit it had won fairly.
Then it walked off into the pigpen as if that had been the plan all along. That is a kitten that does not quit.
qs: Why have the picnic by the pigpen?
It is the only flat bit of ground.
How many routes did the kitten try?
Six different routes.
How did the kitten finally get the ham?
The narrator's sister gave it one.

write.task: Write the picnic from the kitten's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what it could smell.

g4.title: The Picnic and the Kitten
paras: We had the picnic out on the grass beside the pigpen, which is not a spot anybody would pick on its merits, but it is the only genuinely flat ground on that side of the farm.
A kitten came over the wall from the next farm and sat down on the rug with us as though it had been invited, and it did not sit still for one single minute of the entire afternoon.

It insisted on the ham from the start. We did not let it anywhere near the tin, and over the course of about half an hour it tried six distinctly different routes to get at it, each one more inventive than the last.
In the end the kitten got a decent bit of ham, because my sister handed it one while the rest of us were looking elsewhere, and we all had to admit afterwards that it had won the thing fairly.
Then it walked off into the pigpen without hurrying, exactly as if that had been the plan from the beginning and the ham had merely been a stop along the way. That is a kitten that does not quit.
qs: Why is that ground used despite the pigpen?
It is the only genuinely flat ground on that side of the farm.
How did the routes change?
Each one was more inventive than the last.
How did the kitten leave?
Without hurrying, as if it had been the plan all along.

write.task: Write a report on how cats get what they want. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Puppet in the Bucket
paras: Russ has a puppet. The puppet sits in a bucket by the step.
At sunset Russ gets the puppet up. He puts it on his hand.
The puppet has a button for a nose and a bit of rug on top.
Russ did drop a muffin in the bucket. The puppet got upset.
Russ had to undo the lid and get the muffin up. Until then, no puppet.
qs: Where does the puppet sit?
In a bucket by the step.
What does the puppet have for a nose?
The puppet has a button for a nose.
What did Russ drop in the bucket?
Russ did drop a muffin in the bucket.

write.task: Tell what Russ did, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Puppet in the Bucket
paras: Russ keeps his puppet in a bucket by the back step, with the lid on, because that is where the puppet lives and there is no arguing about it.
At sunset he takes the puppet out and puts it on his hand, and from then until bedtime the puppet does most of the talking in that house.
The puppet has a button for a nose and a strip of old rug for hair, and Russ made both of those himself when he was five.
On Sunday he dropped a muffin into the bucket by accident and put the lid back on without noticing, and the puppet, he says, got extremely upset.
Russ had to undo the lid and dig the muffin out from under the puppet. Until that was done, there was no puppet and no talking at all.
qs: Why does the puppet live in the bucket?
That is where it lives and there is no arguing about it.
Who made the nose and hair?
Russ made both himself when he was five.
What stopped the talking?
The muffin in the bucket, until it was dug out.

write.task: Is it good for a child to have a puppet speak for them? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Puppet in the Bucket
paras: Russ keeps his puppet in a bucket by the back step with the lid pressed down on it, because that is where the puppet lives, and there has never been any serious arguing about the arrangement from anybody.

At sunset he lifts the puppet out and puts it on his hand, and from that moment until he goes to bed the puppet does a clear majority of the talking in that house, including most of the talking that is addressed to adults.
The puppet has a button for a nose and a narrow strip of old rug for hair, and Russ made both of those himself when he was five, which is a fact he mentions to every single person who meets it.

On Sunday he dropped a muffin into the bucket entirely by accident and put the lid back down on top of it without noticing he had done so, and the puppet, by his own account, got extremely upset about the whole business.
Russ had to undo the lid and dig the muffin out from underneath the puppet with a spoon. Until that job was finished there was no puppet on his hand and, as a direct result, no talking of any kind.
qs: Who does the puppet mostly talk to?
Everybody, including adults.
What does Russ tell everyone who meets the puppet?
That he made the nose and hair himself at five.
What did he dig the muffin out with?
A spoon.

write.task: Write the Sunday from the puppet's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Cupcake Mistake
paras: Jane will make a cupcake for the bake sale.
She did make a mistake. She left the egg in the box on the side.
The cupcake came up flat as a plate. It did not taste bad, but it was flat.
Dad had the flat cupcake. He did not make a face.
Jane will make the next cupcake with the egg in it. A mistake is not big if you can fix it.
qs: What is Jane making the cupcake for?
For the bake sale.
What mistake did she make?
She left the egg in the box.
What did the cupcake come up like?
It came up flat as a plate.

write.task: Tell what went wrong with the cupcake, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Cupcake Mistake
paras: Jane set out to make a dozen cupcakes for the bake sale on Saturday, and she started at seven in the morning to be safe.
She made one mistake. The egg stayed in its box on the side, and she did not notice until the tray was already in the oven.
The cupcakes came up flat as a plate, every one of them. They did not taste bad in the slightest, but there was no getting round how flat they were.
Dad ate two of them and did not make a face, and then asked for a third, which told Jane more than anything he said.
She is making the next batch with the egg in. A mistake is not a large one if you can see exactly where it happened and fix it.
qs: How many cupcakes was Jane making?
A dozen.
When did she notice the egg?
Not until the tray was already in the oven.
What told Jane the most?
That Dad asked for a third one.

write.task: Are mistakes a good way to learn? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Cupcake Mistake
paras: Jane set out to make a dozen cupcakes for the bake sale on Saturday, and she started mixing at seven in the morning so that there would be time to make a second batch if anything went badly wrong.

She made exactly one mistake in the whole process. The egg stayed sitting in its box on the side by the window, and she did not notice it there until the tray was already in the oven with the door shut.

The cupcakes came up as flat as a plate, every single one of the twelve, with no rise in them at all. They did not taste bad in the slightest, which surprised everybody, but there was no getting round quite how flat they were.
Dad ate two of them without making any kind of face, which he is good at, and then asked for a third, which told Jane considerably more than anything he actually said about them did.

She is making the next batch with the egg in it and has moved the egg box to the middle of the table. A mistake is not a large one if you can see exactly where it happened and put it right the following week.
qs: Why did Jane start at seven?
So there would be time for a second batch if anything went wrong.
Where had the egg box been sitting?
On the side by the window.
What has Jane changed for next time?
She has moved the egg box to the middle of the table.

write.task: Write a report on avoiding mistakes when baking. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Invite Inside
paras: Mike sent me an invite. The invite said to come inside at five.
I got to his home at five. The sunshine was still on the step.
Mike had a pile of games inside. We did not pick just one.
We did combine two games. It did take us a bit of time.
At sunset I went home. Mike did invite me to come back on the ninth.
qs: What did the invite say?
It said to come inside at five.
What did Mike have inside?
Mike had a pile of games.
What did they do with two games?
They did combine two games.

write.task: Is it a good idea to combine two games? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Invite Inside
paras: Mike sent me an invite in the post, which nobody does any more, and the invite said to come inside at five rather than knock.
I got to his home at five exactly. The sunshine was still lying along the step and the door was already standing open.
Mike had a pile of games stacked inside the front room, about nine of them, and we could not pick just one between us.
So we did the obvious thing and combined two of them, which took a bit of time to work out and a good deal longer to play.
At sunset I walked home. Mike invited me back on the ninth, and I think the combined game is now simply the game.
qs: What does nobody do any more?
Send an invite in the post.
How many games were in the pile?
About nine.
What has the combined game become?
Simply the game they play.

write.task: Write the afternoon from Mike's point of view. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Invite Inside
paras: Mike sent me an invite through the post, on actual card, which is a thing that nobody does any more, and the invite said to come inside at five rather than knocking and waiting on the step like a stranger.

I arrived at his home at five exactly, because the invite had said five. The sunshine was still lying in a stripe along the front step and the door was already standing open, which I decided to treat as instruction enough.

Mike had a pile of games stacked up inside the front room, nine of them at least, and between the two of us we could not pick a single one, having given it a serious and genuinely fair attempt for some minutes.
So we did the obvious thing instead and combined two of them into one, which took a bit of time to work out on paper and then a very great deal longer to actually play through to the end.

At sunset I walked home the long way. Mike invited me back on the ninth before I had got to the gate, and I am fairly sure the combined game has now simply become the game, and that the other seven are finished.
qs: What was the invite made of?
Actual card, sent through the post.
Why did he walk straight in?
The door was open, which he treated as instruction enough.
What does he think has happened to the other games?
That they are finished, because the combined game is now the game.

write.task: Explain how to invent a new game from two old ones. Organise it into steps and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Note in the Envelope
paras: Mom got an envelope in the post. Inside it was a note.
The note was from Rose. It said Rose will come home in a bit.
Mom did not sit at home and mope. She did a lot of jobs.
At six the bell went. Rose was on the step with a big stone in her hand.
The stone was from the hillside by her home. Mom put it on the stove top. It is on the stove still.
qs: What was inside the envelope?
Inside it was a note.
Who was the note from?
The note was from Rose.
Where did Mom put the stone?
Mom put it on the stove top.

write.task: Write three facts about the stone. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Note in the Envelope
paras: Mom got an envelope in the post on Monday with no stamp on it and a note folded twice inside.
The note was from Rose, and all it said was that Rose would be home before the end of the week, which was more than we had been told in a month.
Mom did not sit at home and mope about it for the rest of the week. She did every job in the house that had been waiting since spring.
At six on Friday the bell went, and Rose was standing on the step with a bag over one shoulder and a large stone in her hand.
The stone had come from the hillside above the place she had been. Mom put it on the stove top, where it still sits, and nobody has suggested moving it.
qs: What was odd about the envelope?
It had no stamp on it.
What did Mom do instead of moping?
Every job in the house that had been waiting since spring.
Where had the stone come from?
The hillside above the place Rose had been.

write.task: Write the Friday from Rose's point of view. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Note in the Envelope
paras: Mom got an envelope in the post on Monday morning with no stamp on it anywhere, which means somebody put it through the door by hand, and a single note folded twice over inside.

The note was from Rose, and the whole of what it said was that Rose would be home before the end of the week. That was a good deal more information than we had been given at any point in the previous month.

Mom did not sit at home and mope about it for four days. She went through the house and did every job in it that had been waiting since the spring, including two that had been waiting a great deal longer than that.

At six o'clock on Friday the bell went, and Rose was standing on the step with a bag over one shoulder, mud to the knee, and a large grey stone held in her free hand as though it were perfectly normal luggage.

The stone had come off the hillside above the place she had been staying. Mom put it on the stove top the same evening, where it sits to this day, and in all that time nobody has once suggested moving it.
qs: What does the missing stamp mean?
Somebody put the envelope through the door by hand.
What did Mom do beyond the spring jobs?
Two jobs that had been waiting a great deal longer.
How did Rose hold the stone?
As though it were perfectly normal luggage.

write.task: Why do people keep objects from places they have been? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: Undo, Unpack, Unlock
paras: Mom will unpack the box. I will undo the tape on top.
The tape will not undo. It is stuck fast and it is unkind tape.
Dad got a blade and did unlock the lid. He said it was unsafe for me to do it.
Inside was a lot of fun stuff. It was not a mess at all.
Mom will unpack the rest in the sun. I will undo the next box.
qs: What will Mom do with the box?
Mom will unpack the box.
Why did Dad use a blade?
The tape would not undo and it was unsafe for a child.
What was inside?
A lot of fun stuff, not a mess.

write.task: Tell how they got the box open, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Undo, Unpack, Unlock
paras: Mom said she would unpack the box if I would undo the tape across the top of it, which seemed like a fair split at the time.
The tape would not undo. It had been wound round four times and then folded under itself, and it is unkind tape, whoever made it.
Dad came in with a blade and unlocked the lid in about a second. He said it was unsafe for me to use and he was probably right about that.
Inside was a lot of very good stuff and no rubbish at all, which is unusual for a box that has sat in a shed since before I was born.
Mom will unpack the rest of it out in the sun on Saturday. I have been told I may undo the next box, which I take as progress.
qs: What was the split they agreed?
Mom would unpack and the narrator would undo the tape.
How was the tape wound?
Round four times and then folded under itself.
How long had the box been in the shed?
Since before the narrator was born.

write.task: Should children be allowed to use sharp tools? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: Undo, Unpack, Unlock
paras: Mom said that she would unpack the box if I would undo the tape across the top of it, which seemed like a perfectly fair split of the work at the moment it was proposed and much less fair about a minute later.

The tape would not undo. It had been wound right round the box four separate times and then folded back under itself at the end, and it is unkind tape, whoever it was that made it and whatever they thought they were doing.

Dad came in with a blade and unlocked the lid in something close to a second, having watched me fail at it for a while first. He said the blade was unsafe for me to be using, and he was almost certainly right about that.
Inside the box was a lot of genuinely good stuff and almost nothing that could fairly be called junk, which is unusual for a box that has sat unopened in a shed since a point before I was born.
Mom will unpack the rest of it out in the sun on Saturday if the weather holds. I have been told that I may undo the next box myself, blade and all, which I am choosing to take as progress.
qs: When did the split stop seeming fair?
About a minute after it was proposed.
What did Dad do before using the blade?
He watched the narrator fail at it for a while.
What has the narrator been allowed next time?
To undo the next box, blade and all.

write.task: Write a report on opening and storing things safely. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: Nonstop Nonsense
paras: Dad can talk nonstop. It is a lot of nonsense, but it is fun.
Mom has a nonstick pan. She makes us a nonfat dish in it.
The mat in the tub is nonslip. Dad still fell in the tub.
He got up and did talk nonstop at us until bed.
Mom said it was nonsense. Dad said it was nonstop fun. It was both.
qs: How does Dad talk?
Dad can talk nonstop.
What does Mom make in the nonstick pan?
She makes us a nonfat dish.
What happened in the tub?
Dad still fell, even on the nonslip mat.

write.task: Is Dad's talk nonsense or fun? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: Nonstop Nonsense
paras: Dad can talk nonstop from the moment he comes in until the moment he sits down, and most of it is nonsense, and all of it is good.
Mom has a nonstick pan that she will not let anybody else wash, and she makes a nonfat dish in it on Fridays that is better than it sounds.
The mat in the tub is nonslip and it says so on the label. Dad went over in that tub on Sunday regardless of the label.
He got straight back up and talked nonstop about it the whole way to bed, which is how we all came to hear the story four times.
Mom said the whole business was nonsense. Dad said it was nonstop entertainment. On the evidence available, both of them were right.
qs: When does Dad talk nonstop?
From the moment he comes in until he sits down.
Who may wash the nonstick pan?
Only Mom.
How many times did they hear the story?
Four times.

write.task: Explain how to stay safe in a bathroom. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Nonstop Nonsense
paras: Dad can talk nonstop from the moment he gets in through the front door until the moment he finally sits down in his chair, and the clear majority of it is nonsense, and all of it without exception is good to listen to.

Mom has a nonstick pan that she will not let any other person in the house wash, dry, or move, and she makes a nonfat dish in it on Tuesdays that is a great deal better than the description of it ever manages to sound.

The mat in the tub is nonslip and the label on the underside of it says so in three places. Dad went over in that tub on Sunday evening regardless of the label and of everything the label is supposed to prevent.

He got straight back up, entirely unhurt, and talked nonstop about the incident the whole way to bed, which is how every member of this family came to hear the complete story of it four separate times in one evening.

Mom said afterwards that the whole business was nonsense from start to finish. Dad said it had been nonstop entertainment for everybody. On the evidence actually available to me, both of them were right.
qs: What may nobody else do with the pan?
Wash, dry, or move it.
Where does the label say nonslip?
In three places on the underside.
What is the narrator's verdict?
That both Mom and Dad were right.

write.task: Write the Sunday evening from Mom's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Mild Wild Cat
paras: The cat in the shed is wild. It is not a mild cat at all.
No child can pet it. No child ever has.
It hunts in the wild grass by the back wall.
Last week a child left fish on the step. The wild cat did eat it.
Now the wild cat is a bit more mild. It sits by the step when that child is there.
qs: What kind of cat is in the shed?
It is a wild cat, not a mild one.
Where does it hunt?
In the wild grass by the back wall.
What did a child leave on the step?
A child left fish on the step.

write.task: Tell how the cat changed, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Mild Wild Cat
paras: The cat that lives in the shed is wild, properly wild, and nothing about it is mild in the way a house cat is mild.
No child has ever petted it, and the children on this road have between them tried every method anybody has suggested.
It hunts in the wild grass along the back wall at dusk, and it is very good at it, which is why it has never needed us.
Last week a child left a bit of fish on the step and went away, and the wild cat came down and ate the lot of it.
The cat is a shade milder now. It sits near the step at the same time each evening when that particular child is in the garden, and no closer.
qs: What have the children tried?
Every method anybody has suggested for petting it.
Why has the cat never needed people?
It is very good at hunting in the wild grass.
How close does it sit now?
Near the step and no closer.

write.task: Should people feed a wild cat? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Mild Wild Cat
paras: The cat that lives in the shed at the end of the garden is wild, properly and genuinely wild, and there is nothing mild about it in the way that a house cat is mild when it has had its tea.

No child has ever petted it, not once, and the children on this road have between them tried every single method that anybody has ever suggested to them, including several that were never going to work.
It hunts in the wild grass along the back wall at dusk every evening, and it is extremely good at it, which is the whole reason it has never at any point needed anything from any of us.
Last week one child left a bit of fish on the step and then deliberately walked away and sat down at a distance, and the wild cat came down off the shed roof and ate the entire lot of it.

The cat is a shade milder now than it was. It sits near that step at the same time every evening when that one particular child is out in the garden, and at no point has it ever come any closer than that.
qs: What made the child's method different?
The child left the fish and deliberately walked away to a distance.
Where did the cat come down from?
The shed roof.
What has not changed?
It has never come closer than near the step.

write.task: Write a report on wild animals that live near people. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Old Cold Shed
paras: Dad has an old shed. In the fall it gets cold in there.
He told me to hold the box of nails while he sold the rest of them.
In the box was a bit of gold. It was cold to hold.
Dad was bold. He told Mom he had sold the old shed as well.
Mom told him the old shed was hers. Dad did not hold on to that plan.
qs: When does the shed get cold?
In the fall it gets cold in there.
What was in the box?
A bit of gold that was cold to hold.
What did Mom tell Dad?
Mom told him the old shed was hers.

write.task: Should Dad have sold the shed? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Old Cold Shed
paras: Dad has an old shed at the side of the house, and in the fall it gets cold enough in there to see your breath by nine in the morning.
He told me to hold the box of nails for him while he sold off the rest of the stock to a man who had driven over for it.
At the bottom of that box was a thin piece of gold, which nobody has explained, and which was cold to hold even through a glove.
Dad was bold about the whole afternoon. He told Mom he had sold the old shed to the same man, along with everything in it.
Mom told him, without raising her voice at all, that the old shed was hers and always had been. Dad did not hold on to that plan for long.
qs: How cold does the shed get?
Cold enough to see your breath by nine in the morning.
What was at the bottom of the box?
A thin piece of gold, cold to hold even through a glove.
How did Mom answer?
Without raising her voice at all.

write.task: Write the afternoon from Mom's point of view. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Old Cold Shed
paras: Dad has an old shed down the side of the house, and in the fall it gets cold enough in there that you can see your own breath by nine in the morning without any help from the weather outside.
He told me to hold the box of nails steady for him while he sold off the rest of the stock to a man who had driven the whole way over from the coast that morning specifically to collect it.
At the very bottom of that box of nails was a thin flat piece of gold that nobody in the family has ever explained to my satisfaction, and it was cold to hold even through a work glove.
Dad was bold about the entire afternoon, bolder than the facts supported. He told Mom that he had sold the old shed itself to the same man, along with every single thing still inside it.

Mom told him, without raising her voice by so much as a word, that the old shed was hers, had been hers since before they met, and was not his to sell. Dad did not hold on to that plan for very long at all.
qs: How far had the buyer come?
The whole way from the coast that morning.
What has never been explained?
The thin flat piece of gold at the bottom of the box.
On what grounds was the shed Mom's?
It had been hers since before they met.

write.task: Should one person be able to sell what the family shares? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Post at the Gate
paras: A tall post stands at the gate. It holds up most of the fence.
Most of the post is sunk down in the mud.
Mom is the host when we have a picnic. She hangs a flag on the post.
Almost all of us sit by the post. It is the best spot in the yard.
The post has been there the most time of all. It will stand when the rest is gone.
qs: What does the post hold up?
It holds up most of the fence.
What does Mom hang on the post?
She hangs a flag on the post.
Where do almost all of them sit?
Almost all of them sit by the post.

write.task: Write three facts about the post. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Post at the Gate
paras: A tall post stands at the gate, and it holds up most of the fence on that side, which is more than it was ever meant to do.
Most of the post is sunk down in the mud, and the part you can see is the smaller half of it by some distance.
Mom is the host whenever we have a picnic, and the first thing she does is hang a flag on that post so people can find the place.
Almost all of us end up sitting by the post rather than up near the house, because it is the best spot in the whole garden and always has been.
That post has stood there the most time of anything in the garden. It will still be standing when the rest of the fence has gone.
qs: Why does the post do more than it was meant to?
It holds up most of the fence on that side.
Which part of the post is bigger?
The part sunk in the mud.
Why does Mom hang the flag?
So people can find the place.

write.task: Write about one picnic at the post. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Post at the Gate
paras: A tall post stands at the gate at the bottom of the garden, and it holds up most of the fence along that entire side, which is a great deal more than anybody ever intended it to be doing.
Most of the post is sunk down in the mud below the surface, and the part of it that you can actually see from the path is comfortably the smaller half of the thing by some considerable distance.

Mom is the host whenever this family has a picnic, which is most fine Sundays from May onwards, and the very first thing she does on the day is hang a flag on that post so that people can find the place without ringing.

Almost all of us end up sitting down by the post rather than up near the house where the chairs are, because it is the best spot in the entire garden, it has always been the best spot, and nobody has ever argued the point.

That post has stood in that one position for the most time of anything out there, including two of the trees. It will still be standing long after the rest of the fence has gone over, and everybody in this family knows it.
qs: How often are the picnics?
Most fine Sundays from May onwards.
Why can people find the place without ringing?
The flag on the post.
What has the post outlasted?
Two of the trees, and it will outlast the fence.

write.task: Is the oldest thing in a place the most important? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: A Kind Find
paras: I did find a nest behind the shed.
Mom said to mind the eggs and to be kind.
I did not mind. I did find a way to see it from the back step.
A blind old cat sits behind the gate. It will not find the nest.
Be kind and you will find that birds will stay.
qs: Where did the narrator find a nest?
Behind the shed.
What did Mom say?
She said to mind the eggs and be kind.
Who sits behind the gate?
A blind old cat sits behind the gate.

write.task: Should the nest be left alone? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: A Kind Find
paras: I found a nest behind the shed in April, down low in the ivy where nobody would think to look for one.
Mom told me to mind the eggs and to be kind about it, which in practice meant looking and not touching, ever.
I did not mind that. I found a way of seeing the nest from the back step with a mirror, and never went near it again.
A blind old cat sits behind the gate most afternoons. It will not find that nest, and that is the only reason it is still there.
Four chicks came out of it in May. Be kind, and you find that birds stay and come back the year after.
qs: Where exactly was the nest?
Down low in the ivy behind the shed.
How did the narrator watch it?
From the back step with a mirror.
How many chicks came out?
Four chicks, in May.

write.task: Explain how to watch birds without disturbing them. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: A Kind Find
paras: I found a nest behind the shed in the middle of April, down low in the thick of the ivy where nobody with any sense would ever think to go looking for one.
Mom told me to mind the eggs and to be kind about the whole business, which in actual practice meant looking at the nest and never once touching it or anything within a foot of it.

I did not mind that condition in the slightest. I worked out a way of seeing the nest clearly from the back step using an old shaving mirror, and after the first week I never went near the ivy again at all.

A blind old cat sits behind the gate most afternoons in the sun. It will not find that nest, it has no way of finding that nest, and that is very probably the only reason the nest is still there in one piece.

Four chicks came out of it in the second week of May, which Mom counted from the kitchen window. Be kind about these things and you find that birds stay, and that the same pair come back the following year.
qs: Why would nobody look there?
It was down low in the thick of the ivy.
What did the narrator use the mirror for?
To see the nest clearly from the back step.
What does being kind lead to?
Birds stay, and the same pair come back the following year.

write.task: Write the spring from the nesting bird's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Roll and the Troll
paras: Gran can roll a soft bread roll with just her hands.
I had a roll with jam in it. It did roll off the plate and on to the mat.
The troll in my tale will roll a big rock. He asks a toll at the gate.
I did not pay the toll. I did roll the rock back at him.
Gran said that was a kind of roll she did not mean.
qs: What can Gran do with her hands?
She can roll a soft bread roll.
Where did the roll with jam go?
It did roll off the plate on to the mat.
What does the troll ask for?
The troll asks a toll at the gate.

write.task: Tell what happened with the roll, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Roll and the Troll
paras: Gran can roll a soft bread roll with nothing but her two hands, no board and no pin, and she has done it that way for sixty years.
I had a roll with jam in it on Sunday. It got away from me, rolled the length of the plate, and went on to the mat jam side down.
The troll in the book I am reading will roll a boulder across a road and then ask a toll of everybody who wants past the gate.
I would not pay that toll. I would roll the rock straight back down the hill at him and take my chances, which Gran says is not how books work.
Gran said the kind of roll she meant was the one with jam in it, and that I should think about the mat before I think about trolls.
qs: How long has Gran rolled bread that way?
For sixty years.
Which way up did the roll land?
Jam side down.
What does Gran say about books?
That rolling the rock back is not how books work.

write.task: Should the troll be paid or stood up to? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Roll and the Troll
paras: Gran can roll a soft bread roll using nothing whatsoever but her two hands, with no board and no rolling pin involved at any stage, and she has been doing it exactly that way for something close to sixty years.

I had a roll with jam in it on Sunday afternoon and it got away from me completely. It rolled the entire length of the plate, went over the edge, and landed on the mat jam side down, as these things invariably do.

The troll in the book I am reading at the moment will roll an enormous boulder across the road at the narrow part and then demand a toll from every single person who wants to get past the gate beyond it.

I would not pay that toll under any circumstances. I would roll that rock straight back down the hill at him and take whatever came of it, which Gran says, quite firmly, is not how books of this kind are supposed to work.

Gran said afterwards that the kind of roll she had meant was the one with the jam in it, and that I would do better to give some thought to the state of her mat before giving any more thought at all to trolls.
qs: What does Gran use to roll bread?
Nothing but her two hands — no board and no rolling pin.
Where does the troll put the boulder?
Across the road at the narrow part.
What does Gran think deserves more thought?
The state of her mat.

write.task: Write a report on how stories set up a problem. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Colt and the Bolt
paras: We have a colt in the field. A colt is a small horse.
The gate has a bolt on it. The colt can lift the bolt with his nose.
He did it with a jolt. The gate went back and the colt got free.
Dad put a chain on the bolt. The colt did not like that one bit.
Now the colt stands by the bolt and waits. He will get it yet.
qs: What is a colt?
A colt is a small horse.
How does the colt lift the bolt?
He can lift the bolt with his nose.
What did Dad put on the bolt?
Dad put a chain on the bolt.

write.task: Tell how the colt got out, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Colt and the Bolt
paras: We have a colt in the top field. A colt is a young horse, and this one is eleven months old and cleverer than it has any need to be.
The gate into that field has a sliding bolt on it, and the colt worked out in about a fortnight that he can lift the bolt with his nose.
He does it with a sharp jolt of the head. The gate swings back on its own, and the colt is free and halfway down the lane.
Dad has put a chain through the bolt and clipped it shut. The colt did not like that at all and made his position clear for most of an evening.
He stands by the bolt now and waits, watching it. Dad says he will get it in the end, and Dad does not say that about many animals.
qs: How old is the colt?
Eleven months old.
How long did it take him to work out the bolt?
About a fortnight.
What does Dad expect?
That the colt will get the bolt in the end.

write.task: Is a clever animal harder to keep? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Colt and the Bolt
paras: We have a colt up in the top field. A colt is a young horse, and this particular one is eleven months old and a good deal cleverer than he has any practical need to be for the life he leads.

The gate into that field has a long sliding bolt on the outside of it, and the colt worked out within about a fortnight of arriving that he can get his nose under the handle and lift the bolt clear of its keeper.

He does it with one sharp jolt of the head, which is the part that took him the longest to learn. The gate then swings back under its own weight, and the colt is free and halfway down the lane before anybody has looked up.

Dad has since put a short chain through the bolt and clipped the chain shut with a spring link. The colt did not care for that arrangement at all and made his position on it entirely clear for the better part of an evening.

He stands beside that bolt now and simply waits, watching it for long stretches at a time. Dad says the colt will get it in the end, and Dad is not a man who says that sort of thing about very many animals.
qs: What took the colt longest to learn?
The sharp jolt of the head.
How is the chain fastened?
Shut with a spring link.
Why does Dad's prediction carry weight?
He is not a man who says that about many animals.

write.task: Write the escape from the colt's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Knot I Know
paras: I know how to tie a knot. Gran did teach me when I was six.
She can knit as well. She knit me a cap and a pair of socks.
On Sunday the knot got stuck. I had to use a knife to cut it.
Gran did knock on the glass. She did know the knot would stick.
Now I know a knot that will not stick. Gran did know that one all along.
qs: Who taught the narrator to tie a knot?
Gran did teach me when I was six.
What did Gran knit?
She knit me a cap and a pair of socks.
What did Gran know all along?
She did know a knot that will not stick.

write.task: Tell how the knot got cut, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Knot I Know
paras: I know how to tie a proper knot, because Gran showed me when I was six and made me do it again every time I got it wrong.
She can knit as well as she can tie. She knitted me a cap and a pair of socks in a week and did not once look at what her hands were doing.
On Sunday the knot I had tied in the rope got stuck hard, and in the end I had to cut it out with a knife, which I had been told not to do.
Gran knocked on the kitchen glass while I was doing it. She had known from the start that the knot would stick, and she let me find out anyway.
I know a better knot now, one that holds and still comes undone when you pull the short end. Gran had known that knot all along and had been waiting.
qs: How did Gran teach the knot?
She made the narrator do it again every time it was wrong.
How fast did she knit the cap and socks?
In a week, without looking at her hands.
Why did she not say the knot would stick?
She let the narrator find out instead.

write.task: Is it better to be told or to find out? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Knot I Know
paras: I know how to tie a proper knot, and the reason I know is that Gran showed me when I was six years old and then made me untie it and do it again every single time I got any part of it wrong.

She can knit every bit as well as she can tie. She knitted me a cap and a pair of socks inside one week and did not once, at any point in that week, look down at what her own hands were doing while she worked.

On Sunday the knot I had put in the rope by the shed got stuck hard, hard enough that I could not get a finger into it, and in the end I had to cut the whole thing out with a knife, which I had specifically been told not to do.

Gran knocked on the kitchen glass while I was in the middle of cutting it. She had known from the moment I started tying it that the knot would stick, and she chose to let me get all the way there and find it out for myself.

I know a better knot now, one that holds under load and still comes undone cleanly when you pull on the short end. Gran had known that knot all along, for about sixty years, and had simply been waiting for me to need it.
qs: What did Gran make the narrator do when it was wrong?
Untie it and do it again, every single time.
What had the narrator been told not to do?
Cut the knot out with a knife.
How long had Gran known the better knot?
About sixty years.

write.task: Write a report on how skills pass from one person to another. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Wren and the Wrong Note
paras: I did write a note for Gran. I wrote it with my left hand.
The note was wrong. I had the day wrong in it.
Gran had to wrap it up and write it again for me.
A wren sat on the sill and did not care at all.
I did write it right the next time. My wrist was sore when I was done.
qs: Who was the note for?
I did write a note for Gran.
What was wrong with it?
I had the day wrong in it.
What sat on the sill?
A wren sat on the sill.

write.task: Write three facts about the note. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Wren and the Wrong Note
paras: I wrote a note for Gran on Saturday, and I wrote the whole of it with my left hand because my right one was in a sling.
The note was wrong. I had put the wrong day in it, which meant that anybody who read it would have turned up a day early.
Gran had to wrap the first one up in the bin and write the thing out again herself, in handwriting that is still better than mine.
A wren sat on the sill through all of this and did not care about any of it, which I found steadying at the time.
I wrote the next one right, and my wrist was sore by the end of it. Gran kept the wrong one. She says she likes the wrong one better.
qs: Why did the narrator use the left hand?
The right one was in a sling.
What would the wrong day have caused?
People would have turned up a day early.
Which note did Gran keep?
She kept the wrong one, and likes it better.

write.task: Write the Saturday from Gran's point of view. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Wren and the Wrong Note
paras: I wrote a note for Gran on Saturday morning, and I wrote the whole of it with my left hand, because my right hand was in a sling at the time and had been for most of a fortnight.

The note was wrong. I had put the wrong day in it, in the one place where the day actually mattered, which meant that anybody who read it and acted on it would have turned up a full day early and found nobody home.

Gran had to wrap the first one up and put it in the bin, and then write the thing out again herself from the start, in handwriting that is still a great deal better than mine has ever been and probably ever will be.
A wren sat on the sill outside the window through the whole of this and did not care about any part of it, which I remember finding oddly steadying while the rest of the morning was going wrong.

I wrote the next one right, slowly, and my wrist was genuinely sore by the time I had finished it. Gran kept the wrong one anyway and put it in the drawer. She says, and has said more than once, that she likes the wrong one better.
qs: How long had the sling been on?
Most of a fortnight.
Why did the wrong day matter so much?
It was in the one place where the day actually mattered.
Where did the wrong note end up?
In Gran's drawer.

write.task: Why might somebody keep a mistake? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Bright Night Light
paras: At night I need a light by my bed.
The light I had was bright. It was so bright it was not right.
Mom said I might sleep with it set low.
She put the light up high on the shelf. Now it is just right.
At night I get a soft light and no more. I do not fight it and I sleep tight.
qs: What does the narrator need at night?
A light by the bed.
What was wrong with the old light?
It was so bright it was not right.
Where did Mom put the light?
She put the light up high on the shelf.

write.task: Should a light be left on at night? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Bright Night Light
paras: At night I need a light on in my room, and I have needed one for as long as I can remember, and I have stopped apologising for it.
The light I had until March was far too bright. It put a hard white square on the wall and lit the room as though it were the middle of the day.
Mom said I might sleep better with it set low, and that there was no rule anywhere saying a night light has to be a bright one.
She moved it up high on the shelf and turned it down, and the whole room changed. From the bed it is now just a warm glow along the wall.
I do not fight the dark any more and I sleep tight most nights. It turns out the problem was never the dark. It was the light.
qs: How long has the narrator needed a light?
For as long as they can remember.
What did the old light do to the wall?
It put a hard white square on it.
What was the real problem?
The light, not the dark.

write.task: Explain how to make a room good for sleeping. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Bright Night Light
paras: At night I need a light on in my room. I have needed one for as long as I can actually remember needing anything, and somewhere around the start of this year I stopped apologising to people about it.

The light I had until March was far too bright for the job it was supposed to be doing. It threw a hard white square up on the wall above the desk and lit the whole room as though it were the middle of the afternoon.

Mom said that I might well sleep a good deal better with it set low, and that there is no rule written down anywhere, by anybody, which says that a night light has to be a bright light in order to count as one.

She moved it up high onto the top shelf and turned it right down, and the entire character of the room changed in about a second. From where I lie in the bed it is now nothing but a warm glow spread across the ceiling.

I do not fight the dark any more and I sleep tight on most nights of the week. It turns out, after all that, that the problem was never once the dark itself. The problem was the light I had been using against it.
qs: When did the narrator stop apologising?
Around the start of this year.
Where exactly did the white square fall?
On the wall above the desk.
What is the passage's conclusion?
The problem was the light being used against the dark, not the dark.

write.task: Write one night before and one night after the change. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Book in the Wood
paras: I took a good book to the wood by the pool.
I sat on a log and did look at it until the moon came up.
A deer stood by a tree. It did look at me and did not run.
Soon it got too cool to sit there. I took the book home.
I will look for that deer soon. I will take the book too.
qs: What did the narrator take to the wood?
A good book.
What stood by a tree?
A deer stood by a tree.
Why did the narrator go home?
Soon it got too cool to sit there.

write.task: Tell what happened in the wood, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Book in the Wood
paras: I took a good book down to the wood by the pool on Sunday, which is a thing I had been meaning to do since the start of the summer.
I sat on a fallen log and read until the moon came up over the far side of the water and I could no longer see the page properly.
A deer stood by a tree about twenty feet off and looked at me for a long time without moving, and it did not run when I finally shut the book.
Soon after that it got too cool to sit still, so I took the book home with the last of the light and walked back up the track.
I will look for that deer again soon, at the same time and on the same log. I will take the book too, because I think the book was part of it.
qs: How long had the narrator meant to do this?
Since the start of the summer.
How far off did the deer stand?
About twenty feet.
Why take the book again?
Because the narrator thinks the book was part of it.

write.task: Is it better to read indoors or outdoors? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Book in the Wood
paras: I took a good book down to the wood by the pool on Sunday evening, which is something I had been meaning to get round to doing since the very start of the summer and had not once actually managed.

I sat on a fallen log at the water's edge and read steadily until the moon came up over the far side of the pool and the light got so poor that I could no longer make out the page in front of me at all.

A deer stood by a tree about twenty feet away for a good part of that time and looked at me without moving so much as a foot, and it still did not run when I finally shut the book and the sound carried across the water.
Soon after that it got too cool to go on sitting still, so I took the book home with the last of the light, walked back up the track, and did not see the deer again on the way.

I will look for that deer again soon, at the same hour of the evening and on the same fallen log. I will take the book with me as well, because I have a strong suspicion that the book was somehow part of the whole thing.
qs: Why could the narrator no longer read?
The light got too poor to make out the page.
What did not make the deer run?
The sound of the book being shut.
What will the narrator repeat exactly?
The same hour, the same log, and the same book.

write.task: Write a report on watching wildlife quietly. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Mouse in Our House
paras: A mouse got in our house.
It did not make a loud sound. We found it by the sack of seed.
Mom did shout, but just a bit. The mouse did run round the house.
We did count six holes in the ground out back.
We put the mouse out. It is in the ground by the south wall now.
qs: What got in the house?
A mouse got in our house.
Where did they find it?
They found it by the sack of seed.
How many holes did they count?
They did count six holes in the ground.

write.task: Should the mouse have been put out? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Mouse in Our House
paras: A mouse got into our house in October, through a gap under the back door that nobody had ever thought about until then.
It did not make a loud sound, which is how it went unnoticed for a week. We found it in the end by the sack of seed in the pantry.
Mom did shout, but only a bit, and mostly from surprise. The mouse ran round the whole ground floor twice before it went under the stove.
Out the back we counted six holes in the ground along the foot of the wall, which rather suggested this mouse was not working alone.
We put the mouse out by the south wall and blocked the gap under the door. It lives in the ground out there now, and so, I assume, do the others.
qs: How did the mouse get in?
Through a gap under the back door.
Why did it go unnoticed for a week?
It did not make a loud sound.
What did the six holes suggest?
That the mouse was not working alone.

write.task: Write the week from the mouse's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what it could smell.

g4.title: The Mouse in Our House
paras: A mouse got into our house in the middle of October, through a narrow gap under the back door that nobody in this family had ever once thought about in all the years we have lived here.

It did not make a loud sound at any stage, which is precisely how it managed to go entirely unnoticed for the better part of a week. We found it in the end down by the sack of seed at the back of the pantry.

Mom did shout when she saw it, but only a bit, and mostly out of plain surprise rather than anything else. The mouse ran round the whole of the ground floor twice at considerable speed before disappearing under the stove.

Out the back we counted six separate holes in the ground running along the foot of the wall, all of them fresh, which rather strongly suggested that this particular mouse had not been working on its own.
We put the mouse out by the south wall and blocked the gap under the door with a strip of wood the same afternoon. It lives in the ground out there now, and so, I can only assume, do all the others.
qs: What had nobody thought about?
The narrow gap under the back door.
Why did Mom shout?
Mostly out of plain surprise.
What made the six holes telling?
All of them were fresh.

write.task: Explain how to keep mice out of a house. Organise it into steps and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Brown Owl in Town
paras: A brown owl sits in the old tower down in town.
How it got there, no one knows. It was not there last year.
A crowd will stand down on the road and look up at it.
The owl will frown at us. Then it will look down and not move.
Now the town has an owl. We will not let it go.
qs: Where does the owl sit?
In the old tower down in town.
What does the crowd do?
A crowd will stand down on the road and look up at it.
What does the owl do when it is looked at?
It will frown at us and then look down.

write.task: Write three facts about the owl. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Brown Owl in Town
paras: A brown owl sits in the old tower down in the middle of town, in the gap where a window used to be, and it has sat there since March.
How it got there is something nobody knows. There were no owls in town last year, and there is no wood within three miles of that tower.
A small crowd stands down on the road most evenings and looks up at it, and the crowd is bigger at weekends than it is on a Monday.
The owl frowns down at the crowd, or appears to, and then looks away and does not move again for an hour at a time.
The town has an owl now, and the town has decided that it is the town's owl. Nobody is going to let it go quietly.
qs: Where exactly in the tower does it sit?
In the gap where a window used to be.
Why is its arrival strange?
There is no wood within three miles of the tower.
When is the crowd biggest?
At weekends.

write.task: Write an evening from the owl's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what it could see.

g4.title: The Brown Owl in Town
paras: A brown owl sits in the old tower down in the middle of town, up in the gap where a window used to be before the frame came out, and it has been sitting there without a break since the end of March.

How it got there is something that nobody in this town has ever been able to work out. There were no owls here at all last year, and there is no wood of any size within three miles of that tower in any direction.

A small crowd gathers down on the road most evenings and stands there looking up at it, and that crowd is reliably a good deal bigger at weekends than it ever is on a Monday or a wet Tuesday in the rain.
The owl frowns down at the crowd, or at any rate gives every appearance of frowning down at it, and then looks away across the roofs and does not move again for an hour or more at a stretch.
The town has an owl now, and the town has quietly decided that it is the town's own owl rather than simply an owl that happens to be here. Nobody in it is going to let that bird go quietly.
qs: What changed about the window?
The frame came out, leaving a gap.
When is the crowd smallest?
On a Monday or a wet Tuesday in the rain.
What has the town decided?
That it is the town's own owl, not just an owl passing through.

write.task: Can a town claim a wild animal as its own? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: A Handful of Helpful
paras: Dad said I was helpful on Sunday. That is a big thing for him to say.
I was careful with the eggs. I was careful with the jam as well.
A handful of helpful things is all it takes.
Mom said the list was useful. Dad said it was restful to get help.
I will be helpful next week too. I will be careful and thankful.
qs: What did Dad say about Sunday?
Dad said I was helpful.
What was the narrator careful with?
Careful with the eggs and the jam.
What did Mom say about the list?
Mom said the list was useful.

write.task: What is the most helpful thing a child can do? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: A Handful of Helpful
paras: Dad said I had been helpful on Sunday, and that is not a thing he says lightly or, as far as I know, very often.
I had been careful with the eggs, which is the job nobody wants, and careful with the jam as well, which is worse.
A handful of helpful things is all it takes, as it turns out. Not a whole day of them. Four or five, done properly.
Mom said the list I made was useful and has pinned it up. Dad said it was restful to have help in the house for once.
I will be helpful again next week, and the week after. I intend to be careful about it and, with luck, thankful rather than smug.
qs: How often does Dad say that?
Not lightly, and not very often.
Which job does nobody want?
Being careful with the eggs.
How many helpful things does it take?
Four or five, done properly.

write.task: Explain how to be useful at home. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: A Handful of Helpful
paras: Dad said that I had been helpful on Sunday, and that is not a thing he says lightly, nor, so far as anybody in this house has ever been able to establish, a thing he says with any great frequency.

I had been careful with the eggs, which is the job that nobody in this family wants and which gets handed down to whoever is youngest, and I had been careful with the jam as well, which is considerably worse.

A handful of helpful things is all it actually takes, as it turns out, and this was news to me. Not a whole day of them, start to finish. Four or five of them, chosen sensibly and done properly all the way through.

Mom said the list I had made was useful and has pinned it up on the inside of the cupboard door where she will see it. Dad said it was restful, for once, to have some help in the house that he had not needed to ask for.

I intend to be helpful again next week, and the week after that, and to stay careful about the whole business. I would also like to manage being thankful about it rather than becoming insufferably pleased with myself.
qs: Who gets the egg job?
Whoever is youngest in the family.
Where has the list been pinned?
Inside the cupboard door where Mom will see it.
What does the narrator want to avoid becoming?
Insufferably pleased with themselves.

write.task: Write the Sunday from Dad's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Spotless Shed
paras: Our shed was a mess. Now it is spotless.
It took us an endless day to do it. I was restless by lunch.
The old mop was useless. Dad got one that was not.
A spot of mud is harmless. A shed full of mud is not harmless at all.
Now the shed is spotless. We will not be careless with it again.
qs: What was the shed like at first?
Our shed was a mess.
How long did it take?
It took us an endless day.
What was wrong with the old mop?
The old mop was useless.

write.task: Tell how the shed got clean, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Spotless Shed
paras: Our shed was a mess from one end to the other, and had been for about four years. It is spotless now, which still surprises me every time I open the door.
It took an endless Saturday to do. I was restless by lunch and bored stiff by three, and Dad did not let that count as a reason to stop.
The old mop turned out to be useless, so halfway through Dad went and bought one that worked, which we should have done at the start.
A spot of mud in a shed is harmless and nobody minds it. Four years of mud is not harmless, and ours had quietly stopped being harmless a long time ago.
The shed is spotless now and we have agreed not to be careless with it again, which is easy to agree to in March and harder to keep up in November.
qs: How long had the shed been a mess?
About four years.
What did Dad not accept as a reason to stop?
That the narrator was restless and bored.
When will the agreement be hard to keep?
In November.

write.task: Is it worth keeping things spotless? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Spotless Shed
paras: Our shed was a mess from one end of it to the other, and it had been in that state for something close to four years. It is entirely spotless now, which still surprises me every single time I open the door on it.

It took one endless Saturday from eight in the morning to do the whole thing. I was restless by lunch and bored absolutely stiff by three, and Dad did not at any point accept either of those as a reason to stop and come back to it.

The old mop turned out to be completely useless once there was actual work for it to do, so halfway through the afternoon Dad drove out and bought one that worked, which is obviously what we should have done before starting.

A single spot of mud in a shed is harmless and no sensible person minds it in the slightest. Four solid years of accumulated mud is not harmless at all, and ours had quietly stopped being harmless some considerable time ago.

The shed is spotless now and the two of us have agreed, out loud, not to be careless with it again. That is an easy thing to agree to in March and a considerably harder thing to keep up through a wet November.
qs: When did the Saturday start?
At eight in the morning.
When did the mop's uselessness show?
Once there was actual work for it to do.
Why name March and November?
Agreeing is easy in March and keeping it up is hard in a wet November.

write.task: Write a report on keeping a space tidy over time. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Kindness in the Dark
paras: I did not like the darkness in the hall at night.
Mom did a kindness. She put a lamp on the shelf by the stairs.
Now the darkness is soft. The softness of it helps me sleep.
Gran said that is just goodness and a bit of sense. She said the darkness is not my foe.
The sadness I had at night is gone. The kindness did it.
qs: What did the narrator not like?
The darkness in the hall at night.
What kindness did Mom do?
She put a lamp on the shelf by the stairs.
What did Gran say the darkness is not?
Gran said the darkness is not my foe.

write.task: Write three facts about the hall at night. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Kindness in the Dark
paras: I did not like the darkness in the hall at night, and for about a year I would not cross it on my own after the lights went off.
Mom did a kindness without making anything of it. She put a small lamp on the shelf by the stairs and said nothing about why.
The darkness in that hall is soft now rather than solid, and the softness of it is the whole difference. I cross it without thinking.
Gran said it was goodness and a bit of plain sense, and that the darkness had never been my foe in the first place, whatever it had felt like.
The sadness I used to get at bedtime has gone with it. It was not bravery that fixed it. It was one lamp and one kindness that nobody made a fuss about.
qs: How long would the narrator not cross the hall?
For about a year.
What makes the difference now?
The softness of the darkness, because of the lamp.
What fixed the sadness?
One lamp and one kindness, not bravery.

write.task: Write the first night with the lamp. Use time-order words and describe what you could see.

g4.title: The Kindness in the Dark
paras: I did not like the darkness in the hall at night, and for the better part of a year I would not cross that hall on my own once the lights downstairs had gone off for the evening.

Mom did a kindness about it without ever making the smallest thing of it. She put a small lamp on the shelf by the stairs one afternoon and said absolutely nothing to me about why it had appeared there.

The darkness in that hall is soft now rather than solid, and the softness of it turns out to be the entire difference between the two states. I cross the hall at any hour now without thinking about it at all.

Gran said that what Mom had done was goodness and a decent amount of plain sense, and that the darkness had never once been my foe in the first place, whatever it had very convincingly felt like at the time.

The sadness I used to get at bedtime has gone along with the fear of the hall. It was not bravery that fixed any of it, and it was never going to be. It was one small lamp and one kindness that nobody made a fuss about.
qs: When would the narrator not cross the hall?
Once the lights downstairs had gone off.
What did Mom say about the lamp?
Absolutely nothing.
What was never going to fix it?
Bravery.

write.task: Is a quiet kindness worth more than a loud one? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Basement and the Pavement
paras: We have a basement under our house. It is cold and dark down there.
Dad got a shipment of wood to fix it up.
The men left it on the pavement by the gate. It sat there a moment too long.
A man came by and did make a statement to Dad about the pavement.
Dad got the wood in the basement in one long movement. He said the payment was for wood, not for talk.
qs: What is under the house?
We have a basement under our house.
What did Dad get?
Dad got a shipment of wood.
Where did the men leave it?
On the pavement by the gate.

write.task: Tell what happened to the wood, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Basement and the Pavement
paras: We have a basement under our house that is cold and dark and has been doing nothing useful for as long as anybody can remember.
In April Dad ordered a shipment of wood to fix it up, with the firm intention of turning it into a room somebody would actually want to sit in.
The men left the whole shipment stacked on the pavement by the gate rather than in the drive, and it sat out there a good moment too long.
A man from up the road came by and made a statement to Dad about blocking a public pavement, at some length and with some feeling.
Dad shifted every piece of that wood into the basement in one long movement, without stopping once. He said afterwards that the payment had been for wood, not for commentary.
qs: How long has the basement been useless?
As long as anybody can remember.
What was Dad's intention?
To turn the basement into a room somebody would want to sit in.
What was the man's complaint?
That the wood was blocking a public pavement.

write.task: Was the neighbour right to complain? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Basement and the Pavement
paras: We have a basement underneath our house that is cold and dark and that has been doing nothing remotely useful for as long as any member of this family is able to remember with any confidence.

In April Dad ordered a shipment of wood to fix the place up, with the firm and repeatedly stated intention of turning it into a room that somebody in the house might one day actually choose to sit in.
The men delivering it left the entire shipment stacked up on the pavement by the front gate rather than inside the drive where there was room for it, and it sat out there a very good moment too long.

A man from further up the road came by on his way past and made a statement to Dad about the blocking of a public pavement, at considerable length and with a quantity of feeling that nobody had expected at that hour.

Dad then shifted every last piece of that wood down into the basement in one long movement, without stopping once and without answering. He said afterwards that the payment had been made for the wood and not for the commentary.
qs: Where should the wood have gone?
Inside the drive, where there was room for it.
What surprised people about the complaint?
The quantity of feeling at that hour.
How did Dad answer the man?
He did not answer — he moved the wood without stopping.

write.task: Write a report on being a good neighbour. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: Slowly and Softly
paras: Gran walks slowly and she talks softly.
I walk quickly and I talk loudly. We still get on well.
Lately she has told me to slow down a bit.
So I walk slowly with her to the gate. She kindly lets me run back.
Sadly the walk is short. Gladly I will do it again.
qs: How does Gran walk and talk?
Gran walks slowly and talks softly.
How does the narrator walk and talk?
I walk quickly and I talk loudly.
What does Gran kindly let the narrator do?
She kindly lets me run back.

write.task: Is it better to go slowly or quickly? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: Slowly and Softly
paras: Gran walks slowly and talks softly, and she has done both for as long as I have been alive, and not one of those two things is going to change now.
I walk quickly and talk loudly, which she has never once asked me to stop doing. We get on perfectly well in spite of the obvious mismatch.
Lately she has asked me to slow down a bit on the way to the gate, and I have worked out that she means on that stretch only, not in general.
So I walk slowly beside her all the way down, matching her, and then she kindly lets me run back up the lane at my own speed.
Sadly the walk is short and getting shorter. Gladly, and for as long as there is a walk at all, I will keep doing it exactly that way.
qs: What has Gran never asked?
She has never asked the narrator to stop walking quickly or talking loudly.
Where does she want the slowing down?
On the stretch down to the gate only.
Why is the walk getting shorter?
Sadly, Gran can manage less of it.

write.task: Write one walk to the gate. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: Slowly and Softly
paras: Gran walks slowly and she talks softly, and she has done both of those things for the whole of the time that I have been alive, and neither one of them is going to change at this stage.

I walk quickly and I talk loudly, and she has never once in my entire life asked me to stop doing either. The two of us get on perfectly well in spite of what is obviously a considerable mismatch of speeds.

Lately she has started asking me to slow down a bit on the way down to the gate, and after a while I worked out for myself that she means on that one stretch of path only and not as a general instruction about my life.

So I walk slowly the whole way down beside her now, matching her step for step and not hurrying her at any point, and then at the gate she kindly lets me run all the way back up the lane at whatever speed I like.

Sadly the walk is short and it has been getting shorter every year for three years. Gladly, and for as long as there is any walk left to do at all, I am going to keep on doing it in precisely that way.
qs: What is the mismatch between them?
A considerable mismatch of speeds.
What did the narrator work out about the instruction?
That it applied to one stretch of path, not to life in general.
How long has the walk been shortening?
Every year for three years.

write.task: Write a report on spending time with older relatives. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Walk to the Shop
paras: Last week I walked to the shop with Gran.
I asked for bread. Gran asked for jam and a red bag.
We picked up the bag and filled it right up.
On the way back it rained. We jumped the pools and did not stop.
We landed at home wet. Gran said it was the best walk we had had.
qs: Who did the narrator walk with?
I walked to the shop with Gran.
What did they ask for?
I asked for bread and Gran asked for jam.
What happened on the way back?
On the way back it rained.

write.task: Tell what happened on the walk, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Walk to the Shop
paras: Last week I walked down to the shop with Gran, which we had planned on Monday and then put off twice.
I asked for bread at the counter and Gran asked for jam, and then she asked for a red bag because she had forgotten hers at home.
We picked up the bag between us and filled it right to the top, which meant it had to be carried rather than swung.
On the way back it rained hard. We jumped the pools instead of going round them, and not one of us suggested stopping.
