We landed at home soaked to the knee. Gran said, while wringing out her sleeve, that it had been the best walk the two of us had ever had.
qs: How often had the walk been put off?
Twice.
Why did Gran ask for a bag?
She had forgotten hers at home.
What did Gran say at the end?
That it had been the best walk the two of them had ever had.

write.task: Is it better to jump the puddles or go round them? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Walk to the Shop
paras: Last week I walked all the way down to the shop with Gran, a walk the two of us had planned on the Monday and then put off twice for reasons that neither of us can now remember clearly.
I asked for bread at the counter and Gran asked for jam, and then she asked the man for a red bag as well, because she had forgotten her own one on the hook by the door at home.
We picked the bag up between the two of us and filled it right to the top, which meant that from then on it had to be carried properly rather than swung along at the side.
On the way back it rained harder than it had all month. We jumped the pools rather than walking round them, and at no point did either of us suggest that we might shelter and wait it out.

We landed back at the house soaked through to the knee and dripping on the mat. Gran said, while wringing out one sleeve into the sink, that it had been the best walk that the two of us had ever taken together.
qs: Why was the walk put off?
For reasons neither of them can now remember clearly.
Where had Gran's bag been left?
On the hook by the door at home.
What did neither of them suggest?
Sheltering and waiting out the rain.

write.task: Write a report on walking in bad weather. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: Singing and Baking
paras: Gran is singing in the kitchen. She is making bread.
I am helping. I am mixing and she is making the rest.
The ring on her hand is old. She keeps taking it off when she is baking.
A king could not get bread like this. That is a big thing to say.
Nothing is as good as singing and baking on a wet day.
qs: What is Gran doing in the kitchen?
She is singing and making bread.
What job is the narrator doing?
I am mixing.
What does Gran do with her ring?
She keeps taking it off when she is baking.

write.task: Write three facts about baking bread. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: Singing and Baking
paras: Gran is singing in the kitchen again, which means she is making bread, because the singing and the bread arrive together or not at all.
I am helping, which in practice means I am doing the mixing and she is doing every single other part of it herself.
The ring on her hand is old and thin and she keeps taking it off and setting it on the sill whenever she is baking, and twice she has nearly lost it.
A king could not get bread like this, and I say that having eaten bread from three different shops in town this month alone.
Nothing in the world is as good as singing and baking in a warm kitchen on a wet grey day, and I expect to go on thinking so.
qs: How do you know Gran is making bread?
The singing and the bread arrive together.
What does helping actually mean?
The narrator does the mixing and Gran does everything else.
What has nearly happened twice?
Gran has nearly lost the ring.

write.task: Write a baking morning in the kitchen. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: Singing and Baking
paras: Gran is singing in the kitchen again, which in this house means without any doubt that she is making bread, because the singing and the bread have always arrived at the same time or else not arrived at all.
I am helping her, which in actual practice means that I am doing the mixing and standing where I am told, and that she is doing every single other part of the entire job herself without being asked.

The ring on her hand is old and has worn thin, and she keeps taking it off and setting it on the window sill whenever she is baking, and on two separate occasions she has very nearly lost it that way.

A king could not get bread like this anywhere, and I say that as somebody who has eaten bread from three different shops in this town in the past month and found all three of them wanting in one way or another.
Nothing in the world is as good as singing and baking in a warm kitchen on a wet grey afternoon, and I fully expect to go on thinking exactly that for the rest of my life, whatever else changes.
qs: What does the singing reliably mean?
That Gran is making bread.
What else does helping involve?
Standing where the narrator is told.
What was found wanting?
Bread from three different shops in town.

write.task: Is food made at home better than food bought in? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Oldest Tree
paras: The oldest tree in the park is the tallest one as well.
It has the biggest nest in it. That nest is the best I have seen.
The fastest way up is on the west side, but it is the hardest too.
Mom said that was the daftest plan I had had all week.
So I sat and had a rest. The safest spot is the ground.
qs: What is the oldest tree in the park?
It is the tallest one as well.
What is in the tree?
It has the biggest nest in it.
Which is the safest spot?
The safest spot is the ground.

write.task: Should the narrator have climbed the tree? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Oldest Tree
paras: The oldest tree in the park is also the tallest, which is not always how it works, and it has stood at the top of the slope longer than the park has been a park.
It has the biggest nest in it that I have ever seen in a tree, right up in the highest fork, and it is the best nest in the whole of this town by a long way.
The fastest way up that trunk is on the west side where the bark is deeply ridged, but the fastest way is also the hardest and there is no second-best route.
Mom said, when I explained the plan to her, that it was the daftest one I had come up with all week, and it had been a week with a lot of plans in it.
So I sat down at the bottom and had a rest instead, and watched the nest from there. The safest spot in that park is the ground, and I have decided I am content with it.
qs: How long has the tree stood there?
Longer than the park has been a park.
Where exactly is the nest?
Right up in the highest fork.
What did Mom call the plan?
The daftest one of the week.

write.task: Explain how to stay safe around tall trees. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Oldest Tree
paras: The oldest tree in the park is also comfortably the tallest one in it, which is not always how these things work out, and it has stood up there at the top of the slope for longer than the park has been a park at all.

It has the biggest nest in it that I have ever seen in any tree anywhere, sitting right up in the highest fork of the trunk, and on any fair assessment it is the best nest in the whole of this town by a considerable margin.

The fastest way up that trunk is on the west side, where the bark is ridged deeply enough to hold a boot, but the fastest way up is also by some distance the hardest way up, and there is no sensible second-best route to be had.

Mom said, after I had explained the entire plan to her in some detail at the kitchen table, that it was the daftest one I had come up with all week, and it had been a week with a very large number of plans in it.

So I sat down at the bottom of the trunk and had a rest instead, and watched the nest from down there for an hour. The safest spot in that whole park is the ground, and I have decided that I am content with the ground.
qs: Why is the west side climbable?
The bark is ridged deeply enough to hold a boot.
Why is there no second-best route?
The fastest way is also the hardest, and nothing else works.
What did the narrator do instead?
Sat at the bottom and watched the nest for an hour.

write.task: Write the hour at the bottom of the tree. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: A Windy Day with Sandy
paras: It was a windy day and the sky was grey.
Sandy and I were happy to stay in.
We had a jolly time. Mom was busy with the baby.
By three it was sunny. We ran out to play.
Many a day is windy. Not many are as funny as that one.
qs: What was the day like at first?
It was a windy day and the sky was grey.
Who was Mom busy with?
Mom was busy with the baby.
What happened by three?
By three it was sunny.

write.task: Tell how the day changed, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: A Windy Day with Sandy
paras: It was a windy day in January and the sky over the garden was the sort of grey that does not look likely to lift at any point.
Sandy came over early and the two of us were perfectly happy to stay indoors, which is not something we would usually admit to.
We had a jolly morning of it on the stairs with a box of old games, while Mom was busy with the baby and glad enough to have us quiet.
By three the sky had gone sunny without any warning at all, and we ran straight out to play and did not come back in until it got dark.
Many a day in January is windy and grey. Not many of them turn out to be as funny as that one did, and we still talk about it.
qs: What was the grey sky like?
The sort that does not look likely to lift.
What would they not usually admit?
Being happy to stay indoors.
When did they come back in?
Not until it got dark.

write.task: Is a day indoors ever better than a day outside? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: A Windy Day with Sandy
paras: It was a windy day in the middle of January and the sky sitting over the garden was exactly the sort of flat grey that gives you no reason at all to believe it is going to lift at any point before evening.

Sandy came over early in the morning and the two of us were perfectly happy to stay indoors all day, which is not something that either of us would normally be willing to admit to anybody in so many words.

We had a genuinely jolly morning of it sitting on the stairs with a box of very old games, while Mom was busy upstairs with the baby and was glad enough to have the pair of us occupied and quiet for once.

By three in the afternoon the sky had gone completely sunny without any warning whatsoever, and we ran straight out into the garden to play and did not come back inside the house again until it had gone properly dark.

Many a January day here is windy and grey from start to finish and nothing comes of it. Not many of them turn out to be anything like as funny as that one did, and the two of us still talk about it now.
qs: What does that grey sky promise?
No reason to believe it will lift before evening.
Why was Mom glad?
To have both of them occupied and quiet.
What makes that day stand out?
They still talk about it now.

write.task: Write a report on how weather changes plans. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Broken Oven
paras: The oven in the kitchen is broken.
It has been broken since ten past seven.
Mom has eaten nothing. She is not happy when that happens.
Dad has taken the back off it. He has written down the bits.
Then he will open the shop book and get a part. We will eat at ten.
qs: What is broken?
The oven in the kitchen is broken.
How long has it been broken?
It has been broken since ten past seven.
What has Dad taken off?
Dad has taken the back off the oven.

write.task: Tell what the family did about the oven, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Broken Oven
paras: The oven in the kitchen is broken, properly broken, and it has been broken since ten past seven this morning when it made a noise and stopped.
Mom has eaten nothing since then, because everything she had planned for the day needed the oven, and she is never happy when that happens.
Dad has taken the back off the oven and spread the bits out on a sheet of paper, and he has written down where every one of them came from.
Then he will open the shop book, order the part that has gone, and wait for it, which is the part of the job he is worst at.
We will eat at ten tonight, in the kitchen, off the stove. Nobody in this house is pretending to be happy about it, and nobody is complaining out loud.
qs: When did the oven stop?
At ten past seven, after it made a noise.
Why has Mom eaten nothing?
Everything she had planned needed the oven.
Which part of the job is Dad worst at?
Waiting for the part to arrive.

write.task: Should a broken thing be mended or replaced? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Broken Oven
paras: The oven in the kitchen is broken, and it is properly broken rather than merely sulking. It has been broken since ten past seven this morning, when it made a short unpleasant noise and then simply stopped doing anything at all.

Mom has eaten nothing whatsoever since then, because every single thing she had planned for the entire day needed that oven at some stage, and she has never once been happy on any day that this has happened.

Dad has taken the whole back off the oven and spread every piece out across a sheet of paper on the table, and he has written down in order exactly where each one of them came from, which is the sensible thing to do.

Then he will open the shop book, order the part that has actually gone, and sit and wait for it to arrive in the post, and the waiting is far and away the part of any job like this that he is worst at managing.

We will be eating at ten tonight, in the kitchen, off the top of the stove, as we did on Tuesday. Nobody in this house is pretending to be happy about any of it, and nobody is complaining about it out loud either.
qs: How did the oven stop?
It made a short unpleasant noise and stopped doing anything.
Why write down where the pieces came from?
So they can go back in order — it is the sensible thing to do.
What is nobody doing?
Pretending to be happy, or complaining out loud.

write.task: Write the day from Mom's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Boxes of Dishes
paras: Mom has six boxes of dishes in the hall.
The dishes are old. Gran washes them and then wishes she had not.
The boxes sit by the benches at the back of the hall.
Dad matches the lids to the boxes. It takes him ages.
Now all the dishes are in the boxes. Mom wishes for a shelf.
qs: What is in the boxes?
Mom has six boxes of dishes.
What does Gran do with the dishes?
Gran washes them.
What does Dad match?
Dad matches the lids to the boxes.

g3.title: The Boxes of Dishes
paras: Mom has six boxes of dishes stacked in the hall, and they have been standing there since the day they came out of Gran's old house in March.
The dishes in them are old enough to be worth something. Gran washes them one at a time and then wishes she had left them alone, because the pattern lifts.
The boxes sit by the benches at the back of the hall, where nobody can get past them without turning sideways and everybody has stopped mentioning it.
Dad matches the lids to the boxes, which takes him ages, because somebody carried them in without keeping the pairs together and nobody will say who.
All the dishes are in the boxes now and the boxes are shut. Mom wishes for a shelf wide enough to take them, and has wished for it since March.
qs: Where did the dishes come from?
Gran's old house, in March.
Why does Gran wish she had not washed them?
The pattern lifts.
Why does matching the lids take ages?
The pairs were not kept together when they were carried in.

write.task: Write the day the boxes arrived. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Boxes of Dishes
paras: Mom has six boxes of dishes stacked up along one wall of the hall, and they have been standing in exactly that position since the day they came out of Gran's old house back in March and were carried in here.

The dishes inside them are old enough that somebody once suggested they might be worth something. Gran washes them one at a time at the sink and then wishes she had left them alone, because the pattern on them lifts under warm water.

The boxes sit by the benches at the back of the hall, in the one spot where nobody in this house can get past them without turning sideways to do it, and everybody has now quietly stopped mentioning this at mealtimes.

Dad matches the lids to the boxes whenever he has an evening free, which takes him ages every time, because whoever carried them in from the van did not keep the pairs together and to this day nobody will admit to having been the one.

All the dishes are back in the boxes now and the boxes are properly shut. Mom wishes for a shelf wide enough and strong enough to take the lot of them, and she has been wishing out loud for that shelf since March.
qs: What has somebody suggested about the dishes?
That they might be worth something.
What have people stopped doing?
Mentioning the boxes at mealtimes.
What will nobody admit to?
Carrying the boxes in without keeping the pairs together.

write.task: Should old family things be used or kept safe? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Misprint on Page Ten
paras: My book has a misprint on page ten.
It made me misread the rest of the tale.
I did not mistrust the book and I did not mistrust Mom.
Miss Dale said it was a mishap at the shop, not a mistake by me.
I will not mislay that book. A book with a misprint is odd and good.
qs: What is on page ten?
My book has a misprint on page ten.
What did the misprint make the narrator do?
It made me misread the rest of the tale.
What did Miss Dale say?
She said it was a mishap at the shop, not a mistake by me.

write.task: Is a book with a misprint worth keeping? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Misprint on Page Ten
paras: My book has a misprint on page ten, where two lines have been set in the wrong order and nobody at the printers noticed it.
It made me misread the whole of the rest of the tale, because the two lines happen to carry the part that explains who the man at the gate is.
I did not mistrust the book over it, and I did not mistrust Mom when she said the book was fine, because the book is fine apart from page ten.
Miss Dale at school said it was a mishap at the printers rather than a mistake by me, which was a relief, and then she asked to borrow it.
I am not going to mislay that book. A book with a misprint in it is an odd thing to own and I would not swap it for a clean one.
qs: What is wrong on page ten?
Two lines have been set in the wrong order.
Why did that matter so much?
Those lines explain who the man at the gate is.
What did Miss Dale do after explaining?
She asked to borrow the book.

write.task: Write the moment of reading page ten. Use time-order words and describe what you were thinking.

g4.title: The Misprint on Page Ten
paras: My book has a misprint on page ten, where two whole lines have been set in the wrong order round the other way, and apparently not one person at the printers noticed it before the thing went out.

It made me misread the entire remainder of the tale from that point onwards, because those two particular lines happen to be the ones that carry the explanation of who the man standing at the gate actually is.

I did not mistrust the book itself over it, and I did not mistrust Mom when she told me the book was fine, because the book is in fact entirely fine everywhere apart from the ten or so words on page ten.

Miss Dale at school said it was a mishap at the printers rather than any sort of mistake on my part, which was a considerable relief to hear out loud, and then she asked whether she could borrow it for a week.
I have no intention whatsoever of mislaying that book. A book with a genuine misprint in it is an odd thing to own, and I would not swap mine for a clean copy of it under any circumstances.
qs: How were the two lines set?
In the wrong order, round the other way.
What did Mom say, and why was she right?
That the book was fine — it is fine apart from ten or so words.
What would the narrator not do?
Swap it for a clean copy.

write.task: Write a report on how books are made and checked. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Subway in to Town
paras: We took the subway in to town on Monday.
The subway runs under the shops. It is a train under the ground.
On the subway I read a book. My best subject at school is math.
We did subtract and add all the way in. Dad had to submit a note at the gate.
On the way back the subway was packed. I had a seat on the subway and Dad did not.
qs: How did they get in to town?
We took the subway in to town.
Where does the subway run?
The subway runs under the shops.
What is the narrator's best subject?
My best subject at school is math.

write.task: Tell what happened on the subway, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Subway in to Town
paras: We took the subway in to town on Monday morning, which Dad had been putting off for a fortnight because he does not like being underground.
The subway runs directly under the shops on the main street, and the whole of it is a train running under the ground with no windows worth looking out of.
On the subway I read my book for the first ten minutes and then gave up, because my best subject at school is math and Dad had a sheet of it with him.
We did subtract and add all the way in, out loud, which the man opposite did not enjoy. At the gate Dad had to submit a note about my half fare.
On the way back the subway was packed from end to end. I had a seat on the subway and Dad stood the whole way, and he did not complain about it once.
qs: Why had Dad put the trip off?
He does not like being underground.
What did the man opposite not enjoy?
The adding and subtracting out loud.
Who stood on the way back?
Dad stood the whole way.

write.task: Explain how an underground train works. Group your ideas and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Subway in to Town
paras: We took the subway in to town on Monday morning, a trip which Dad had been quietly putting off for a fortnight on the grounds that he has never in his life enjoyed being underground for any length of time.

The subway runs directly underneath the shops along the main street for most of its length, and the whole thing is simply a train running under the ground with no windows worth the trouble of looking out of.
On the subway I read my book for the first ten minutes or so and then gave up on it entirely, because my best subject at school is math and Dad had a folded sheet of it in his coat pocket.

We did subtract and add the whole way in, out loud and at normal speaking volume, which the man sitting directly opposite us very plainly did not enjoy. At the gate Dad had to submit a note about my half fare.

On the way back out the subway was packed solid from one end of the carriage to the other. I had a seat on the subway for the whole journey and Dad stood the entire way, and he did not complain about it even once.
qs: How long had the trip been put off?
A fortnight.
Where had Dad kept the math sheet?
Folded in his coat pocket.
What is notable about Dad standing?
He did not complain about it even once.

write.task: Should children get a cheaper fare than adults? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g2.title: The Postman and the Postcard
paras: The postman came at ten.
He put a postcard in the postbox by the gate.
It was from Gran. She had to postpone her trip and pay more postage.
Mom put the postcard up on the wall next to a poster.
The postman will be back. Gran will post again.

The postman came at ten.
Where did he put the postcard?
In the postbox by the gate.

She had to postpone her trip.

g3.title: The Postman and the Postcard
paras: The postman came at ten on Saturday, which is late for him, and he had one thing in his hand when he came up the path.
He put a postcard in the postbox by the gate rather than through the door, because the dog has an opinion about the door.
The postcard was from Gran. She had to postpone her trip by a month and had paid extra postage to get the card here before we set off to meet her.
Mom put the postcard up on the kitchen wall next to an old poster of the same coast, and the two of them match better than you would expect.
The postman will be back on Monday. Gran will post again before then, because Gran always posts again, and she has never once picked up a handset for this sort of thing.
qs: Why use the postbox and not the door?
The dog has an opinion about the door.
Why did Gran pay extra postage?
To get the card there before they set off to meet her.
What does Gran never use?
A handset, for this sort of thing.

write.task: Is a postcard better than a message on a screen? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Postman and the Postcard
paras: The postman came at ten o'clock on Saturday morning, which is a good deal later than he usually manages, and he had exactly one thing in his hand when he came up the path to the house.

He put the postcard into the postbox out by the gate rather than pushing it through the door, as he has done every single day since the spring, because the dog in this house has a strongly held opinion about the door.

The postcard was from Gran. She had been obliged to postpone her trip by a full month and had paid extra postage on the card specifically so that it would reach us before we set off on the long drive to meet her.

Mom put the postcard up on the kitchen wall directly next to an old poster of the same stretch of coast that has hung there for years, and the two of them match one another a great deal better than anybody expected.

The postman will be back on Monday morning as usual. Gran will have posted again before then, because Gran always posts again, and in all the years I have known her she has never once used a handset for this sort of thing.
qs: How long has he used the postbox?
Every day since the spring.
By how long was the trip postponed?
A full month.
What hangs next to the postcard?
An old poster of the same stretch of coast.

g2.title: The Coin in the Soil
paras: I found a coin in the soil by the gate.
It had been in that soil so long it would not come clean in oil.
Dad said to boil it. That did spoil it a bit.
Now it sits on a coil of foil on my shelf.
I will join the club at school and point at my coin.
qs: Where did the narrator find a coin?
In the soil by the gate.
What did Dad say to do?
Dad said to boil it.
Where does the coin sit now?
On a coil of foil on my shelf.

g3.title: The Coin in the Soil
paras: I found a coin in the soil by the gate in April, turned up by the spade while I was planting, and it was green all over.
It had been down in that soil so long that it would not come clean in oil, which is what Gran swore by and which did nothing at all.
Dad said to boil it, so we boiled it for ten minutes, and that spoiled a little of the pattern on one side without getting it any cleaner.
It sits on a coil of foil on my shelf now, green side down, and I have stopped trying to improve it in any way.
I am going to join the history club at school in September and point at my coin until somebody tells me what it is.
qs: How was the coin turned up?
By the spade while planting, in April.
What did Gran swear by?
Oil, which did nothing at all.
Why join the history club?
To point at the coin until somebody says what it is.

write.task: Explain how to look after something old you have found. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Coin in the Soil
paras: I found a coin in the soil by the gate in the middle of April, turned up by the edge of the spade while I was planting out the back border, and it was green all the way over on both faces.
It had been down in that soil for so long that it would not come clean in oil, which is the method Gran swore by for anything metal, and which in this particular case did absolutely nothing at all.

Dad said to boil it, so the two of us boiled it on the stove for ten minutes, and that spoiled a little of the pattern along one side of it without getting the thing any cleaner than it had been to start with.
It sits on a coil of foil on the shelf above my bed now, green side down so that the good face shows, and I have given up entirely on any further attempt to improve its condition.
I am going to join the history club at school in September and point at my coin at the first meeting until somebody in that room is able to tell me with any confidence what it actually is.
qs: Where was the narrator planting?
The back border.
What did boiling cost?
A little of the pattern along one side, with no gain in cleanliness.
How is the coin displayed?
Green side down, so the good face shows.

g2.title: The Boy and the Toy Truck

I did annoy him once. I did not do it again.
The toy is old and it is a joy to see it run.
He is a loyal boy. He will not let that toy be destroyed.

The boy next door has a toy truck.

g3.title: The Boy and the Toy Truck
paras: The boy next door has a toy truck that belonged to his father before him, and the paint has gone from the whole of one side.
He will not enjoy it on his own, which I think is the point of it, so he comes to the fence and asks whether I am coming out.
I did annoy him once, badly, by driving the truck down the step to see what it would do. I have not done it again and I will not.
The toy is older than both of us and it is still a joy to watch it run the length of the path with nobody touching it.
He is a loyal boy about that truck. He will not let it be destroyed by anybody, and I have come round to thinking he is right.
qs: Who owned the truck before?
His father owned it before him.
How did the narrator annoy him?
By driving the truck down the step.
What has the narrator come round to?
Thinking he is right to protect it.

write.task: Write the day of the step from the other boy's point of view. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Boy and the Toy Truck
paras: The boy next door has a toy truck that belonged to his father before him and to somebody else before that, and the paint has gone entirely from one whole side of it where it has been run along walls.
He will not enjoy that truck on his own, which I have slowly come to understand is more or less the entire point of it, so he comes down to the fence every afternoon and asks whether I am coming out.

I did annoy him once, and badly, by taking the truck and driving it down the stone step at the side of the house purely to see what it would do. I have not done it since and I am not going to do it again.
The toy is older than the two of us put together and it is still a genuine joy to watch it run the full length of the path on its own with nobody touching it and nobody pushing it along.

He is loyal to that truck in a way I did not understand at all to begin with. He will not let it be destroyed by anybody, however careless, and I have come round entirely to thinking that he is right about it.
qs: How did the paint come off?
It has been run along walls.
What is the point of the truck?
Not enjoying it on his own.
How has the narrator's view changed?
From not understanding his loyalty to agreeing with it entirely.

g2.title: The Cause of the Pause
paras: Paul had to pause on the path to school.

It was not Paul's fault. The cat would not haul itself up.
In August that cat sits in the sun all day because it is warm there.
Paul will pause for that cat. He says the cat is the author of the rule.
qs: Who had to pause?
Paul had to pause on the path to school.
What was the cause?
A big cat sat in the way.
When does the cat sit in the sun all day?
In August.

g3.title: The Cause of the Pause
paras: Paul has to pause on the path to school every morning at the same spot, about halfway along, and he has done since the start of August.
The cause is a large cat that sits square in the middle of the path and has no intention of being anywhere else.
It is not Paul's fault, and the cat is not at fault. The cat will not haul itself up for anybody, and Paul will not step over an animal.
In August the cat sat there all day because the stones hold the heat, and now that it is cooler it still sits there out of habit.
Paul pauses for that cat without complaining about it. He says the cat is the author of the rule and that he is only the one keeping it.
qs: Where on the path does he stop?
About halfway along.
Why did the cat sit there in August?
The stones hold the heat.
What does Paul say about the rule?
The cat is the author of it and he only keeps it.

write.task: Should Paul step over the cat? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Cause of the Pause
paras: Paul has to pause on the path to school every single morning at precisely the same spot, about halfway along where the wall ends, and he has been doing so without a break since the start of August.

The cause of the pause is a large cat that sits square in the middle of the path with all four feet tucked under it and has never once given any indication of intending to be anywhere else at that hour.

It is not Paul's fault and it is not really the cat's fault either. The cat will not haul itself up out of the way for anybody who comes along, and Paul has a settled rule against stepping over any animal.

Through August the cat sat on that path all day long, because the stones there hold the heat from morning until late evening, and now that the weather has turned it goes on sitting there out of nothing but habit.

Paul pauses for that cat each morning without complaining about it to anybody, including me. He says that the cat is the author of the rule and that he is merely the person who happens to be keeping it.
qs: What marks the spot?
It is where the wall ends.
What is Paul's settled rule?
He will not step over any animal.
Why does the cat still sit there?
Out of nothing but habit, now the weather has turned.

write.task: Write a report on habits, in animals and in people. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Hawk on the Lawn
paras: At dawn I saw a hawk on the lawn.
It had a bit of straw in its claw.
I did not draw it. I just sat and did not yawn.

I did draw the hawk when I got in. It was awful, but it was mine.
qs: What did the narrator see at dawn?
A hawk on the lawn.
What did the hawk have?
A bit of straw in its claw.
What is the law of the house?
We do not go on the lawn at dawn.

write.task: Write three facts about the hawk. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Hawk on the Lawn
paras: At dawn on Sunday I saw a hawk standing on the lawn, not twelve feet from the window, which has never happened before.
It had a long bit of straw caught in one claw and it spent some time trying to shake the straw off without losing any dignity.
I did not draw it while it was there. I sat on the stairs and watched and did not yawn once, which at that hour took some doing.
The law of this house is that nobody goes out on the lawn at dawn, because that is when the birds have it, and the law is Mom's.
I did draw the hawk from memory when I got back upstairs. The drawing was awful, but it was mine, and I know what it is meant to be.
qs: How close was the hawk?
Not twelve feet from the window.
What was the hawk trying to do?
Shake the straw off its claw without losing dignity.
Why is nobody allowed on the lawn at dawn?
Because that is when the birds have it.

write.task: Write the dawn from the hawk's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what it could see.

g4.title: The Hawk on the Lawn
paras: At dawn on Sunday morning I saw a hawk standing out on the lawn, not twelve feet away from the kitchen window, which in all the years we have lived in this house has never once happened before.

It had a long piece of straw caught round one claw and it spent a considerable stretch of time attempting to shake that straw off again without, as far as I could tell, losing any of its dignity in the process.

I did not draw it while it was actually standing there. I sat halfway down the stairs with my knees up and watched it instead, and I did not yawn once in all that time, which at that hour of the morning took real effort.
The law of this house is that nobody at all goes out onto the lawn at dawn, because dawn is when the birds have the run of it and we do not, and that law is Mom's and has never been open to argument.
I drew the hawk from memory when I got back upstairs to my room. The drawing was genuinely awful by any standard you care to apply, but it was mine, and I know perfectly well what it is meant to be.
qs: What makes the sighting remarkable?
It has never happened in all the years they have lived there.
Where did the narrator watch from?
Halfway down the stairs.
Why does the bad drawing still matter?
It is the narrator's own, and they know what it is meant to be.

write.task: Does a drawing have to be good to be worth keeping? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Table by the Stable
paras: There is an old table in the stable.
It is not able to hold much. One leg is not stable at all.
Gran keeps a bundle of straw on it and a marble in a tin.
She says the table is humble but it is able to do its job.
I think the table is a bit of a muddle. Gran is not able to see that.
qs: Where is the old table?
There is an old table in the stable.
What is wrong with it?
One leg is not stable at all.
What does Gran keep on it?
A bundle of straw and a marble in a tin.

write.task: Should the old table be kept? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Table by the Stable
paras: There is an old table in the stable at the end of the yard, and it has been in there longer than the horse has.
It is not able to hold very much any more. One leg is not stable and has been packed up with a folded bit of card for years.
Gran keeps a bundle of straw on one end of it and a marble in a tin on the other, and not one of those has moved since I was small.
She says the table is humble but that it is still able to do the one job it has, which is holding things off a wet floor.
I think the table is a muddle and always has been. Gran is not able to see that, and I have stopped pointing it out to her.
qs: What is older, the table or the horse?
The table has been in the stable longer.
How is the leg packed up?
With a folded bit of card.
What is the table's one job?
Holding things off a wet floor.

write.task: Write about a morning in the stable. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Table by the Stable
paras: There is an old table standing in the stable at the far end of the yard, and by everybody's reckoning it has been in that stable a good deal longer than the horse currently living in it has.

It is not able to hold very much of anything any more. One leg is not stable and has not been stable for years, and it has been packed up underneath with a folded piece of card that nobody has ever replaced with anything better.

Gran keeps a bundle of straw on one end of that table and a single marble in a tin on the other end, and neither of those two things has moved so much as an inch since I was small enough to be carried into the stable.
She says the table is a humble thing but that it is still perfectly able to do the one job it has ever been asked to do, which is to hold things up off a floor that is wet for most of the winter.
I think the table is a muddle, and I think it has been a muddle for as long as I have known it. Gran is not able to see that at all, and I gave up pointing it out to her some time ago.
qs: What has nobody replaced?
The folded piece of card under the leg.
How long have the straw and marble sat there?
Since the narrator was small enough to be carried in.
Why does the floor matter?
It is wet for most of the winter.

write.task: Write a report on why people keep old furniture. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Cycle by the Circle
paras: Uncle Ben has an old cycle in the shed. A cycle is the same as a bicycle.
He rides the cycle round the circle of grass at the park.
There is a crack in one handle. My uncle will not fix it.
My uncle says a cycle is a simple thing and must stay simple.
I rode his cycle round the circle once. Now I want a cycle of my own.
qs: What does Uncle Ben have?
Uncle Ben has an old cycle in the shed.
Where does he ride it?
Round the circle of grass at the park.
What does my uncle say about a cycle?
He says a cycle is a simple thing and must stay simple.

write.task: Write three facts about the cycle. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Cycle by the Circle
paras: Uncle Ben has an old cycle in the shed that he bought second hand in a year he will not name.
He rides it round the circle of grass at the park on Sunday mornings, always the same way round, and always eleven times.
There is a crack in one handle that has been there since before I was born. He will not have it fixed and will not discuss it.
My uncle says a cycle is a simple article and that it has to stay a simple one, and that anything you cannot mend at the roadside has no business being on a cycle.
I rode the cycle once, as far as the gate and back. I want a cycle of my own now, and I would like one exactly as simple as his.
qs: How often does he ride the circle?
Eleven times, every Sunday morning.
How old is the crack?
It has been there since before the narrator was born.
What is his rule about parts?
Anything you cannot mend at the roadside has no business on a bike.

write.task: Is a simple machine better than a complicated one? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Cycle by the Circle
paras: Uncle Ben has an old cycle hanging up in the shed that he bought second hand a very long time ago, in a year which he has consistently declined to name to anybody who has asked him directly.

He rides it round the circle of grass at the park on Sunday mornings between eight and nine, always in the same direction, and always exactly eleven times round before he stops and leans it on the railings.

There is a crack running through one of the handles which has been there since before I was born. He will not have it fixed by anybody and he will not discuss having it fixed, and the subject is closed.

My uncle says that a cycle is a simple article and that it is obliged to remain a simple article, and that any part of a machine which you cannot mend at the side of the road with your hands has no business being on a bicycle at all.
I rode it once, as far as the gate at the end of the lane and back again, under supervision. I want a cycle of my own now, and what I want is one that is exactly as simple as his is.
qs: When exactly does he ride?
Between eight and nine on Sunday mornings.
Where does he leave the cycle afterwards?
Leaning on the railings.
What test must a part pass?
You must be able to mend it at the roadside with your hands.

write.task: Write the one ride to the gate and back. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Candle and the Puddle
paras: We had a candle on the middle of the table.
The wind got in and it went out. Dad did not fiddle with it.
He got a bundle of sticks and made a fire in the grate.
I had to paddle out to the shed in a puddle to get more.
Now we sit in the middle of the room. The candle can wait.
qs: Where was the candle?
On the middle of the table.
What did Dad get?
He got a bundle of sticks.
What did the narrator paddle through?
A puddle, out to the shed.

write.task: Tell what happened when the candle went out, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Candle and the Puddle
paras: We had a candle standing in the middle of the table on Friday because the power had gone off across the whole village.
The wind got in under the door and the candle went out twice. Dad did not fiddle about with it a third time.
He went and got a bundle of dry sticks from under the stairs and made a proper fire in the grate instead, which took him four minutes.
I had to paddle out to the shed through a puddle the size of the path to fetch more wood, in boots that are not as waterproof as advertised.
We sat in the middle of the room for the rest of the evening with the fire going. The candle can wait until the next time, and there will be a next time.
qs: Why was there a candle?
The power had gone off across the whole village.
How long did the fire take to make?
Four minutes.
What was wrong with the boots?
They are not as waterproof as advertised.

write.task: Explain what to do when the power goes off. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Candle and the Puddle
paras: We had a candle standing upright in the middle of the kitchen table on Friday evening, because the power had gone off across the whole of the village at about six and nobody could say when it would be back.
The wind got in underneath the back door and put the candle out twice inside ten minutes. Dad did not fiddle about with trying to relight it for a third time, which I thought showed good sense.

He went and got a bundle of dry sticks from the store under the stairs and built a proper fire in the grate instead, and from striking the first match to having it drawing well took him a little under four minutes.

I had to paddle out to the shed through a puddle that covered the entire width of the path to fetch more wood for it, wearing a pair of boots that are a great deal less waterproof than the people who sold them claimed.

We sat in the middle of the room for the whole of the rest of that evening with the fire going and the candle unlit on the table. The candle can wait until the next time, and in this village there is always a next time.
qs: How long did the candle last?
It went out twice inside ten minutes.
What does four minutes measure?
From the first match to the fire drawing well.
Why will there be a next time?
In this village the power goes off regularly.

write.task: Is a fire better than a candle in a power cut? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Eagle and the Single Tree
paras: A single tree stands up on the hill.
An eagle sits in it. It will not struggle to hold on in the wind.
We giggle when it fluffs up like a bundle of rags.
Dad says do not giggle at an eagle. It can see a single mouse from up there.
The eagle sits in that single tree all day. It will not budge.
qs: What stands up on the hill?
A single tree stands up on the hill.
What sits in the tree?
An eagle sits in it.
What can the eagle see?
It can see a single mouse from up there.

write.task: Write three facts about the eagle. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Eagle and the Single Tree
paras: A single tree stands up on the hill above the farm, with nothing else within half a mile of it in any direction.
An eagle sits in that tree most afternoons and does not struggle to hold on, even on days when the wind is bending the top branches right over.
We giggle at it when it fluffs itself up and looks, for a moment, exactly like a bundle of old rags somebody left in a tree.
Dad says not to giggle at an eagle, because an eagle can pick out a single mouse in the grass from up there and we cannot pick out a rabbit.
It sits in that single tree all day in October and will not budge for us, the dog, or the tractor going past underneath it.
qs: How far is the nearest other tree?
Half a mile in any direction.
What does the eagle look like when fluffed up?
A bundle of old rags left in a tree.
What will not move it?
Not the family, the dog, or the tractor.

write.task: Write an afternoon from the eagle's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what it could see.

g4.title: The Eagle and the Single Tree
paras: A single tree stands up on the hill above the farm buildings, and there is nothing else of any height at all within half a mile of it in any direction you care to walk.

An eagle sits in that tree most afternoons through October and does not appear to struggle to hold on in the slightest, even on the days when the wind is bending the whole top of the tree right over to one side.

We giggle at it from the yard when it fluffs itself up against the cold, because for a few seconds at a time it looks exactly like a bundle of old rags that somebody has thrown up into the branches and left there.

Dad says that we should not giggle at an eagle, on the grounds that an eagle can pick out a single mouse moving in the grass from that height, and that none of us standing in the yard could reliably pick out a rabbit.
It sits up in that single tree the whole day long and will not budge for any of us, or for the dog barking at the gate, or for the tractor going past directly underneath the branches twice a day.
qs: When is the eagle there?
Most afternoons through October.
What is Dad's comparison?
An eagle spots a mouse; the family could not spot a rabbit.
How often does the tractor pass?
Twice a day, directly underneath.

write.task: Should we admire animals that can do what we cannot? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Apple and the Maple
paras: We have one apple tree and one maple by the wall.
The apple tree is simple to climb. The maple is not.
Gran has a sample of each leaf in a book.
She says a simple apple is the best thing in the world.
I think so too. An apple from that tree beats an apple from a shop.
qs: What two trees are by the wall?
One apple tree and one maple.
Which tree is simple to climb?
The apple tree is simple to climb.
What does Gran keep in a book?
A sample of each leaf.

write.task: Which tree is better, the apple or the maple? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Apple and the Maple
paras: We have one apple tree and one maple standing by the wall at the bottom of the garden, and they were planted on the same day.
The apple tree is simple to climb because the branches start low. The maple is not simple at all and I have never got above the first fork.
Gran keeps a sample of each leaf pressed in a book on the shelf, with the date of the day they were planted written underneath in pencil.
She says a simple apple off your own tree is the best thing in the world and that nobody who has had one would argue with her.
I think so too. An apple off that tree beats an apple from the shop by a distance, and the maple has never produced anything at all.
qs: When were the trees planted?
On the same day.
Why is the apple tree simple to climb?
The branches start low.
What is written under the leaves?
The date of the day they were planted.

write.task: Explain how to press and keep a leaf. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Apple and the Maple
paras: We have one apple tree and one maple standing together by the wall at the bottom of the garden, and according to Gran the two of them were planted on the very same afternoon.

The apple tree is simple to climb, because the lowest branches start at about chest height. The maple is not simple in the least, and in eleven years I have never once got myself above the first fork of it.
Gran keeps a sample of each of the two leaves pressed flat in a book on the shelf by the stairs, with the date of the day they were planted written underneath both of them in pencil in her own hand.
She says that a simple apple taken off your own tree is the best thing in the world, and that no person who has ever actually had one is in any position to argue the point with her.

I think so as well, having compared them carefully. An apple off that tree beats an apple from any shop by a considerable distance, and the maple, in all that time, has never produced one single thing.
qs: How high are the lowest branches?
About chest height.
How long has the maple defeated the narrator?
Eleven years.
What has the maple produced?
Not one single thing.

write.task: Write the day the two trees were planted. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Kettle and the Thistle
paras: Mom has a little kettle that she will not throw out.
It has a dent in the side and the handle will rattle.
She sets the kettle on the stove and it starts to whistle.
Out the back there is a thistle as tall as the gate.
Mom will not cut that thistle and she will not toss that kettle.
qs: What will Mom not throw out?
Mom has a little kettle that she will not throw out.
What does the kettle do on the stove?
The kettle starts to whistle.
What is out the back?
A thistle as tall as the gate.

write.task: Tell what the kettle does, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Kettle and the Thistle
paras: Mom has a little kettle that she will not throw out under any circumstances, and it has been on that stove since before the house was ours.
It has a dent in one side where it came off the shelf in a move, and the handle will rattle the whole time the water is heating.
She sets the kettle on the stove at seven every morning and it starts to whistle at about four minutes past, which is how the house knows the day has begun.
Out the back there is a thistle growing by the step that is now as tall as the gate and has been left alone for two full summers.
Mom will not cut that thistle and she will not throw out that kettle, and she has given reasons for both that I have decided not to argue with.
qs: Where did the dent come from?
It came off the shelf in a move.
How does the house know the day has begun?
The kettle whistles at about four minutes past seven.
How long has the thistle been left?
Two full summers.

write.task: Should the thistle be cut down? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Kettle and the Thistle
paras: Mom has a little kettle that she will not throw out under any circumstances that have yet been put to her, and it has been sitting on that same stove since a point before this house was ours at all.
It has a dent in one side where it came off a shelf during a move a long time ago, and the handle will rattle steadily against the body of it for the entire time the water inside is heating up.

She sets the kettle on the stove at seven o'clock every single morning and it starts to whistle at about four minutes past, which is the signal by which everybody in this house knows that the day has properly begun.
Out the back there is a thistle growing up beside the step which is now very nearly as tall as the gate beside it, and which has been deliberately left alone for two complete summers running.

Mom will not cut that thistle down and she will not throw out that kettle, and she has given clear reasons for both of those positions which I have thought about carefully and decided not to argue with.
qs: What does the handle do while heating?
It rattles steadily against the body of the kettle.
What is the signal for the day beginning?
The whistle at about four minutes past seven.
Why does the narrator not argue?
Mom has given clear reasons that the narrator has thought about carefully.

write.task: Write a report on why people keep things that look worn out. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Station and the Question
paras: We met at the station at ten.
I had one question for Mom: what is the action plan?
Her solution was simple. The action was to sit and wait.
A man made a big production of it and ran for his train.
That was the end of my question. Our train came in at the station on time.
qs: Where did they meet?
We met at the station at ten.
What was the question?
What is the action plan?
What was Mom's solution?
The action was to sit and wait.

write.task: Tell what happened at the station, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Station and the Question
paras: We met at the station at ten on Saturday, under the board, because that is where this family has always met and no discussion has ever been needed.
I had one question for Mom while we stood there, which was what the action plan would be if the train did not come at all.
Her solution was simple and I should have guessed it. We would sit on the bench by the station wall and wait, and we would not fuss.
A man further along the platform made a great production of it instead, and ran the length of the station for a train that was not his.
That rather settled my question. Our train came into the station two minutes early, which in my whole life I have never known to happen before.
qs: Where does the family always meet?
Under the board at the station.
What was Mom's solution?
To sit on the bench by the station wall and wait without fussing.
What happened to the train?
It came into the station two minutes early.

write.task: Is it better to wait calmly or to act quickly? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Station and the Question
paras: We met at the station at ten o'clock on Saturday morning, directly under the departures board, because that is where this family has always met one another and no discussion about it has ever been necessary.
I had exactly one question for Mom while the two of us stood there waiting, which was what the action plan was going to be in the event that the train simply did not come at all.

Her solution was perfectly simple, and I should have been able to guess it without asking. We would sit down on the bench by the station wall and we would wait, and under no circumstances would we fuss.

A man further along the platform made an enormous production of the same situation instead, and ran the entire length of the station in his coat for a train that turned out not to be his train at all.

That rather conclusively settled my question. Our train came into the station two full minutes early, which is something that in the whole of my life travelling from that station I have never once known to happen.
qs: Where exactly do they meet?
Directly under the departures board.
Why should the narrator have guessed?
Mom's solution is always to sit, wait and not fuss.
What settled the question?
The train came in two full minutes early.

write.task: Write a report on how people behave while waiting. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Mission and the Decision
paras: Dad set me a mission on Sunday.
The mission was to sort the shed with no help. It was a big mission.
I had to make a decision: toss it out or keep it.
My vision for that shed was a big one. I got half of it done.
Dad said half a mission is still a mission. That was his decision.
qs: What did Dad set on Sunday?
Dad set me a mission.
What was the mission?
To sort the shed with no help.
What did Dad say at the end?
He said half a mission is still a mission.

write.task: Was half the mission good enough? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Mission and the Decision
paras: Dad set me a mission on Sunday morning, which is what he calls a job he does not want to do himself but will not say so about.
The mission was to sort out the whole shed on my own, with no help from anybody and no discussion about the method.
Every single thing in there needed a decision made about it: throw it out, or keep it and find it a place. There were about sixty things.
My vision for that shed was an ambitious one, with shelves and labels and a clear floor. I got through rather less than half of it by dark.
Dad said that half a mission is still a mission, which was his decision and not mine, and I have accepted it on the grounds that I am tired.
qs: What does Dad mean by a mission?
A job he does not want to do himself.
How many things needed a decision?
About sixty.
What was the narrator's vision?
Shelves, labels and a clear floor.

write.task: Write the Sunday in the shed. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Mission and the Decision
paras: Dad set me a mission on Sunday morning, and a mission in this house is what he calls a job that he has no intention of doing himself and no intention of admitting that about either.
The mission was to sort out the entire shed on my own, from the door to the back wall, with no help from anybody in the house and no discussion whatsoever about the method I was to use.

Every single object in that shed required a decision to be made about it, one way or the other: throw it out for good, or keep it and find it somewhere sensible to live. There were, at a conservative count, about sixty objects.

My vision for that shed was an ambitious one by any standard, involving shelves along two walls, written labels on everything, and a completely clear floor. I got through rather less than half of all that before the light went.

Dad said afterwards that half a mission is still a mission, which was entirely his own decision and in no sense mine, and I have decided to accept it without argument on the straightforward grounds that I was extremely tired.
qs: What does Dad not admit?
That a mission is a job he has no intention of doing himself.
What two outcomes did each decision have?
Throw it out for good, or keep it and find it somewhere to live.
Why did the narrator accept the verdict?
On the grounds of being extremely tired.

write.task: Should a job be judged on effort or on what gets finished? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Keys Dad Couldn't Find
paras: Dad can't find his keys. He says they aren't in the car.
Mom didn't move them. She hasn't been in the car all week.
I don't know where they are and I won't look again.
They weren't in his coat. They weren't on the hook by the door.
Gran didn't say a word. She just held them up. Dad couldn't say much to that.
qs: What can't Dad find?
Dad can't find his keys.
Where weren't they?
They weren't in his coat or on the hook.
Who had them?
Gran had them and just held them up.

write.task: Tell how the keys were found, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Keys Dad Couldn't Find
paras: Dad can't find his keys, and he is certain they aren't in the car, because he says he checked the car twice before he started shouting.
Mom didn't move them and hasn't been anywhere near that car all week, which she pointed out once and then didn't repeat.
I don't know where they are and I won't go and look again, because I have looked three times and I wasn't the one who lost them.
They weren't in his coat pocket and they weren't on the hook by the door, which are the only two places he ever puts them.
Gran didn't say a word through any of it. She just held them up at the end, and Dad couldn't think of much to say to that.
qs: Why is Dad certain about the car?
He checked it twice before he started shouting.
How many times has the narrator looked?
Three times.
Where does Dad normally put them?
In his coat pocket or on the hook by the door.

write.task: Who should look for a lost thing — the owner or everybody? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Keys Dad Couldn't Find
paras: Dad can't find his keys anywhere in the house, and he is entirely certain that they aren't in the car, because by his own account he checked the car twice over before he started raising his voice about it.
Mom didn't move them and hasn't been anywhere near that car at any point all week. She pointed this out exactly once, in a level voice, and then didn't say it again however the search went.
I don't know where they are and I won't go and look for them again, because I have already looked in three rooms, twice, and I wasn't the person who lost them in the first place.
They weren't in his coat pocket and they weren't on the hook by the back door, and those two places between them are the only places he has ever put a set of keys in the whole of his adult life.
Gran didn't say one word through any part of this. She waited until it had gone properly quiet and then simply held them up, and Dad couldn't find a great deal to say to that.
qs: What did Mom do after making her point?
She didn't say it again, however the search went.
Why does the narrator refuse to look?
They have looked three rooms twice and did not lose them.
When did Gran produce the keys?
After it had gone properly quiet.

write.task: Write the search from Gran's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: That's Dad's Cap
paras: That's Dad's cap on the hook by the door.
It's not Mom's cap and it's not mine.
He's had it since he was ten. He's not going to toss it.
Gran's take is that it's time for a fresh one.
Dad's take is that it's fine. He's right, if you ask me.
qs: Whose cap is on the hook?
That's Dad's cap.
How long has he had it?
He's had it since he was ten.
What does Gran say?
Gran's take is that it's time for a fresh one.

write.task: Should Dad get a new cap? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: That's Dad's Cap
paras: That's Dad's cap on the hook by the back door, and it's been on that hook or on his head every day since we moved in.
It's not Mom's cap and it's certainly not mine, and nobody in this house has ever picked it up by mistake, because there's no mistaking it.
He's had it since he was ten years old, which he'll tell you himself without being asked. He's not going to throw it out and that's settled.
Gran's position is that it's long past time for a fresh one and that there's no shame in it. She's said so at every birthday for six years.
Dad's position is that it's perfectly fine and that a cap's job is to keep the sun off. He's right, if anybody's asking me.
qs: How long has it been on the hook?
Every day since they moved in.
How often does Gran say it?
At every birthday for six years.
What does Dad say a cap's job is?
To keep the sun off.

write.task: Explain why people get attached to old clothes. Group your ideas and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: That's Dad's Cap
paras: That's Dad's cap hanging on the hook by the back door, and it's been either on that hook or on his head every single day since the week we moved into this house, with no exceptions that anybody can name.

It's not Mom's cap and it's certainly not mine, and nobody living here has ever once picked it up by mistake on the way out, for the straightforward reason that there is no mistaking it for anything else.

He's had it since he was ten years old, a fact he'll tell you himself inside two minutes of the cap coming up in conversation. He's not going to throw it out at this stage, and as far as he's concerned that's settled.

Gran's view is that it's long past time he got a fresh one and that there's no shame whatsoever in retiring a cap. She's said exactly that at every single birthday of his for the last six years running.
Dad's view is that it's perfectly fine as it stands and that a cap's only real job is keeping the sun off a person's face. He's right about that, if anybody in this house is actually asking me.
qs: Why has nobody taken it by mistake?
There is no mistaking it for anything else.
How quickly will he tell you its age?
Inside two minutes of the cap coming up.
What is Gran's second point?
That there's no shame in retiring a cap.

write.task: Write the story of the cap from when he was ten. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: We'll Go at Ten
paras: I'll go to the shop at ten. We'll get bread and jam.

g3.title: We'll Go at Ten
paras: I'll go down to the shop at ten and we'll get bread, jam and whatever else is on the list by the kettle.

g4.title: We'll Go at Ten
paras: I'll go down to the shop at ten o'clock and we'll get bread, jam, and whatever else has been added to the list that lives on the shelf by the kettle and gets written on by everybody.
Mom says she'll come along with me if the rain has stopped before then, and on the look of the sky from the kitchen window this morning she'll very probably be able to manage that without difficulty.
If it hasn't stopped by ten, I'll go on my own with the big canvas bag and the rest of them will simply have to wait for their bread until I'm back, which they'll survive perfectly well.
You'll see how it goes. It'll be entirely fine, nobody in this house is going to starve in the meantime, and whatever my brother says about it between now and then can safely be ignored.

We'll be back before one o'clock at the very latest. That'll give everybody in the house time to eat properly before the match starts, which, if we're honest about it, is the only part of any of this that actually matters.
qs: Who writes on the list?
Everybody.
What will the others have to do?
Wait for their bread until the narrator is back.
What is the only part that matters?
Eating before the match starts.

g3.title: We've Got the List
paras: I've got the list in my pocket and we've got the big bag, which between them are the only two things anybody in this house ever forgets.
They've shut the shop on Sundays since the spring, so you've got to go on a Monday now, and half the village still turns up on a Sunday and finds the door locked.
I've been in that shop twice already this week and both times the man behind the counter asked after Gran before he asked what I wanted.

g4.title: We've Got the List
paras: I've got the list folded up in my coat pocket and we've got the big canvas bag by the door, which between the two of them are the only things that anybody in this house has ever managed to forget on a shopping morning.

They've shut the shop on Sundays since the spring, so you've got to go on a Monday instead now, and a good half of this village still turns up on a Sunday morning out of habit and finds the door firmly locked.

I've been into that shop twice already this week, and on both occasions the man behind the counter asked after Gran and how she was keeping before he got round to asking me what it was that I had actually come in for.

We've had the same list stuck to the shelf by the kettle for the better part of a month now, and I've not lost it once in all that time, which, given my long and well-documented record with pieces of paper, is worth saying out loud.

They've said the shop will be opening at ten this morning rather than at nine as it usually does. We've got plenty of time, and we've decided between us to walk down rather than take the car for once.
qs: Where is the list kept and carried?
Stuck to the shelf by the kettle, and folded in a coat pocket.
What does half the village still do?
Turns up on a Sunday out of habit and finds the door locked.
What have they decided?
To walk down rather than take the car.

g2.title: The Artist and the List
paras: Mom is an artist. She has a list of jobs on the wall.
The dentist is on that list. So is the florist.
I made a fist and did a twist. The artist did not look up.
An artist must insist on time to work.
That list will exist until the last job on it is done.

Mom is an artist.
Who is on the list?
The dentist is on that list, and so is the florist.

An artist must insist on time to work.

g3.title: The Artist and the List
paras: Mom is an artist, and she keeps a list of jobs pinned to the wall by the door that is longer at the end of every week than it was at the start.
The dentist is on that list and has been since February. So is the florist, for reasons nobody has yet explained to me.
I made a fist and did a twist and a whole dance in front of her easel on Thursday. The artist did not look up once.
An artist has to insist on having time to work, she says, because nobody is going to hand that time over without being asked for it.
That list will exist on that wall until the very last job on it has been done, and on current form the list is going to outlive us all.
qs: How does the list change each week?
It is longer at the end than at the start.
What did the artist do during the dance?
She did not look up once.
Why must an artist insist on time?
Because nobody hands that time over without being asked.

write.task: Should people be left alone while they work? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Artist and the List
paras: Mom is an artist by trade, and she keeps a list of jobs pinned to the wall beside the kitchen door which is reliably longer at the end of each week than it was at the beginning of that same week.
The dentist has been on that list since February without moving up or down it at all. So has the florist, for reasons that nobody in this house has yet been willing or able to explain to me properly.

I made a fist and did a twist and then a complete and frankly excellent dance directly in front of her easel on Tuesday afternoon. The artist did not look up from the canvas even once during any of it.
An artist has to insist on having the time to work, she says, because nobody anywhere is ever going to simply hand that time over to her without being asked for it clearly and more than once.
That list will exist on that wall until the very last job written on it has actually been done, and on the evidence of the last six months the list is comfortably going to outlive every one of us.
qs: How has the dentist entry changed?
It has not moved up or down since February.
What does the artist's focus show?
She did not look up from the canvas even once.
What does the evidence suggest about the list?
It will outlive all of them.

g3.title: The Old Table
paras: Our old table is still perfectly able to hold everything we put on it, and on Sundays that is eleven plates and a pot.
Dad says it is not valuable in the slightest and never has been, but that it is comfortable to sit at, which he rates far higher.
The cable from the lamp runs under the table and up the back of the chair, which is not tidy but is the only route that works.
The cloth on it is washable, and that is the single most useful thing about it given what happens at this table on a Sunday.
An old table that is able to do the job it was bought for is good enough for anybody, and I have never heard a good argument against that.
qs: What goes on it on Sundays?
Eleven plates and a pot.
What does Dad rate higher than value?
Being comfortable to sit at.
Why does the washable cloth matter?
Given what happens at the table on a Sunday.

write.task: Explain how to choose furniture that lasts. Group your ideas and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Old Table
paras: Our old table is still entirely able to hold everything that we put on top of it, and on a Sunday afternoon that means eleven plates, a pot, and whatever anybody has carried in from somewhere else.

Dad says that it is not valuable in the slightest and that it never has been at any point in its life, but that it is comfortable to sit at for hours, and comfort is a quality he rates a great deal higher than value.

The cable from the standing lamp runs underneath the table and then up the back of the chair in the corner, which is not tidy by anybody's standards but is the only route through that room which actually works.

The cloth laid over it is washable at high temperature, and that is far and away the single most suitable thing about it, given everything that regularly happens at this table on a Sunday with eleven people round it.

An old table that is still able to do the job it was originally bought to do is good enough for anybody at all, and in all the years I have been making that argument nobody has given me a good answer to it.
qs: What else ends up on the table?
Whatever anybody has carried in from somewhere else.
Why is the cable routed badly?
It is the only route through the room that works.
How has the narrator's argument fared?
Nobody has given a good answer to it.

write.task: Write a Sunday around that table. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Pond Is Horrible
paras: Is it possible to get a fish from that pond?

The fish are visible from the bank. They are not edible.
The smell from that pond is horrible. It is terrible in June.
It is not possible to sit there long. That is a sensible thing to know.

He says it is possible but not sensible.
Can you see the fish?
The fish are visible from the bank.
What is the smell like?
The smell from that pond is horrible.

g3.title: The Pond Is Horrible
paras: It is possible to get a fish out of the pond at the bottom of the lane, and my brother has done it twice, which settles the question of whether it can be done.
Dad says that it being possible and it being sensible are two entirely separate matters, and that only one of them applies to that pond.
The fish are clearly visible from the bank on a still day, lying just under the surface, and not one of them is edible by any standard.
The smell coming off that water is horrible in April and truly terrible by the middle of June, when the weed comes up and the level drops.
It is not possible to sit on that bank for more than about ten minutes in summer, and knowing that in advance is the sensible part.
qs: Who has got a fish out, and how often?
The narrator's brother, twice.
Where do the fish lie?
Just under the surface, visible from the bank.
What makes June worse?
The weed comes up and the level drops.

write.task: Explain why some water goes bad in summer. Group your ideas and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Pond Is Horrible
paras: It is entirely possible to get a fish out of the pond at the bottom of the lane, and my brother has managed to do exactly that on two separate occasions, which settles for good the question of whether the thing can be done at all.

Dad says that a thing being possible and that same thing being sensible are two completely separate matters which people confuse constantly, and that only one of the two has ever applied to that particular pond.

The fish are clearly visible from the bank on any still day, lying just below the surface and barely moving, and not a single one of them is edible by any standard that anybody sensible would want to apply.
The smell coming up off that water is horrible as early as April and becomes genuinely terrible by the middle of June, which is when the weed comes up through it and the water level drops away.

It is not possible to sit on that bank for more than about ten minutes at a stretch in high summer, and knowing that fact in advance of going down there is the only sensible part of the whole business.
qs: What do people constantly confuse?
A thing being possible with that thing being sensible.
How do the fish behave?
They lie just below the surface, barely moving.
What is the sensible part?
Knowing in advance you cannot sit there long.

write.task: Should the pond be cleaned up or left alone? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.
