g3.title: The Olive Tree Gran Keeps
paras: Gran is more active at her age than most people are at fifty. She will drive into town and back at five in the afternoon without thinking anything of it.
She keeps an olive tree in a pot by the door that is somehow still alive after eleven winters in a country it has no business growing in.
The tree is native to a warm, dry land and ours is not warm and not dry, which is why she carries the pot indoors every November without fail.
She will give me an olive off it if I ask her, and they are massive ones, far bigger than anything in the shops, and far more bitter as well.
An active Gran with a living olive tree in a pot is a fine thing for anybody to have in the family, and I am aware that I am lucky.
qs: How does Gran compare with others?
She is more active at her age than most people are at fifty.
How long has the olive tree survived?
Eleven winters.
How do the olives compare with shop ones?
Far bigger and far more bitter.

write.task: Write the November the tree comes indoors. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Olive Tree Gran Keeps
paras: Gran is a great deal more active at eighty than most people I know are at fifty. She will drive into town and back again at five in the afternoon in bad light and think absolutely nothing of it afterwards.
She keeps an olive tree in a heavy pot beside the front door which is somehow still alive after eleven complete winters in a country where it has no business whatsoever attempting to grow at all.

The tree is native to a warm and dry climate and ours is reliably neither of those two things, which is the entire reason she carries that pot indoors every November without once forgetting or needing reminding.
She will give me an olive off it if I ask her for one, and they are massive things, far larger than anything you can buy in a shop, and also a great deal more bitter than anybody expects them to be.
An active Gran with a living olive tree standing in a pot by her door is a fine thing for any family to have, and I am entirely aware of how lucky that makes me, and I try to say so.
qs: What does she do in bad light?
Drive into town and back at five.
Why does the pot come indoors?
Our climate is neither warm nor dry.
What does the narrator try to do?
Say out loud how lucky they are.

write.task: Is it worth growing a plant that does not suit the climate? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

Mom had to return the lamp to the shop.

He said he would replace it, not repair it.

g3.title: The Lamp We Had to Return
paras: Mom had to return the lamp to the shop on Saturday, three days after she had bought it, which is not how any of us had planned to spend the morning.
It did not work at all, not even for a second, and she had no wish to repeat the trip a second time if there was any way of avoiding it.
The man behind the counter said that he would replace the lamp rather than repair it, because repairing a lamp that new would cost more than the lamp.
I had to remind her twice to take the box with us, because the shop will not replace anything that does not come back in its own box.
We did not have to return a third time. The replacement lamp works perfectly and has done since the day it came home.
qs: How long after buying did she return it?
Three days.
Why replace rather than repair?
Repairing a lamp that new would cost more than the lamp.
Why did the box matter?
The shop will not replace anything that does not come back in its own box.

write.task: Should shops always replace things that break? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Lamp We Had to Return
paras: Mom had to return the lamp to the shop on Saturday morning, three days after she had bought it and carried it home, which is not remotely how any of us had planned on spending that particular morning.

It did not work at all, not for so much as a second after it was plugged in, and she had no desire whatsoever to repeat the whole trip a second time if there turned out to be any way at all of avoiding it.

The man behind the counter said straight away that he would replace the lamp rather than attempt to repair it, on the sensible grounds that repairing a lamp that new would cost rather more than the lamp itself had.
I had to remind her twice before we left the house to bring the box along with us, because the shop will not replace anything at all that does not come back to them inside its own original box.
We did not have to return to that shop a third time. The replacement lamp has worked perfectly from the day it came home and is still working now, several months later.
qs: How long did the lamp work?
Not for so much as a second after it was plugged in.
What were the grounds for replacing?
Repairing it would cost more than the lamp had.
How long has the replacement lasted?
Several months, and it is still working.

g4.title: Dad Will Prepare the Meal
paras: Dad will prepare the whole of the meal himself on Sunday, which in practice means that he will preheat the pan at about half past ten in the morning for a dish that does not go into it until twelve.

I predict that it will be good, because it is good the overwhelming majority of the time, and the handful of occasions when it has not been good were all occasions when somebody talked him into changing one thing.

Mom will prepay for the trip up to Gran's house on Monday so that not one person has to think about money on the day itself, which is more or less how she prefers to arrange absolutely everything in her life.

Gran will be present at that meal for the first time since March, and that is the actual reason that any of this is happening at all, and yet nobody in the house has said so out loud at any point this week.
We will all pretend not to be particularly glad about it, because that is simply the way this family operates and always has. To prepare properly and to prevent any kind of fuss is the entire plan.
qs: When has the food disappointed?
Only when somebody talked him into changing one thing.
How does Mom prefer to arrange things?
So nobody has to think about money on the day.
What has nobody said out loud?
That the meal is really because Gran will be there.

g3.title: The Frog Project
paras: We have a project at school this term that we chose ourselves, which is not how projects usually work in our class.
I promised in front of everybody to do my part of it, and I have found since that promising in front of people makes a real difference.
Mom will provide the card and the paste out of her own money, and we will produce a sign big enough to be read from the road.
The plan is to protect the frogs in the pond by the gate, because there are fewer of them every spring and nobody has asked why.

Big enough to be read from the road.

g4.title: The Frog Project
paras: We have a project at school this term which the class chose entirely for itself, and that is not in any way how projects have ever worked in our class before this year.

I promised in front of everybody in the room that I would do my part of it properly, and I have discovered since then that promising a thing in front of other people makes a genuine difference to whether it gets done.
Mom will provide the card and the glue out of her own money without being asked twice, and between us we will produce a sign large enough to be read clearly from the far side of the road.

The plan is to protect the frogs in the pond by the gate at the bottom of the lane, because there have been fewer of them every single spring for four years and not one person in authority has asked why that might be.

We will protest if the council decides to fill that pond in, and we have said so in writing. That is a proper project, and it is the first piece of school work I have genuinely cared about since I started there.
qs: What did the narrator discover about promising?
Promising in front of people makes a real difference to whether it gets done.
How long has the decline gone on?
Four years.
What have they already done?
Said in writing that they will protest.

g3.title: The Bus Will Depart at Ten
paras: The bus will depart from the end of the lane at ten exactly and it will not delay for anybody, which everybody in this village has learned the hard way.
We depend on that bus to get to school on the days we do not walk, and the whole morning is built around the fact that it does not wait.
Mom will decide whether we go by bus or by car when she looks out of the window at half past nine, and it depends entirely on the rain.
The man will deliver the bread at nine, before any of that is settled, and he has never once been late in the four years he has been doing it.
I can detect the smell of that bread from the front step before he has got out of the van, and I will defend my share of it against anybody in this house.
qs: What has the village learned the hard way?
That the bus will not delay for anybody.
When does Mom decide?
At half past nine, when she looks out of the window.
How reliable is the bread man?
Never once late in four years.

write.task: Explain how to get out of the house on time. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Bus Will Depart at Ten
paras: The bus will depart from the end of our lane at ten o'clock exactly and it will not delay for anybody at all, which is something that every single person in this village has learned the hard way at least once.
We depend on that bus to get to school on any day that we are not walking in, and the entire shape of the morning in this house is built around the plain fact that the bus does not wait for a soul.

Mom will decide whether we are going by bus or by car at the moment she looks out of the kitchen window at half past nine, and the decision depends entirely and only on what the rain is doing at that moment.
The man will deliver the bread at nine, well before any of that has been settled one way or the other, and in the four years he has been driving this round he has not once been late to our gate.
I can detect the smell of that bread from the front step before he has even got himself out of the van, and I will defend my own share of it against anybody else living in this house, including Dad.
qs: What is the morning built around?
The plain fact that the bus does not wait.
What does the decision depend on?
Only on what the rain is doing at half past nine.
Who is included in the narrator's defence?
Anybody in the house, including Dad.

write.task: Should buses wait for late passengers? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g3.title: The Form on the Desk
paras: Dad has a form on his desk that has been there since last Wednesday, and it is the same form he filled in at the start of the year.
He has to inform the school that I will be out on Monday, and the only way the school will accept that information is on this form.

paras: Mom was on a call that mattered on Thursday afternoon, and I walked in and interrupted her twice inside about a minute.

g4.title: Do Not Interrupt
paras: Mom was on a call that genuinely mattered on Thursday afternoon, and I walked straight into the room and interrupted her twice within the space of about a minute without noticing I was doing it.

She told me afterwards, perfectly calmly, that to interrupt a person in the middle of a sentence is rude whatever your reason happens to be, and that she was not going to stand there arguing the point with me.

The call itself ended rather abruptly after the second interruption, because the man at the other end of it had somewhere else that he needed to be and quite reasonably took the opening when it appeared.

I am not going to interrupt a call like that again if I can help it. A single interruption at exactly the wrong moment can disrupt an entire afternoon's work and, on a bad day, the rest of the week as well.

Mom was not cross with me for anything like as long as I deserved. She simply does not care for an abrupt interruption, and having thought about it properly I have come round to precisely the same opinion.

Not as long as the narrator deserved.

g4.title: The Duct Under the House

paras: My grade went up this term by one step, and it was a gradual thing built out of about forty evenings rather than any sort of jump.

g4.title: Progress Is Gradual
paras: My grade went up by one full step this term, and it was an entirely gradual thing, built out of something like forty separate evenings at the kitchen table rather than any kind of sudden jump.

Mom will not rush my progress and she never has at any point. She has watched a number of other parents rush their own children through things and she has formed a settled and unmoving opinion about the results.

She says that progress is gradual or else it is not actually progress at all, and that what people usually call a sudden leap is simply a good week that happened to land on exactly the right day of the term.

My brother will graduate in June after two solid years in which there was very little visible progress of any kind to point at, which rather neatly proves her entire point for her without her having to say a word.

A grade is only a mark written on a sheet of paper at the end of a term by somebody who was not there for any of it. The gradual progress underneath that mark is the part that actually counts for anything.
qs: Where did the forty evenings happen?
At the kitchen table.
What is a so-called sudden leap?
A good week that landed on the right day of the term.

Somebody who was not there for any of it.

g3.title: The Current in the River
paras: The current in that river is strong all year round and it is strongest in the narrow stretch below the bridge where it looks slowest.

g4.title: The Current in the River
paras: The current in that river runs strong the whole year round, and it is at its very strongest in the narrow stretch just below the bridge, which is precisely the stretch where the surface looks slowest and safest.

It will occur to almost every person who stands on that bank on a hot day that going in would be a reasonable idea. Nobody who actually grew up in this village has ever done it, and there are good reasons for that.

Mom keeps the written record of every incident there in cursive in a hard-backed notebook, and while her cursive is genuinely difficult to read, her account of what happened on each occasion is accurate to the minute.

A slip can occur in the space of a second if the current shifts at the bend, which it reliably does whenever there has been any real rain anywhere upstream within the previous two days, whatever the weather is doing here.
We keep the boat secure on a chain at both ends now rather than one. That single change is the only reason the same thing has stopped recurring every spring the way it used to.
qs: Why is the look of the water misleading?
The slowest-looking stretch has the strongest current.
How accurate is the notebook?
Accurate to the minute.
What change ended the yearly trouble?
Chaining the boat at both ends rather than one.

g4.title: Gran's Visit in May
paras: Gran will visit us in May, exactly as she has done every single May for the last eleven years without once missing one, arriving on the Thursday afternoon and going home again on the Sunday after lunch.

She will not take a video of any part of that visit and will ask anybody else holding a device to put it away. She says a visit is not a thing for recording, and that you are supposed to be inside it rather than filming it.

My vision of a genuinely good day is any one day out of that visit. It is visible to me now from a month away, and that visibility is honestly most of the pleasure of the thing.

A full week beforehand.

Being able to see the visit coming from a month away.

g4.title: The Audience at the Back
paras: The play on Friday evening had a big audience, considerably bigger than that hall has managed to hold in several years, and something close to a third of all of them were left standing along the back wall.

The audio was poor from the opening line onwards. Half of everything said on that stage was simply not audible past about the eighth row, and nobody at any point during the evening did anything whatsoever about it.
I was sitting in the audience with Gran, three rows from the very back, and she told me twice during the first act alone that she could not hear a single word of what was being said down there.

We did applaud properly at the end, and the applause went on for a genuinely long time, because the acting itself was good all evening even during the long stretches when it was effectively inaudible.

An audience that cannot hear will applaud once out of plain politeness and will then quietly not come back the following year. That is the thing the people who run that hall need to understand before next season.

Standing along the back wall.

Nothing, at any point during the evening.

Quietly not come back.

g3.title: Two Versions of the Shed
paras: We are going to convert the shed at the side of the house into a den, and the work starts the Saturday after next.

g4.title: Two Versions of the Shed
paras: We are going to convert the shed at the side of the house into a den, and the work on it is due to start on the Saturday after next if the weather does anything like what it is supposed to.

Dad has a version of the plan drawn out on the back of an electricity bill in pencil. Mom has a version of her own, drawn properly on squared paper, to scale, with measurements written along every edge.

The two versions are very nearly the exact reverse of one another: his door goes precisely where her window goes, and his workbench stands precisely where her set of shelves is meant to be fixed to the wall.

Both versions do agree on one single point, which is that the back wall has to be genuinely vertical or the whole conversion will come down in the first serious gale of the winter and take the fence with it.

In the end we will convert that shed using pieces taken from both versions, and within a year of it being finished nobody in this house will be able to tell you whose version actually won the argument.

Measurements written along every edge.

The fence.

Whose version won the argument.

g4.title: The Transplant by the Wall

The pot it arrived in is transparent all the way round, which is precisely how we know that the roots have gone right round the bottom of it in a circle and will need teasing out by hand before planting.

My interest is in the play itself. My interest has never once been in the interval, and I would happily give the whole twenty minutes back.

Twenty minutes.

That is where the whole thing finally turns.

The internal doors stick in damp weather.

g4.title: The Interval in the Play
paras: There is an interval in the play at half past one in the afternoon, and it runs for a full twenty minutes regardless of whether a single person in that building actually wants twenty minutes of it.

I take a genuine interest in the half of the play that comes after the interval, for the straightforward reason that the second half is where the entire thing finally turns on itself and starts to make sense.

You are not supposed to interrupt anybody during the interval, because the interval is the one stretch in the whole afternoon when the rest of them actually talk properly to one another about anything at all.

The internal doors of that hall stick badly in damp weather and always have done, which means that the interval reliably begins with a long queue in the corridor and nobody responsible has ever got round to fixing them.

My interest is entirely in the play itself. My interest has never once been in the interval, and I would hand all twenty minutes of it straight back if anybody in that building ever thought to offer me the choice.

g3.title: The Picture on Gran's Wall
paras: Gran has a picture of the farm on her wall by the stairs, taken in nineteen sixty something, and nobody has ever moved it.
It is a picture of nature rather than a picture of people. There is not one person anywhere in it, which I think was deliberate.
In the future I am going to take a picture from exactly the same spot, at the same hour, and hang the two of them side by side.

A picture can capture a place at one moment. Nature will keep changing that place every year, and the picture will stay exactly as it is.

In nineteen sixty something.

That there is not one person in the picture.

The mixture of grass and mud, unchanged in sixty years.

g4.title: The Picture on Gran's Wall
paras: Gran has a picture of the farm hanging on the wall by the stairs, taken in nineteen sixty something by a person whose name nobody now remembers, and in all that time nobody has ever moved it even slightly.

It is a picture of nature rather than a picture of any people. There is not one single human figure anywhere in the frame, and I have always thought that must have been entirely deliberate on somebody's part.

In the future I am going to take a picture from precisely the same spot, at the same hour of the same month, and then hang the two of them side by side on that wall and let people work out which is which.

The mixture of long grass and churned mud in the foreground of it has not changed in sixty years of weather, and that unremarkable detail is the thing that makes the entire picture work as well as it does.

A picture can capture a place at one single moment and hold it there. Nature will carry on changing that place every season for as long as it exists, and the picture on the wall will not alter by one degree.
qs: What is forgotten about the picture?

It is unremarkable, yet unchanged in sixty years.

g4.title: The Famous Man in the Shop

g4.title: The Music at the Fair

g3.title: The Calendar on the Door
paras: Gran has a calendar hanging on the back of the kitchen door and has had one there, in the same spot, for as long as anybody can remember.
She is absolutely regular about it. Every Sunday evening she sits down and marks the coming week on it in pen, never pencil.

qs: When does she fill it in?
Every Sunday evening.
What is the fifth kind of mark?
The one day she will not be in the house.
What is her record?
She has never missed an appointment in thirty years.

write.task: Explain how to keep track of what is coming up. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Calendar on the Door
paras: Gran has a calendar hanging on the back of the kitchen door and she has had one in that identical spot, on the same nail, for longer than any member of this family is able to remember with any confidence.

She is absolutely regular about the thing. Every Sunday evening without exception she sits down at the table and marks up the coming week on it in pen, never in pencil, because pencil invites you to change your mind.

The marks on it are remarkably similar from one month to the next: bins, bread, bank, sugar, and the single day in each month on which she will not be in the house and does not intend to explain where she is.

A calendar on a door has never been popular with Dad, who carries the whole of his year around in his head and has done so since well before I was born, and who has lost one afternoon to it in all that time.

Gran says that a calendar costs about a dollar and that it saves you a great deal more than a dollar over a year. In thirty years of keeping one she has not missed a single appointment, and Dad has missed four.
qs: Why pen and not pencil?
Pencil invites you to change your mind.
What will she not explain?
Where she is on that one day each month.
How do their records compare?
Gran has missed none in thirty years; Dad has missed four.

write.task: Is it better to write things down or keep them in your head? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Blue Statue
paras: The old statue in the park is blue.
It is true that no one knows who made it.
I had one clue: a date cut in the base of the statue.
The value of it is not in cash. It is due to be cleaned in May.
We will not argue about that statue. It is blue and that is true.
qs: What colour is the statue?
The old statue in the park is blue.
What is true about it?
No one knows who made it.
What clue did the narrator have?
A date cut in the base of the statue.

write.task: Write three facts about the statue. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Blue Statue
paras: The old statue at the top of the park has gone blue over the years, and it was certainly not blue when it was put there.
It is true that nobody now living knows who made that statue, and the records that would say so were lost when the town hall burned.
I had exactly one clue to work from: a date cut into the base of the statue, half worn away, which gives a year and nothing else.
The value of the statue is not in money, whatever the council thinks. It is due to be cleaned in May for the first time in twenty years.
We will not argue about that statue in this house. It is blue, it is ours, and that is true enough for anybody.
qs: Why is the maker unknown?
The records were lost when the town hall burned.
What does the clue give?
A year, and nothing else.
When was it last cleaned?
Twenty years ago.

write.task: Should the statue be cleaned? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Blue Statue
paras: The old statue standing at the top of the park has gone a deep blue over the years with the weather, and it was quite certainly not blue on the day that somebody first put it up there.

It is true that nobody now living in this town knows who actually made that statue, and the records that would have said so were all lost in the fire that took the old town hall in the nineteen thirties.
I had exactly one clue to work from in the whole business: a date cut into the stone base of the statue, half worn away now, which gives a year and gives nothing else whatsoever beside it.

The value of that statue is not in money at all, whatever the council may happen to think about it at any given meeting. It is due to be cleaned in May for the first time in slightly over twenty years.
We will not argue about that statue in this house, and we never have. It is blue, it is ours, it has always been there, and that is true enough for anybody who asks.
qs: When was the town hall lost?
In the fire in the nineteen thirties.
What else does the base give?
Nothing whatsoever beside the year.
What is the family's position?
They do not argue about it; it is blue, theirs, and always there.

write.task: Write the day the statue was first put up. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Weird Ceiling
paras: The ceiling in the hall is weird.
It has a vein of paint across it that no one will claim.
Neither Mom nor Dad will say they did it.
I did receive the blame for it. That is not fair.
Either we paint the ceiling or we live with the weird vein.
qs: What is weird?
The ceiling in the hall is weird.
What is across it?
A vein of paint that no one will claim.
Who received the blame?
I did receive the blame for it.

write.task: Should the ceiling be painted? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Weird Ceiling
paras: The ceiling in our hall is weird and has been weird since the summer we moved in, and visitors notice it before they notice anything else.
There is a vein of grey paint running right across that ceiling from the light to the corner, and not one person in this house will claim it.
Neither Mom nor Dad will say that they did it, and both of them were in the house on the only afternoon it could possibly have happened.
I did receive the blame for it at the time, and I was seven, and I could not have reached that ceiling with a ladder and a brush taped to a pole.
Either we paint the whole ceiling this year or we go on living with the weird vein, and I know perfectly well which one of those will happen.
qs: What do visitors notice first?
The weird ceiling.
Where does the vein run?
From the light to the corner.
Why could the narrator not have done it?
They were seven and could not have reached it.

write.task: Write the afternoon the paint got there. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Weird Ceiling
paras: The ceiling in our hall is weird and it has been weird since the summer that we first moved into this house, and visitors standing in the doorway tend to notice it before they notice a single other thing.

There is a vein of grey paint running the whole way across that ceiling from the light fitting to the far corner above the stairs, and not one person living in this house has ever been willing to claim it.

Neither Mom nor Dad will say that they were the one who did it, and both of them were demonstrably in the house on the only afternoon of that entire summer on which it could possibly have happened at all.
I did receive the blame for it at the time, and I have never fully received an apology since. I was seven years old and could not have reached that ceiling with a ladder and a brush taped to a pole.
Either we paint that whole ceiling properly this year or else we carry on living with the weird vein across it, and I know perfectly well which of those two things is actually going to happen.
qs: Where does the vein end?
The far corner above the stairs.
What was never fully received?
An apology.
What does the narrator predict?
That they will go on living with the vein.

write.task: Does an old family blame ever need putting right? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The New Crew at the Yard
paras: We have a new crew at the boat yard.
I knew a few of them from school.
One threw a rope and the rest drew the boat in.
The cook made a stew. We all had a bowl and did chew in peace.
The crew grew by three this week. The new ones are fine.
qs: What is new at the yard?
We have a new crew at the boat yard.
How many did the narrator know?
I knew a few of them from school.
What did the cook make?
The cook made a stew.

write.task: Tell what the crew did, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The New Crew at the Yard
paras: We have a new crew down at the boat yard this spring, taken on all at once, which has not happened there in about a decade.
I knew a few of them already from school, two of them well, and it is strange to see people you sat next to doing proper work.
On Tuesday one of them threw a rope the length of the slip and the rest of the crew drew the boat in hand over hand without a word.
The cook made a stew for them at twelve and the whole crew sat on the wall and ate it, and for twenty minutes nobody said anything at all.
The crew grew by three again this week. The new ones are good, and the yard has not looked like this since before I started going down there.
qs: How unusual is the hiring?
It has not happened all at once in about a decade.
How was the boat drawn in?
Hand over hand, without a word.
What happened during the stew?
Nobody said anything for twenty minutes.

write.task: Explain how a team learns to work together. Group your ideas and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The New Crew at the Yard
paras: We have a new crew down at the boat yard this spring, taken on all together in the same fortnight, which according to my father has not happened down there in something like a decade.
I knew a few of them already from school and two of them reasonably well, and it is a strange thing to watch people you used to sit beside in a classroom doing proper paid work with their hands.

On Tuesday morning one of them threw a rope the entire length of the slip without looking, and the rest of the crew drew the boat in hand over hand on it without one of them saying a single word to any other.

The cook made a stew for the lot of them at twelve and the whole crew sat along the harbour wall and ate it, and for a solid twenty minutes not one person on that wall said anything at all to anybody.
The crew grew by another three this week. The new ones are good at it already, and that yard has not looked the way it looks now since well before I first started going down there as a child.
qs: What is strange to watch?
People from the classroom doing proper paid work with their hands.
What did the rope throw not need?
Looking, or any word between them.
How far back does the comparison go?
Before the narrator first went down there as a child.

write.task: Write a morning at the boat yard. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: Eight of Us and the Weight
paras: The box did weigh a lot. Eight of us could not lift it.
Our neighbour came to help. He is eighty.
He said to weigh it first, then lift.
The weight was all on one side. That was the whole thing.
With eight of us and one neighbour it went up at the eighth try.
qs: How many could not lift it?
Eight of us could not lift it.
Who came to help?
Our neighbour came to help.
Where was the weight?
The weight was all on one side.

write.task: Tell how the box got lifted, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Eight of Us and the Weight
paras: The box did weigh a great deal more than it looked like it should, and eight of us standing round it could not get it off the ground.
Our neighbour came over the fence to help without being asked. He is eighty and he did not touch the box at any point.
He said to weigh it up properly before trying again, and to work out where the weight actually was before anybody lifted anything.
The weight was all on one side, under the lid, where nobody had looked. That one fact was the whole of the problem.
With eight of us lifting and one neighbour telling us where to stand, the box went up at the eighth attempt and straight onto the trailer.
qs: What did the neighbour not do?
He did not touch the box at any point.
Where was the weight hidden?
On one side under the lid, where nobody had looked.
How many attempts did it take?
Eight.

write.task: Is advice as useful as help? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: Eight of Us and the Weight
paras: The box did weigh a very great deal more than anything of that size had any business weighing, and eight of us standing round it on the grass could not get it off the ground by so much as an inch.

Our neighbour came over the fence to help without anybody asking him to and without saying very much at all. He is eighty years old and he did not put a hand on that box at any point in the entire afternoon.

He said that we should weigh the thing up properly before trying again, and work out exactly where the weight inside it actually sat, before any one of us attempted to lift any part of it a second time.

The weight was all on one side, underneath the lid, in a compartment that not a single person present had thought to open and look inside. That one fact turned out to be the whole of the problem we had.
With eight of us lifting and one eighty-year-old neighbour standing back telling each of us precisely where to put our feet, the box went up at the eighth attempt and straight onto the trailer.
qs: What had nobody thought to do?
Open the compartment under the lid and look inside.
What was the neighbour's actual contribution?
Telling each person precisely where to put their feet.
How much had eight people managed before?
Not so much as an inch.

write.task: Write a report on lifting heavy things safely. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Fruit Stand Dad Built
paras: Dad built a fruit stand at the gate.
He built it from wood that was not suitable, but it still stands.
We sell fruit and juice from it all summer.
I got a bruise when I built the top shelf. That was my own fault.
A fruit stand you built is worth more than one you buy.
qs: What did Dad build?
Dad built a fruit stand at the gate.
What do they sell from it?
We sell fruit and juice from it.
How did the narrator get a bruise?
When I built the top shelf.

write.task: Is it better to build something or buy it? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Fruit Stand Dad Built
paras: Dad built a fruit stand at the gate the first summer we lived here, over two evenings, from whatever was stacked behind the shed.
He built it out of wood that was not remotely suitable for standing outdoors, and six years later it has not moved or rotted through.
We sell fruit and juice from that stand every summer, on an honesty box, and in six years the box has been short exactly twice.
I got a bruise across one hand when I built the top shelf onto it last year, which was entirely my own fault and my own hammer.
A fruit stand you built yourself is worth more to you than any stand you could buy, and it is worth about the same to everybody who stops at it.
qs: How long did it take to build?
Two evenings.
How often has the honesty box been short?
Exactly twice in six years.
Whose fault was the bruise?
Entirely the narrator's own, with their own hammer.

write.task: Write the two evenings the stand was built. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Fruit Stand Dad Built
paras: Dad built the fruit stand that sits at our gate during the first summer we lived in this house, over the course of two evenings, using nothing except what was already stacked up behind the shed waiting to be burned.

He built it out of wood that was not remotely suitable for standing outdoors in this climate, and six full years later it has not moved, has not rotted through anywhere, and has not needed a single repair.

We sell fruit and juice from that stand every summer on an honesty box nailed to the side, and in six years of doing it the box has come up short on exactly two occasions, both of them in the same week.

I got a bruise right across the back of one hand while I was building the top shelf onto it last year, which was entirely my own fault, with my own hammer, in front of two people who had stopped to buy plums.

A fruit stand that you built yourself is worth a great deal more to you than any stand you could possibly buy ready-made, and it appears to be worth about the same to every single person who stops at it.
qs: What was the wood waiting for?
To be burned.
When were the two shortfalls?
Both in the same week.
Who witnessed the bruise?
Two people who had stopped to buy plums.

write.task: Write a report on running an honesty stall. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: It Is Impossible to Improve the Car
paras: It is impossible to improve a thing you will not look at.
Dad said that about the car. The impact of the words was big.
The car is imperfect. It has been imperfect for years.
He is impatient with it, but he will not sell it.
To improve that car is impossible. To improve his mood is not.
qs: What is impossible?
It is impossible to improve a thing you will not look at.
What is the car like?
The car is imperfect and has been for years.
What is Dad like with it?
He is impatient with it, but he will not sell it.

write.task: Should Dad sell the car? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: It Is Impossible to Improve the Car
paras: It is impossible to improve anything you are not willing to look at properly, which is a thing Dad says about other people's work all the time.
He said it about his own car in March, out loud, in front of me, and the impact of hearing him say it about himself was considerable.
The car is imperfect and has been imperfect for at least six years. The passenger door has not opened from the outside since before I could drive.
He is impatient with that car every single week and he will not sell it, and those two facts have lived side by side for a long time.
To improve that car now is probably impossible. To improve his mood about it turns out to be entirely possible, and it costs nothing.
qs: Who does Dad usually say it about?
Other people's work.
What is wrong with the door?
The passenger door has not opened from the outside for years.
What turns out to be possible?
Improving his mood about the car, and it costs nothing.

write.task: Write the March day he said it. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: It Is Impossible to Improve the Car
paras: It is impossible to improve anything at all that you are not genuinely willing to look at properly first, and that is a thing Dad has said about other people's work for as long as I have been able to understand it.

He said it about his own car back in March, out loud, standing in the drive in front of me, and the impact of hearing him turn that particular line round onto himself was a good deal larger than he intended.

The car is imperfect and has been plainly imperfect for at least the last six years. The passenger door has not opened from the outside since a point before I was old enough to be interested in cars at all.

He is impatient with that car on a weekly basis and he has never once seriously considered selling it, and those two facts have lived comfortably alongside one another in this family for a very long time.
To improve that car at this stage is almost certainly impossible without more money than it is worth. To improve his mood about it turns out to be entirely possible, and it costs nothing whatsoever.
qs: How long has he used that line?
For as long as the narrator could understand it.
What was larger than intended?
The impact of turning the line onto himself.
What would improving the car take?
More money than the car is worth.

write.task: Write a report on deciding whether to repair or replace. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Illegible Note
paras: Gran had an illness in the spring. She is fine now.
Her note to the school was illegible. No one could read it.
It is not illegal to write badly, she said.
That is illogical, said Dad. He was ill at the time as well.
An illness, an illegible note and an ill Dad make for a long week.
qs: What did Gran have in the spring?
Gran had an illness in the spring.
What was wrong with her note?
Her note to the school was illegible.
What did Gran say?
She said it is not illegal to write badly.

write.task: Tell what happened that week, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Illegible Note
paras: Gran had an illness in the spring that kept her in bed for nine days, and she is entirely fine now and does not like it mentioned.
On the fourth day she wrote a note to the school about me, and the note was illegible from the first word to the last.
It is not illegal to write badly, she said when the school rang to ask what the note had meant, and she said it without any apology.
That is illogical, said Dad, because the whole point of a note is that somebody else reads it. He was ill himself by then and losing arguments.
An illness, an illegible note and an ill father between them made for one of the longest weeks this house has had.
qs: How long was Gran in bed?
Nine days.
Why did the school ring?
To ask what the illegible note had meant.
What was Dad's point?
The whole point of a note is that somebody else reads it.

write.task: Does handwriting still matter? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Illegible Note
paras: Gran had an illness in the spring that kept her in bed for nine straight days, and she is entirely fine again now and does not care at all for anybody in this family mentioning it to her.

On the fourth day of that illness she wrote a note to the school about me and sent it in, and the note was completely illegible from the opening word to the final one, including her own name at the bottom.

It is not illegal to write badly, she said when the school rang the house to ask what exactly the note had been intended to mean, and she said it without offering anything resembling an apology to anybody.

That is illogical, said Dad from the next room, on the grounds that the entire purpose of writing a note at all is that some other person is going to read it. He was ill himself by then and was losing most arguments.
An illness, an illegible note, and an ill father all arriving in the same seven days between them made for one of the longest weeks this house has had in years.
qs: What else was illegible?
Her own name at the bottom.
Where was Dad when he objected?
In the next room.
Why was Dad losing arguments?
He was ill himself by then.

write.task: Write the phone call from the school. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Irregular Bus
paras: The bus is irregular on a Sunday.
That does irritate Dad. It does not irritate me.
He says it is irresponsible to run one bus a day.
I say it is irrelevant if you can walk. He stands there with a face like iron.
An irregular bus is a fact. To irritate Dad is a sport.
qs: When is the bus irregular?
The bus is irregular on a Sunday.
Who does it irritate?
That does irritate Dad.
What does Dad say?
He says it is irresponsible to run one bus a day.

write.task: Should there be more buses on a Sunday? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Irregular Bus
paras: The bus out of this village is irregular on a Sunday, which in practice means one in the morning and nothing else until Monday.
That does irritate Dad, every Sunday, in the same way at the same time. It does not irritate me in the slightest and never has.
He says it is irresponsible of the company to run a single bus a day on a route that half the village depends on to get anywhere.
I say it is largely irrelevant if you are able to walk the two miles to the main road. He stands at that stop with a face like iron.
An irregular bus is simply a fact of living here. Managing to irritate Dad about it before nine on a Sunday is closer to a sport.
qs: What does irregular mean here?
One bus in the morning and nothing else until Monday.
Why does Dad call it irresponsible?
Half the village depends on that route.
How far is the main road?
Two miles.

write.task: Explain how people get around without a car. Group your ideas and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Irregular Bus
paras: The bus out of this village is irregular on a Sunday, and what irregular actually means in practice is one bus at twenty past nine in the morning and then absolutely nothing at all until the Monday.

That does irritate Dad every single Sunday, in precisely the same way, at precisely the same point in the morning, and from a seat he has already chosen. It does not irritate me in the slightest and it never has.

He says it is irresponsible of the company to run one single bus a day on a route that a good half of this village genuinely depends on in order to get anywhere else at all, and he is not entirely wrong about that.

I say it is largely irrelevant to anybody who is able to walk the two miles down to the main road and pick up a different service. He stands at that stop every week with a face like iron and says nothing to me.
An irregular bus is simply a fact of living somewhere like this. Managing to irritate Dad about that bus before nine on a Sunday morning is rather closer to a sport than it is to an accident.
qs: What time is the only bus?
Twenty past nine in the morning.
What does the narrator concede?
That Dad is not entirely wrong about the company.
What is the alternative?
Walking two miles to the main road for a different service.

write.task: Should rural bus routes be protected? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: Connect the Pipe to the Tank
paras: We had to connect the pipe to the tank.
Dad said to consider the drop first.
The tank can contain a lot of water, so it must sit level.
We did complete the job by six. I did not complain once.
If you compare the two taps, the one we did connect works best. We sat in comfort after.
qs: What did they have to connect?
We had to connect the pipe to the tank.
What did Dad say to consider?
Dad said to consider the drop first.
When did they complete the job?
We did complete the job by six.

write.task: Tell how they fixed the water, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Connect the Pipe to the Tank
paras: We had to connect the new pipe to the tank on Saturday, because the old pipe had split at the joint and had been dripping since February.
Dad said to consider the drop before touching anything, because water will only run downhill and a pipe that rises anywhere will not work at all.
The tank can contain four hundred litres when it is full, which means it has to sit completely level or it will push itself off the blocks.
We did complete the whole job by six in the evening and I did not complain once, which Dad noticed and mentioned to Mom afterwards.
If you compare the two taps now, the one we connected ourselves runs better than the one that was done by a company. We sat in comfort after that.
qs: Why was the pipe replaced?
The old one had split at the joint and had been dripping since February.
Why consider the drop?
Water will only run downhill, and a pipe that rises will not work.
How do the two taps compare?
The one they connected runs better than the one done by a company.

write.task: Explain how water gets from a tank to a tap. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Connect the Pipe to the Tank
paras: We had to connect the new pipe to the tank on Saturday morning, because the old pipe had split right at the joint some time in February and had been dripping quietly into the gravel ever since without anybody noticing.

Dad said that we should consider the drop carefully before touching anything else at all, on the grounds that water will only ever run downhill and that a pipe which rises at any point along its length will not work at all.

The tank can contain four hundred litres of water when it is completely full, which is why it has to sit perfectly level on its base, or over a few weeks it will shift itself slowly off the blocks underneath it.

We did complete the entire job by six o'clock that evening and I did not complain about any part of it even once, which Dad noticed at the time and then mentioned to Mom in the kitchen afterwards when he thought I was out.

If you compare the two taps in that yard now, the one the two of us connected ourselves runs noticeably better than the one that was put in by a company for money. We sat out there in some comfort afterwards.
qs: Why did nobody notice the split?
It was dripping quietly into the gravel.
What happens if the tank is not level?
Over a few weeks it shifts itself off the blocks.
When did Dad mention the lack of complaining?
To Mom afterwards, when he thought the narrator was out.

write.task: Write the Saturday from Dad's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Initial Plan Was Partial
paras: The initial plan was partial. It had gaps in it.
Mom said the essential part was missing.
An essential thing is one you can not do the job without.
The potential of the plan was good. The initial draft was not.
We made a substantial change. Now it is essential and not partial.
qs: What was the initial plan like?
The initial plan was partial and had gaps.
What did Mom say?
She said the essential part was missing.
What is an essential thing?
One you can not do the job without.

write.task: Write three facts about the plan. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Initial Plan Was Partial
paras: The initial plan we handed in was partial at best, and the gaps in it were the kind that only show up once somebody else reads the thing.
Mom said the essential part had been left out altogether, which was the costing, and that nothing else on the page mattered until that was there.
An essential part of a plan is the part you simply cannot do the job without, and everything else, however good, is decoration around it.
The potential of the plan was genuinely good and she said so first. The initial draft of it was not good and she said that second.
We made one substantial change and handed it in again. It is now essential rather than partial, and it was accepted on the Friday.
qs: When do the gaps show up?
Once somebody else reads the plan.
What was the essential part?
The costing.
In what order did Mom say things?
The potential first, the weakness second.

write.task: Should praise come before criticism? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Initial Plan Was Partial
paras: The initial plan that we handed in was partial at the very best, and the gaps running through it were exactly the kind of gaps that only ever become visible once some other person sits down and reads the thing properly.

Mom said that the essential part of it had been left out of the document altogether, meaning the costing, and that nothing else written anywhere on those pages mattered in the slightest until that section was actually there.

An essential part of any plan is the part that you simply cannot do the job without having settled, and every other section of it, however well written and however interesting, is decoration arranged around that part.

The potential of the plan was genuinely good and she made a point of saying so first, before anything else. The initial draft of it was not good at all, and she said that second and rather more briefly.
We made one substantial change to it over the weekend and handed the whole thing in again on the Monday. It is now essential rather than partial, and it was accepted without comment on the Friday.
qs: What makes those gaps invisible?
They only show when another person reads it properly.
What is decoration?
Every section other than the essential one.
How was the second version received?
Accepted without comment on the Friday.

write.task: Write the weekend the plan was rewritten. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: Cautious on the Ice
paras: Gran is cautious on the ice. She is not cautious on the road.
My brother is ambitious. He wants to run the farm.
The soup she makes is nutritious and it is good as well.
His plan is ambitious, but it is not fictitious. He means it.
I am cautious about his plan. Gran is not cautious about it at all.
qs: Where is Gran cautious?
Gran is cautious on the ice.
What does the brother want?
He is ambitious and wants to run the farm.
What is the soup like?
The soup she makes is nutritious and good as well.

write.task: Is it better to be cautious or ambitious? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: Cautious on the Ice
paras: Gran is extremely cautious on ice and takes the long way round the yard all winter. She is not remotely cautious once she is behind a wheel.
My brother is ambitious in a way nobody in this family expected. He wants to run the farm himself and he has said so since he was nine.
The soup Gran makes on those winter days is nutritious and, which is rarer, actually good, and she will not write the method down for anybody.
His plan for the farm is ambitious but it is not fictitious. He has written it out, costed it, and shown it to two people who know.
I am cautious about that plan because I would be cautious about any plan. Gran is not cautious about it at all, and Gran is usually right.
qs: Where is Gran not cautious?
Behind the wheel.
How long has the brother said it?
Since he was nine.
Why is the plan not fictitious?
He has written it out, costed it and shown it to two people who know.

write.task: Write the day he showed the plan. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: Cautious on the Ice
paras: Gran is extremely cautious on ice and will take the long way round the whole of the yard every day from November to March. She is not in any way cautious the moment she gets behind the wheel of a car.

My brother is ambitious in a way that nobody else in this family expected of him or particularly prepared for. He wants to run this farm himself one day and he has been saying so out loud since he was about nine years old.

The soup Gran makes on those hard winter days is nutritious and, which is a good deal rarer in soup of that kind, genuinely good to eat, and she has never written the method for it down for any person who has asked.

His plan for the farm is ambitious but it is in no sense fictitious. He has written the whole thing out properly, costed every line of it twice, and taken it to two people outside the family who actually know the trade.

I am cautious about that plan, and I would be equally cautious about almost any plan that anybody put in front of me. Gran is not cautious about it in the slightest, and Gran is usually the one who turns out to be right.
qs: Which months does she avoid the ice?
November to March.
How often was each line costed?
Twice.
Why does the narrator's caution mean little?
They would be cautious about almost any plan.

write.task: Write a report on what makes a plan believable. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Electrician Who Plays
paras: The electrician came at nine.
He is also a musician, and a better musician than electrician.
My brother says he is part magician with a wire.
A technician can fix a thing. A musician can lift a room. An optician can not do either.
That electrician is both, so we keep his card on the door.
qs: When did the electrician come?
The electrician came at nine.
What else is he?
He is also a musician.
Why do they keep his card?
Because that electrician is both.

write.task: Write three facts about the electrician. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Electrician Who Plays
paras: The electrician came at nine on Thursday to look at the lights in the back room, and he was gone again by half past ten.
He is also a musician, and by his own cheerful admission a rather better musician than he has ever been an electrician.
My brother says the man is part magician with a length of wire, and having watched him work for an hour I am not going to argue with that.
A technician can fix a thing that is broken. A musician can lift a whole room full of people. An optician, he said, can do neither of those.
That electrician is both of the first two, so we keep his card pinned on the back of the kitchen door where it cannot get lost.
qs: How long was he there?
From nine to half past ten.
What does he admit cheerfully?
That he is a better musician than electrician.
Where is the card kept?
Pinned on the back of the kitchen door.

write.task: Is it good to be skilled at two very different things? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Electrician Who Plays
paras: The electrician came out at nine o'clock on Thursday morning to look at the lights in the back room that had been failing since the spring, and he was finished and gone again by half past ten.

He is also a musician, and by his own entirely cheerful admission he is and always has been a rather better musician than he has ever managed to be an electrician, which is not what you want to hear at the time.

My brother says that the man is part magician with a length of wire in his hands, and having stood and watched him work for the better part of an hour I am not going to stand here and argue with that description.

A technician can fix a thing that is broken and that is a real skill. A musician can lift an entire room full of tired people in about four bars. An optician, he said, while packing up, can do neither of those two things.
That electrician is comfortably both of the first two, which is why we keep his card pinned to the back of the kitchen door where it is not able to get lost among everything else.
qs: How long had the lights been failing?
Since the spring.
What is not what you want to hear?
That he is a better musician than electrician.
How fast can a musician lift a room?
In about four bars.

write.task: Write the hour watching him work. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: A Special Night at the Hall
paras: Friday is a special day at the hall.
It is a social thing. All of the village comes.
There is no official list. You just turn up.
That is the crucial part. No one is left off a list that does not exist.
A special night with no official list is the best kind of social. That is why it is special.
qs: What is Friday at the hall?
Friday is a special day at the hall.
Who comes?
All of the village comes.
What is the crucial part?
No one is left off a list that does not exist.

write.task: Should events have a guest list? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: A Special Night at the Hall
paras: Friday is a special night at the village hall and has been for as long as the hall has stood, which is a hundred and ten years this November.
It is a social thing more than anything else. All of the village comes, or enough of it that the ones who do not come get asked about.
There is no official list of any kind and never has been. You turn up at seven and you are in, and nobody writes your name anywhere.
That is the crucial part of the whole arrangement. Nobody can be left off a list that has never been made, so nobody ever is.
A special night with no official list and no official anything else is the best kind of social evening there is, and other villages ask us how.
qs: How old is the hall?
A hundred and ten years this November.
What happens if you do not come?
You get asked about.
Why can nobody be left out?
There has never been a list to be left off.

write.task: Explain how a village keeps everybody included. Group your ideas and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: A Special Night at the Hall
paras: Friday is a special night at the village hall and it has been a special night for as long as that hall has been standing on the green, which will be a hundred and ten years this November.

It is a social thing far more than it is anything else at all. All of the village comes along, or at any rate enough of the village comes that the handful who do not come get asked about by somebody before the evening ends.

There is no official list of attenders of any kind whatsoever and there never has been one in all that time. You turn up at seven o'clock and you are in, and nobody writes your name down anywhere at any point.

That is the genuinely crucial part of the whole arrangement and the part that visitors never quite believe. Nobody can possibly be left off a list that has never once been made, and so in a hundred and ten years nobody ever has.

A special night with no official list, no official welcome and no official anything else at all is the best kind of social evening there is, and three other villages have now written to ask us how it is done.
qs: What do visitors not quite believe?
That there is no list at all.
What is the result over 110 years?
Nobody has ever been left off.
Who has written to ask?
Three other villages.

write.task: Write one Friday night at the hall. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Delicious Loaf
paras: The bread at the hall is delicious.
Gran is gracious about it, but she is suspicious of the jam.
She says a jam that red is not a precious thing. It is a suspicious thing.
The hall is spacious. There is room for all of us.
A delicious loaf and a suspicious jam is still a good night.
qs: What is delicious?
The bread at the hall is delicious.
What is Gran suspicious of?
She is suspicious of the jam.
What is the hall like?
The hall is spacious.

write.task: Tell what happened at the hall, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Delicious Loaf
paras: The bread they put out at the hall is delicious and it comes from the shop on the corner, which gives it free on a Friday and has for years.
Gran is gracious about the bread in front of the people who carry it in, and she is openly suspicious of the jam in front of exactly the same people.
She says that a jam that red cannot be a precious thing made from fruit. She says it is a suspicious thing made from something else entirely.
The hall itself is spacious enough for all of us with the chairs out, and spacious enough for twice that number once the chairs go back.
A delicious loaf and a jam that Gran finds suspicious still adds up to a good night, and she eats the jam anyway, which she denies.
qs: Where does the bread come from?
The shop on the corner, free on a Friday.
What does Gran think the jam is made from?
Something other than fruit.
What does Gran deny?
That she eats the jam anyway.

write.task: Should you say what you think of food you are given? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Delicious Loaf
paras: The bread they put out on the long table at the hall is delicious, and it comes down from the shop on the corner, which has given it free of charge every single Friday for something in the region of fifteen years.

Gran is entirely gracious about that bread in front of the people who carry it in from the van, and she is equally openly suspicious of the jam in front of those exact same people, which she sees no contradiction in at all.

She says that a jam of that particular red simply cannot be a precious thing made out of fruit by anybody. She says, to anybody within range, that it is a suspicious thing made out of something else entirely.

The hall itself is spacious enough to hold all of us comfortably with every chair out on the floor, and spacious enough for twice that number of people once the chairs have been stacked back against the wall.
A delicious loaf and a jam that Gran has publicly declared suspicious still adds up to a very good night. She eats the jam anyway, every Friday, and denies having done so on the way home.
qs: How long has the shop given bread?
About fifteen years.
What does Gran see no contradiction in?
Praising the bread and doubting the jam to the same people.
When does she deny it?
On the way home.

write.task: Write a report on how a community shares food. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Elephant on Dad's Phone
paras: Dad has a photo of an elephant on his phone.
He took the photo on a trip. The elephant filled the whole photo.
My nephew made a graph of all the trips we have had.
The graph has one tall bar on it. That bar is the elephant trip.
A photo on a phone is fine. A graph on the wall is better.
qs: What is on Dad's phone?
Dad has a photo of an elephant.
Who made the graph?
My nephew made a graph of all the trips.
What is the tall bar?
The tall bar is the elephant trip.

write.task: Write three facts about the graph. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Elephant on Dad's Phone
paras: Dad has one photo of an elephant on his phone and he has never deleted a single thing off that phone since the day he bought it.
He took the photo on a trip eleven years ago, and the elephant fills the whole frame because it walked towards him while he stood still.
My nephew made a graph of every trip this family has taken since then, with a bar for each one and the height set by how often we talk about it.
The graph has exactly one very tall bar on it, far taller than the rest, and that bar is the elephant trip, which nobody disputed.
A photo on a phone is a fine thing to have. A graph on the kitchen wall showing which photo everybody actually remembers is better.
qs: Why does the elephant fill the frame?
It walked towards him while he stood still.
What sets the height of each bar?
How often the family talks about that trip.
What did nobody dispute?
That the elephant trip is the tallest bar.

write.task: Write the moment the photo was taken. Use time-order words and describe what he could see.

g4.title: The Elephant on Dad's Phone
paras: Dad has exactly one photo of an elephant on his phone, and he has never once deleted a single thing from that phone in all the years since the day he first bought it and carried it home.

He took that photo on a trip eleven years ago, and the elephant fills the entire frame of it, not because he moved any closer but because the animal walked steadily towards him while he stood completely still and kept pressing.

My nephew made a graph of every trip this family has taken since that year, with one bar for each separate trip and the height of each bar determined solely by how often we still talk about it at the table.

That graph has exactly one extremely tall bar standing on it, far taller than every other bar on the sheet put together, and that bar is the elephant trip, and not one person in this family disputed the result.
A photo on a phone is a perfectly fine thing to own and to carry about. A graph on the kitchen wall showing you which photo everybody in the house actually remembers is a considerably better thing.
qs: What has he never done to the phone?
Deleted a single thing from it.
Why did he not move closer?
The elephant walked towards him while he stood still.
How tall is the elephant bar?
Taller than every other bar put together.

write.task: Is a photo worth more than a memory? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Chemist on the Main Road
paras: The chemist on the main road has been there for years.
I went in with a stomach ache.
The chemist did not need a scheme or a chart. He just knew.
The shop has an echo in it. It is all tile and glass.
A chemist who knows your stomach is worth more than a school of them.
qs: Where is the chemist?
The chemist on the main road has been there for years.
Why did the narrator go in?
I went in with a stomach ache.
What does the shop have?
The shop has an echo in it.

write.task: Is a small shop better than a big one? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Chemist on the Main Road
paras: The chemist on the main road has been in that same shop for thirty-one years, and his father was in it for twenty-eight before him.
I went in on Monday with a stomach ache that had been going on for three days, which Mom had decided was long enough.
The chemist did not need a scheme or a chart or a machine of any kind. He asked me four questions and then he simply knew.
That shop has an echo in it because it is all tile and glass and nobody has ever put a carpet down or softened a single surface.
A chemist who knows your stomach and knew your mother's is worth more to a village than a whole school of people who do not.
qs: How long has the family been there?
Thirty-one years, and twenty-eight before that.
What did he use instead of a machine?
Four questions.
Why does the shop echo?
It is all tile and glass with nothing soft in it.

write.task: Explain what makes a good local shop. Group your ideas and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Chemist on the Main Road
paras: The chemist on the main road has stood behind the same counter in the same shop for thirty-one years, and his father stood behind that identical counter for twenty-eight years immediately before him.
I went in on Monday afternoon with a stomach ache that had by then been going on for three solid days, which Mom had finally decided was a long enough stretch to be worth somebody else looking at.

The chemist did not need a scheme, a chart, or a machine of any description to work it out. He asked me four questions, listened to the whole of each answer without interrupting once, and then he simply knew.

That shop has a real echo in it, because the whole of it is tile and glass and dark wood, and in fifty-nine years nobody in that family has ever put down a carpet or softened a single surface anywhere in the room.

A chemist who knows your stomach, and knew your mother's stomach before that, is worth a great deal more to a village like this one than an entire school of clever people who happen not to know either.
qs: How long has that counter been in the family?
Fifty-nine years between the two of them.
What did he do while listening?
Listened to the whole of each answer without interrupting.
What has never been added to the shop?
A carpet or any soft surface.

write.task: Write the visit to the chemist. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Rhubarb by the Shed
paras: Gran grows rhubarb by the shed.
She says the rhubarb has a rhythm. It comes up at the same time each year.
I made a rhyme about the rhubarb for school.
The rhyme had no rhythm at all, but it did rhyme.
A rhino would eat that rhubarb in one go. We have no rhino.
qs: What does Gran grow?
Gran grows rhubarb by the shed.
What does she say the rhubarb has?
She says the rhubarb has a rhythm.
What was wrong with the rhyme?
The rhyme had no rhythm at all.

write.task: Write three facts about the rhubarb. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Rhubarb by the Shed
paras: Gran grows rhubarb in the bed beside the shed and has grown it in that same bed since before my mother was born.
She says the rhubarb has a rhythm to it, and she is right: it comes up within the same week of April every single year whatever the winter did.
I wrote a rhyme about that rhubarb for school in March and read it out to her at the kitchen table before I handed it in.
The rhyme had no rhythm in it anywhere, which she pointed out at once, but every line of it did at least rhyme with the line before.
A rhino, she said, would get through that whole bed of rhubarb in about a minute. We have no rhino, and the rhubarb is safe.
qs: How long has the bed been there?
Since before the narrator's mother was born.
When does the rhubarb come up?
Within the same week of April every year.
What did Gran point out at once?
That the rhyme had no rhythm.

write.task: Write reading the rhyme to Gran. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Rhubarb by the Shed
paras: Gran grows rhubarb in the long bed immediately beside the shed, and she has been growing it in that one bed, in that one spot, since a time before my mother was born in the house behind it.

She says that the rhubarb has a rhythm of its own, and on the evidence she is entirely right: it comes up within the same week of April every single year regardless of what the winter before it did or failed to do.
I wrote a rhyme about that rhubarb for school in the middle of March and then read the whole thing out loud to her at the kitchen table one evening before I handed any of it in to be marked.

The rhyme had no rhythm in it at any point from start to finish, a fact which she pointed out to me immediately and without softening it, but every single line of it did at least rhyme properly with the line before.

A rhino, she said while handing the sheet back across the table, would get its way through that entire bed of rhubarb in about a minute. We have no rhino anywhere near this village, and the rhubarb is safe.
qs: Where was Gran's daughter born?
In the house behind the rhubarb bed.
What does the rhubarb ignore?
Whatever the winter before it did.
How did Gran deliver her verdict?
Immediately and without softening it.

write.task: Does a poem need rhythm more than rhyme? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Autumn Hymn
paras: In autumn the hall sings a hymn at the start.
It is a solemn thing. No one talks.
The words are set out in a column on the sheet.
I read the column of words. I did not sing.
An autumn hymn in a cold hall is a solemn way to start.
qs: What does the hall sing in autumn?
In autumn the hall sings a hymn.
What is it like?
It is a solemn thing. No one talks.
How are the words set out?
The words are set out in a column on the sheet.

write.task: Tell what happens at the start, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Autumn Hymn
paras: In autumn the hall sings one hymn at the start of the evening, always the same hymn, and it has been the same one since the hall was built.
It is a solemn thing to stand in. Nobody talks during it, nobody moves, and the people who do not sing stand up all the same.
The words are set out in a single narrow column down the left side of the sheet, in a type that is too small for half the room.
I read the whole column through twice and did not sing a note of it, which Gran noticed and has not yet said anything about.
An autumn hymn sung in a cold hall by people who mostly cannot sing is a solemn way to start an evening, and a good one.
qs: How long has it been the same hymn?
Since the hall was built.
What do the non-singers do?
They stand up all the same.
What is wrong with the sheet?
The type is too small for half the room.

write.task: Should everybody join in, or is standing enough? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Autumn Hymn
paras: In autumn the hall sings exactly one hymn at the start of the evening, always the same hymn in the same key, and as far as anybody has ever been able to establish it has been that same one since the hall was first built.

It is a genuinely solemn thing to stand inside. Nobody talks during it, nobody moves from where they are standing, and the considerable number of people who do not sing a note stand up for the whole of it regardless.

The words are set out in one narrow column running down the left-hand side of the sheet, printed in a type that is plainly too small for a good half of the room to read without holding it at arm's length.
I read the whole of that column through twice over and did not sing a single note of any of it, which Gran noticed at the time and about which she has so far said absolutely nothing to me at all.
An autumn hymn sung in a cold hall by a room full of people who for the most part cannot really sing is a solemn way to start an evening, and in my opinion it is also a very good one.
qs: What stays the same besides the hymn?
The key it is sung in.
How do people read the small type?
By holding the sheet at arm's length.
What has Gran done about it?
Noticed, and said absolutely nothing so far.

write.task: Write the minute of the hymn. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Psalm Book on the Shelf
paras: At the hall they read a psalm as well as a hymn.
The psalm is old. The words are not the words we use now.
Gran keeps the psalm book on the shelf with her maps.
She has two books of psalms and one book of maps.
She says a psalm is a song that lost its tune. I like the psalm. I like the maps more.
qs: What do they read at the hall?
They read a psalm as well as a hymn.
Where does Gran keep the psalm book?
On the shelf with her maps.
What does Gran say a psalm is?
She says a psalm is a song that lost its tune.

write.task: Which would you rather read, a psalm or a map? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Psalm Book on the Shelf
paras: At the hall somebody reads a psalm as well as the hymn, and whoever reads it is chosen on the night and never knows in advance.
The psalm is old enough that the words in it are not the words any of us would use now, and that is most of why it works.
Gran keeps the psalm book at home on the shelf by the window, in between her two books of maps, which is where it has always lived.
She has two books of psalms in total. She has read both of them the whole way through and she has read the maps a great deal more often.
She says a psalm is simply a song that has lost its tune somewhere along the way. I like the psalm well enough. I like the maps more.
qs: How is the reader chosen?
On the night, with no warning in advance.
