Where does the psalm book live?
Between her two books of maps on the shelf by the window.
Which has she read more often?
The maps.

write.task: Explain why old words are kept in some readings. Group your ideas and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Psalm Book on the Shelf
paras: At the hall somebody reads a psalm aloud as well as singing the hymn, and whoever ends up reading it is chosen on the night itself and therefore never has any opportunity to prepare for it in advance.

The psalm is old enough that the words set down in it are not words that any person in that room would ever use in ordinary speech, and that distance is a good part of the reason the whole thing works at all.
Gran keeps her psalm book at home on the shelf by the window, sitting in between her two books of maps, and that is precisely where it has lived for every year that I have been going into that room.

She has two books of psalms on that shelf in total. She has read both of them the whole way through more than once, and she has read the books of maps beside them a very great deal more often than that.
She says that a psalm is simply a song which has lost its tune somewhere along the way and never got it back. I like the psalm well enough when it is read properly. I like the maps a good deal more.
qs: Why does the old language work?
The distance from ordinary speech is a good part of why.
How long has the book been in that spot?
Every year the narrator has been going into that room.
What happened to the psalm's tune?
It was lost along the way and never got back.

write.task: Should old texts be rewritten in modern words? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Microphone That Hums
paras: The hall has one microphone and it hums.
Dad says the hum is in the phone line, not the microphone. He knows phone lines.
Gran has a telephone with a dial on it.
She will not use headphones. She says a symphony needs a room.
A microphone that hums is worse than no microphone at all.
qs: What does the hall have?
The hall has one microphone and it hums.
Where does Dad say the hum is?
Dad says the hum is in the phone line.
What does Gran say about a symphony?
She says a symphony needs a room.

write.task: Should the hall buy a new microphone? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Microphone That Hums
paras: The hall owns exactly one microphone and it has hummed for as long as anybody can remember, at the same pitch, all the way through every event.
Dad says the hum is coming in off the phone line that runs along the same wall and not out of the microphone at all, and he does know phone lines.
Gran still has a telephone with a dial on it and refuses to be talked out of it, and the dial is the reason she never misdials a number.
She will not use headphones for music under any circumstances. She says a symphony needs a room to be in and that headphones take the room away.
A microphone that hums steadily right through a speech is genuinely worse than having no microphone in the hall at all, and we should admit that.
qs: What is odd about the hum?
It is always at the same pitch, right through every event.
Why does Gran never misdial?
Because of the dial on her telephone.
What do headphones take away?
The room a symphony needs to be in.

write.task: Explain how sound reaches a room. Group your ideas and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Microphone That Hums
paras: The hall owns exactly one microphone and that microphone has hummed for as long as anybody now living in this village can remember, at precisely the same pitch, the whole way through every single event held in the building.

Dad says that the hum is coming in off the phone line which runs along the inside of that same wall rather than out of the microphone itself at any point, and he does genuinely know a great deal about phone lines.

Gran still has a telephone with a proper dial on the front of it and has refused for thirty years to be talked out of it, and that dial is the entire reason she has never once misdialled a number in all that time.

She will not use headphones to listen to music under any circumstances whatsoever. She says that a symphony needs a room around it in order to be a symphony, and that a pair of headphones takes the room away from it.
A microphone that hums steadily right the way through a speech is genuinely worse than having no microphone in the hall at all, and the committee should be willing to admit that at the next meeting.
qs: Where exactly does the phone line run?
Along the inside of the same wall.
How long has she refused to change?
Thirty years.
What should the committee admit?
That a humming microphone is worse than none.

write.task: Write an evening ruined by the hum. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Telescope in the Back Room
paras: Gran has a telescope in the back room.
She has a television as well, but she will not watch it.
The telescope is old. It came with a telegram in the box.
The telegram said the telescope was a gift from her dad.
A telescope beats a television on a clear night.
qs: What is in the back room?
Gran has a telescope in the back room.
What came in the box?
It came with a telegram in the box.
What did the telegram say?
It said the telescope was a gift from her dad.

write.task: Tell the story of the telescope, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Telescope in the Back Room
paras: Gran has a telescope standing on a tripod in the back room, pointed at the window, and it has not been moved from that spot in years.
She has a television in the same room as well, under a cloth, and she will not watch it and will not have it taken away either.
The telescope is old enough that it came packed in a wooden box, and folded inside that box there was a telegram.
The telegram is still there. It says, in eleven words, that the telescope is a gift from her father and that she is to use it.
A telescope beats a television on any clear night of the year, and on a cloudy one Gran reads instead and the television stays under its cloth.
qs: Where is the telescope pointed?
At the window.
How long is the telegram?
Eleven words.
What happens on a cloudy night?
Gran reads, and the television stays under its cloth.

write.task: Is a telescope a better gift than a television? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Telescope in the Back Room
paras: Gran has a telescope standing on a wooden tripod in the back room of her house, permanently pointed at the middle pane of the window, and it has not been shifted from that exact position in a great many years.
She has a television sitting in the very same room as well, kept under a cloth, and she will not watch it under any circumstances and will not allow anybody to carry it out of the house either.
The telescope is old enough that it arrived packed in a fitted wooden box with a lid that still shuts properly, and folded flat inside that box, under the lens cap, there was a telegram.
That telegram is still folded in the same place. It says, in eleven words exactly, that the telescope is a gift from her father and that she is to use it rather than keep it.
A telescope beats a television on any clear night of the year without argument. On a cloudy night Gran reads a book instead, and the television stays exactly where it is, under its cloth.
qs: Where precisely is it pointed?
At the middle pane of the window.
What two things does she refuse?
Watching the television and letting anybody remove it.
What did her father instruct?
That she use the telescope rather than keep it.

write.task: Write the night the telescope arrived. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Photograph of the Hall
paras: The photo on the wall is a photograph of the hall.
A photographer came in nineteen fifty to take it.
We made a photocopy of the photograph for school.
The photocopy is grey. The photograph is not grey at all.
A photo can hold a hall that is not there now.
qs: What is the photo of?
The photo on the wall is a photograph of the hall.
Who came in nineteen fifty?
A photographer came to take it.
What is the photocopy like?
The photocopy is grey.

write.task: Write three facts about the photograph. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Photograph of the Hall
paras: The photo hanging on the wall by the door is a photograph of the old hall, taken from the field opposite before the road was widened.
A photographer came out from the town in nineteen fifty to take it, and he took one plate and went home again, which is how it was done then.
We made a photocopy of the photograph for a school project and pinned the copy up in the classroom for a term.
The photocopy is flat and grey and has lost every tone in the sky. The photograph itself is not grey anywhere and never has been.
A photo can hold a building that is not standing any more, and that is the only reason anybody now knows what that hall looked like.
qs: Where was it taken from?
The field opposite, before the road was widened.
How many plates did he take?
One.
What did the photocopy lose?
Every tone in the sky.

write.task: Write the day the photographer came. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Photograph of the Hall
paras: The photo hanging on the wall just inside the door is a photograph of the old hall, taken from the field directly opposite it, some years before the road running past the front was widened to what it is now.

A photographer came out from the town in nineteen fifty specifically to take it. He set up, exposed one single plate, packed everything away again and went home, which is simply how the work was done at that time.
We made a photocopy of that photograph for a school project two years ago and pinned the copy up on the classroom wall, where it stayed for a full term before anybody took it down again.
The photocopy came out flat and grey and had lost every single tone that there had been in the sky behind the roof. The photograph itself is not grey anywhere in it and never has been at any point.
A photo can hold a whole building that is no longer standing anywhere, and that single fact is the only reason that anybody alive now has the faintest idea what that hall actually looked like.
qs: What changed after the photo?
The road past the front was widened.
What did the photographer do after the plate?
Packed everything away and went home.
Why does the photo matter?
It is the only reason anybody knows what the hall looked like.

write.task: Should old buildings be recorded before they go? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: Biology on a Boat
paras: My best class is biology.
We read a biography of a woman who did biology on a boat.
She wrote down what she saw. That is how biology starts.
The bags we use in class are biodegradable.
A biography of a biologist is the best kind of book. I will read a biography a month.
qs: What is the narrator's best class?
My best class is biology.
What did they read?
A biography of a woman who did biology on a boat.
How does biology start?
She wrote down what she saw.

write.task: Is biology the most useful subject? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: Biology on a Boat
paras: My best class at school is biology, and it was not my best class last year or the year before that, so something has changed.
What changed is that we read a biography of a woman who did her biology on a boat for eleven years and published almost nothing until the end.
She wrote down everything she saw, every day, whether it seemed to matter or not, and that is how biology actually starts for anybody.
The sample bags we use in class now are biodegradable, which she would have had no way of getting and would probably have approved of.
A biography of a working biologist is the best kind of book there is, and I have decided to read one biography a month until I run out.
qs: How long was she on the boat?
Eleven years.
What did she write down?
Everything she saw, every day, whether it seemed to matter or not.
What has the narrator decided?
To read a biography a month until they run out.

write.task: Explain how a scientist keeps records. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Biology on a Boat
paras: My best class at school this year is biology, and it was certainly not my best class last year or in the year before that one, which means that something has changed and it is worth saying what.

What changed is that we were given a biography of a woman who carried out her biology on a working boat for eleven consecutive years and published almost nothing at all until the very end of that period.

She wrote down every single thing she saw, every day without exception, whether or not it appeared at the time to matter in the slightest, and that is how biology actually begins for anybody who ends up doing it.

The sample bags we use in class now are biodegradable, which is something she would have had no means of obtaining anywhere and which, on the evidence of her notebooks, she would almost certainly have approved of.
A biography of a working biologist is the best kind of book there is to read at this age, and I have accordingly decided to read one of them every month until I run out of biologists.
qs: What is worth saying?
What changed to make biology the best class.
When did she publish?
Almost nothing until the very end of the eleven years.
What evidence is there about the bags?
Her notebooks suggest she would have approved.

write.task: Write a day on her boat. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: A Paragraph About a Graph
paras: We had to write a paragraph on a graph.
The graph was from a geography book.
It had a line that went up and a line that went down.
My paragraph said the graph was not clear.
The man who drew the graph sent me his autograph. That is a true thing.
qs: What did they have to write?
We had to write a paragraph on a graph.
Where was the graph from?
The graph was from a geography book.
What did the paragraph say?
My paragraph said the graph was not clear.

write.task: Write three facts about the graph. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: A Paragraph About a Graph
paras: We had to write one paragraph about one graph for homework, which sounded easy on the Monday and turned out not to be by the Wednesday.
The graph came out of a geography book that is older than our teacher, and it shows rainfall and crop yield on the same pair of axes.
It has one line going steadily up across the page and one line going steadily down, and nothing anywhere on it explains which is which.
My paragraph said, in the end, that the graph was not clear and that a graph which needs a paragraph to explain it has failed at its job.
The man who drew that graph is still alive. He wrote back to the school about my paragraph and sent me his autograph, which I did not expect.
qs: What does the graph show?
Rainfall and crop yield on the same pair of axes.
What is missing from it?
Anything explaining which line is which.
What did the narrator not expect?
A reply and an autograph from the man who drew it.

write.task: Should a graph explain itself? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: A Paragraph About a Graph
paras: We had to write one single paragraph about one single graph for homework, a task which sounded perfectly easy when it was set on the Monday and had stopped sounding easy to anybody by the Wednesday evening.
The graph itself came out of a geography book that is a good deal older than our teacher is, and it sets out annual rainfall and crop yield together on the same pair of axes without ever saying why.

It has one line running steadily upwards across the whole page and a second line running steadily downwards, and there is nothing printed anywhere on or near that graph which explains which of the two lines is which.

My paragraph said, after three attempts at saying something kinder, that the graph was not clear, and that any graph which requires a written paragraph to explain it has already failed at the one job it had.

The man who originally drew that graph is still alive and living two counties away. He wrote back to the school about my paragraph and enclosed his autograph, which is not an outcome I had prepared for in any way.
qs: What does the graph never say?
Why rainfall and crop yield are on the same axes.
How many attempts preceded the verdict?
Three attempts at saying something kinder.
Where does the man live?
Two counties away.

write.task: Write the arrival of the letter. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: Rock, Beast and Ology
paras: Geology is the study of rock.
Zoology is the study of beasts. Both are a kind of ology, and so is ecology.
Gran says ecology is the one that counts now.
I owe her an apology for saying geology was dull.
Geology is not dull. A rock holds more than a book.
qs: What is geology?
Geology is the study of rock.
What is zoology?
Zoology is the study of beasts.
What does the narrator owe Gran?
I owe her an apology for saying geology was dull.

write.task: Write three facts about geology. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: Rock, Beast and Ology
paras: Geology is the study of rock, which sounds narrow until you notice that everything anybody has ever built is standing on some of it.
Zoology is the study of animals, and both of those are a kind of ology, and so is ecology, which ties the first two together.
Gran says ecology is the one that counts now, and that the other two were only ever ways of getting to it without knowing.
I owe her an apology for telling her last year that geology was dull, because I had not at that point read a single page of it.
Geology is not dull in the least. A rock in the right hands holds more information than most books, and it cannot be edited.
qs: Why is geology not narrow?
Everything ever built stands on rock.
What does ecology do?
It ties geology and zoology together.
Why was the earlier verdict unfair?
The narrator had not read a single page of it.

write.task: Which science matters most now? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: Rock, Beast and Ology
paras: Geology is the study of rock, which sounds like an extremely narrow field of interest right up until the moment you notice that every single thing anybody has ever built is standing on some of it.
Zoology is the study of animals, and both geology and zoology are a kind of ology, and so is ecology, which exists mainly in order to tie the first two of them together into one account.
Gran says that ecology is the one that genuinely counts now, and that the other two were only ever ways of getting towards it slowly without quite knowing that was where they were going.
I owe her a proper apology for telling her flatly last year that geology was a dull subject, because at the time I said it I had not read one single page about geology anywhere.
Geology is not dull in the least and I will argue that now. A rock in the right hands holds a great deal more information than most books do, and unlike a book it cannot be quietly edited afterwards.
qs: When does geology stop sounding narrow?
When you notice everything built stands on rock.
What is ecology mainly for?
Tying geology and zoology into one account.
What can a rock not be?
Quietly edited afterwards.

write.task: Write the conversation where you called it dull. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Chef and His Machine
paras: The chef at the hall has one machine he will not share.
It is a machine that cuts bread.
He got the machine from a brochure that came in the post.
The chef says a machine is only as good as the hand on it.
I would like a machine like that. I am not a chef.
qs: What will the chef not share?
The chef has one machine he will not share.
What does the machine do?
It is a machine that cuts bread.
Where did he get it?
From a brochure that came in the post.

write.task: Should the chef share the machine? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Chef and His Machine
paras: The chef at the hall owns one machine that he will not let anybody else touch, and he carries it in and out himself on every single Friday.
It is a machine for cutting bread, and it cuts a loaf into forty even slices in about nine seconds without tearing one of them.
He ordered the machine from a brochure that came through the door in nineteen ninety and he has never once needed a part for it since.
The chef says that a machine is only ever as good as the hand working it, and then he says that the hand is the part nobody wants to buy.
I would very much like a machine like that one. I am not a chef, and by his own argument the machine would not help me a great deal.
qs: How fast does it cut?
Forty even slices in about nine seconds.
When did he order it?
In nineteen ninety.
What does nobody want to buy?
The hand that works the machine.

write.task: Explain what makes a tool worth owning. Group your ideas and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Chef and His Machine
paras: The chef at the hall owns one machine that he will not allow any other person to touch at any point, and he carries that machine in and back out to his van himself on every single Friday of the year.
It is a machine for cutting bread, and it will cut a full loaf into forty even slices in something close to nine seconds flat without tearing a single one of them or leaving crumbs on the board.
He ordered the machine out of a brochure that came through his door in nineteen ninety, and in all the years since then he has never once had to send away for a replacement part of any kind for it.

The chef says that a machine is only ever as good as the hand that is working it, and then, every time, he adds that the hand is the one part of the arrangement that nobody anywhere has ever wanted to buy.
I would very much like to own a machine like that one. I am not a chef, however, and by the terms of his own argument that machine would not do a great deal for me.
qs: What does it not leave?
Crumbs on the board.
What has he never had to do?
Send away for a replacement part.
What does he add every time?
That nobody has ever wanted to buy the hand.

write.task: Write a Friday in the hall kitchen. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Group That Made Soup
paras: A group of us made soup at the hall.
The soup was for the youth club on a Friday.
We took the long route to get the pot there.
A group that makes soup is a group that stays.
The soup was good. The group was better.
qs: What did the group make?
A group of us made soup at the hall.
Who was the soup for?
The soup was for the youth club on a Friday.
Which way did they go?
We took the long route to get the pot there.

write.task: Tell how the soup got to the club, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Group That Made Soup
paras: A group of six of us made soup in the hall kitchen on Thursday evening, which is not something any of us had done before.
The soup was for the youth club on the Friday, and it had to be ready and cold by nine so that it could be carried over in the morning.
We took the long route round the green to get the pot across rather than the short one, because the short one has three steps and no rail.
A group that makes soup together is a group that stays together, somebody said at the time, and on the evidence so far they were right.
The soup was good, and three people asked who had made it. The group that made it was better than the soup, and we all knew that.
qs: How many were in the group?
Six.
Why avoid the short route?
It has three steps and no rail.
How many asked who made it?
Three people.

write.task: Is cooking together better than cooking alone? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Group That Made Soup
paras: A group of six of us made soup in the hall kitchen on the Thursday evening, which is not a thing that any single one of us had ever done before, in that kitchen or anywhere else.

The soup was intended for the youth club on the Friday, and the whole lot of it had to be finished and properly cold by nine o'clock so that it could be carried over the green first thing in the morning.

We took the long route all the way round the edge of the green to get the pot across rather than the short way through, because the short way has three steps in it and no rail of any kind beside them.
A group that makes soup together is a group that stays together, somebody said while we were washing up, and on all the evidence available since that evening they turned out to be exactly right.
The soup itself was good and three separate people asked who in the group had made it. The group that made it was a good deal better than the soup was, and every one of us knew that at the time.
qs: What had none of them done before?
Made soup, in that kitchen or anywhere else.
When was it said?
While they were washing up.
What did everyone know at the time?
That the group was better than the soup.

write.task: Write a report on cooking for a crowd. Organise it into sections and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Local Hall and Its Metal Roof
paras: The local hall has a metal roof.
In the final week of the year we count the total.
It is not the usual kind of count. We count every animal that came in.
Last year the total was several dogs and one goat.
That is normal for a local hall with a metal roof.
qs: What does the local hall have?
The local hall has a metal roof.
What do they count?
We count every animal that came in.
What was the total last year?
Several dogs and one goat.

write.task: Write three facts about the hall. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Local Hall and Its Metal Roof
paras: The local hall has a metal roof that was put on in the eighties, and in heavy rain nobody inside it can hear a word anybody says.
In the final week of every year the committee sits down and counts the total, and it is not the usual sort of total that a committee counts.
They count every animal that came into the building over the twelve months, because somebody started doing it in nineteen seventy and nobody has stopped.
Last year the total was several dogs, one goat, and a bird that got in through the metal roof and would not go back out the same way.
That is a normal year for a local hall with a metal roof, a field on two sides, and a door that does not shut unless you lift it.
qs: What happens in heavy rain?
Nobody inside can hear a word anybody says.
When did the counting start?
In nineteen seventy.
Why does the door let animals in?
It does not shut unless you lift it.

write.task: Write the day the bird got in. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Local Hall and Its Metal Roof
paras: The local hall has a metal roof that was put on some time in the eighties to replace the original one, and in genuinely heavy rain not one person inside that building can hear a single word that anybody else says.

In the final week of every year the committee sits down at the long table and counts up the total for the year, and it is not at all the usual sort of total that a hall committee anywhere else would be counting.

They count every animal that came into the building over the preceding twelve months, for no better reason than that somebody started keeping the figure in nineteen seventy and nobody since has ever decided to stop.

Last year the total came to several dogs, one goat, and one bird which got in under the edge of the metal roof and then proved entirely unwilling to leave again by the same route it had used coming in.
That is a completely normal year for a local hall with a metal roof, a field along two of its sides, and a front door that will not shut properly unless somebody lifts it while pushing.
qs: What did the metal roof replace?
The original roof.
What is the reason for counting?
Only that somebody started in nineteen seventy and nobody stopped.
How must the door be shut?
Lifted while pushing.

write.task: Are odd traditions worth keeping? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Package with No Name
paras: A package came to the village hall.
There was a message on it but no name.
We put it in storage until we could manage to find out.
The package had no damage on it at all.
In the end the message was for a cottage on the far side of the village.
qs: What came to the hall?
A package came to the village hall.
What was on it?
There was a message on it but no name.
Who was the message for?
A cottage on the far side of the village.

write.task: Tell what happened to the package, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Package with No Name
paras: A package arrived at the village hall on a Tuesday with the morning post, addressed to the hall itself, which nobody could remember happening before.
There was a message written on the outside of it in pen, but there was no name anywhere on the package and no address inside it either.
We put the package into storage in the cupboard by the stage until somebody could manage to work out where it was actually supposed to go.
It sat there for eleven days without any damage to it at all, because the cupboard is dry and because nobody in this village opens other people's post.
In the end the message on it turned out to be meant for a cottage on the far side of the village, and the man who lives there had been waiting.
qs: Why was the delivery unusual?
Nobody could remember a package addressed to the hall itself.
How long did it sit in storage?
Eleven days.
Why was there no damage?
The cupboard is dry and nobody opens other people's post.

write.task: Should the package have been opened? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Package with No Name
paras: A package arrived at the village hall on a Tuesday morning with the ordinary post, addressed to the hall itself rather than to any person in it, which nobody on the committee could remember ever happening before.
There was a message written across the outside of it in pen in a careful hand, but there was no name anywhere on the package at all and nothing written inside it that gave an address either.
We put the package into storage in the cupboard beside the stage until such time as somebody could manage to work out where in the village the thing was actually supposed to have gone.
It sat in there for eleven days without taking any damage whatsoever, partly because that cupboard stays dry all year and partly because nobody in this village has ever opened another person's post.

In the end the message written on it turned out to have been meant for a cottage over on the far side of the village, and the man who lives in that cottage had been quietly waiting for it the whole time.
qs: How was the message written?
Across the outside in pen, in a careful hand.
What two things kept it safe?
The dry cupboard, and nobody opening other people's post.
What had the man been doing?
Quietly waiting for it the whole time.

write.task: Write the eleven days from the waiting man's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Entrance at the Back
paras: The entrance to the hall is at the back.
There is a chance you will not find it. Most do not.
The distance from the gate is short, but the path bends.
At the performance we keep the entrance open for air. A performance in a shut hall is hot.
The importance of that back door is not clear until it rains. Then the chance of a dry seat is low.
qs: Where is the entrance?
The entrance to the hall is at the back.
What is the distance from the gate?
The distance from the gate is short, but the path bends.
Why is the entrance kept open?
At the performance we keep the entrance open for air.

write.task: Should the entrance be moved to the front? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Entrance at the Back
paras: The entrance to the hall is round at the back, which every single person in this village knows and no visitor has ever guessed correctly.
There is a real chance you will not find it on a first visit. Most people do not, and end up standing at the front door reading a notice.
The distance from the gate is only about thirty paces, but the path bends twice behind a hedge and loses you somewhere in the middle of it.
At any performance we keep that entrance propped open for the air, because the hall has no other way of getting any, and a performance in a shut hall gets warm fast.
The importance of that back door is not obvious at all until it rains hard, and then the chance of finding a dry seat anywhere drops to nothing.
qs: Who has never guessed right?
Any visitor.
Why does the path lose people?
It bends twice behind a hedge.
Why is it propped open?
The hall has no other way of getting air.

write.task: Explain how to make a building easy to find. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Entrance at the Back
paras: The entrance to the hall is round at the back of the building, a fact which every single person living in this village knows without being told and which no visitor arriving for the first time has ever once guessed correctly.

There is a very real chance that you will not find it at all on a first visit. Most people do not find it, and end up standing at the front door reading a notice that has been pinned there since before the road was resurfaced.

The distance from the gate to that entrance is only about thirty paces in a straight line, but the path bends twice behind a tall hedge and manages to lose almost everybody somewhere in the middle section of it.

At any performance at all we keep that entrance propped wide open for the air, because the hall has no other means of getting any air into it and the room warms up alarmingly fast once it is full of people.

The importance of that one back door is not in the least obvious until it rains hard during a performance, and at that point the chance of finding yourself a dry seat anywhere in the building drops to nothing.
qs: How old is the notice?
It has been there since before the road was resurfaced.
Where do people get lost?
In the middle section of the bending path.
What happens when it rains during a performance?
The chance of a dry seat drops to nothing.

write.task: Write a visitor's first time finding the hall. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: A Minute of Silence
paras: In the hall there is a minute of silence.
It takes patience to keep a hall in silence.
The difference between a hall and a room is the silence in it.
There is no evidence for that. It is just what I think.
The presence of a hundred people in silence is the best sentence I can write.
qs: What is there in the hall?
In the hall there is a minute of silence.
What does it take?
It takes patience to keep a hall in silence.
What is the difference between a hall and a room?
The difference is the silence in it.

write.task: Write three facts about the minute of silence. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: A Minute of Silence
paras: In the hall every November there is one minute of silence, and it is a real minute, timed on the clock at the back by whoever is nearest to it.
It takes more patience than people expect to keep a hall of that size in silence for sixty seconds, and about half of the work is done by the children.
The difference between a hall and an ordinary room, as far as I can tell, is entirely the silence that a hall can hold without anybody breaking it.
There is no evidence for that statement anywhere and I am not going to pretend otherwise. It is what I think after eleven of those minutes.
The presence of a hundred people standing in silence together is the best sentence I have ever managed to write, and I did not write it.
qs: How is the minute timed?
On the clock at the back, by whoever is nearest.
Who does half the work?
The children.
How many of those minutes has the narrator stood in?
Eleven.

write.task: Does a minute of silence do anything? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: A Minute of Silence
paras: In the hall every November there is one minute of silence, and it is a genuine minute rather than an approximate one, timed on the clock at the back of the room by whoever happens to be standing nearest to it that year.

It takes a great deal more patience than most people would expect to hold a hall of that size in complete silence for sixty full seconds, and something close to half of that work is done quietly by the children.

The difference between a hall and an ordinary room, as far as I have ever been able to tell, lies entirely in the amount of silence that a hall is able to hold in it without any single person breaking the thing.

There is no evidence for that statement available anywhere and I am not going to stand here and pretend that there is. It is simply what I think, having now stood through eleven of those minutes in that room.
The presence of a hundred people standing together in complete silence is the best sentence I have ever managed to write down, and the awkward part of it is that I did not write that sentence at all.
qs: What kind of minute is it?
A genuine minute, not an approximate one.
Where does the difference lie?
In how much silence a hall can hold unbroken.
What is the awkward part?
The narrator did not write the sentence.

write.task: Write the sixty seconds. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Daughter Who Was Taught
paras: Gran taught her daughter to fish.
Her daughter caught more fish than she did.
She taught me as well. I have caught one fish in my life.
She says I was naughty with the rod and that is why.
A daughter who is taught well will out-fish the one who taught her.
qs: Who did Gran teach?
Gran taught her daughter to fish.
Who caught more?
Her daughter caught more fish than she did.

She says I was naughty with the rod.

g4.title: The Boat Dad Bought
paras: Dad bought a boat in April that he thought at the time was perfectly sound, from a man over in the next village who had himself owned the thing for a total of about four weeks before selling it on.

He brought it home on a borrowed trailer with the lights taped onto the back of it, and when it arrived it took two of us and a neighbour from up the road the better part of an hour to get it off the trailer again.

He fought with that boat for the whole of the summer, every single weekend without missing one, and by the middle of August he had replaced rather more of the boat than the man in the next village had actually sold him.

He ought to have got down underneath it and looked at the hull properly before any money at all changed hands. He knows that perfectly well, he has known it since May, and nobody in this family has ever said it to him.

He thought that what he was buying in April was a boat. What he had in fact bought himself was a job, and it is comfortably the job he has enjoyed most in the last ten years. He ought to be pleased, and he is.
qs: How long did unloading take?
The better part of an hour, with three people.
Since when has he known?
Since May.
How does the narrator judge the purchase?
As the job he has enjoyed most in ten years.
